verdict.shared_subject: Wederzijdse bijstand tussen toezichthoudende autoriteiten
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Artikel 61 AVG laat de ontvangende autoriteit een bijstandsverzoek afwijzen wanneer het verzoek inbreuk maakt op toepasselijk Unierecht of nationaal recht. Artikel 37 NIS2 zegt daarentegen dat een verzoek niet mag worden geweigerd, behalve op de daar opgesomde gronden; bij een verzoek dat onder beide bepalingen valt, lijken de toegestane weigeringsgronden dus niet volledig gelijk te lopen.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: De bepalingen kunnen naast elkaar worden toegepast doordat artikel 61 AVG alleen ziet op verzoeken aan een AVG-toezichthoudende autoriteit en artikel 37 NIS2 op bevoegde autoriteiten in de NIS2-samenwerking. Bovendien kan een strijd met toepasselijk recht onder artikel 61 AVG mogelijk samenvallen met de NIS2-grond dat uitvoering strijdig zou zijn met wezenlijke nationale veiligheids-, openbare veiligheids- of defensiebelangen, zodat de teksten niet noodzakelijk een concrete onverenigbaarheid opleveren.
verdict.concrete_scenario: Een AVG-toezichthoudende autoriteit ontvangt in het kader van een grensoverschrijdende NIS2-handhavingsactie een gemotiveerd verzoek om een inspectie of gerichte beveiligingsaudit uit te voeren. De autoriteit meent dat uitvoering van het verzoek inbreuk zou maken op toepasselijk nationaal recht, zodat artikel 61 AVG afwijzing toestaat, terwijl artikel 37 NIS2 weigering alleen op de daar genoemde gronden toestaat en die specifieke wettelijke-inbreukgrond niet noemt.

Nothing in either provision forbids performing the other role or requires conflicting conduct.

verdict.shared_subject: Processing activities and real-world testing of high-risk AI systems
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A concerns an exemption from maintaining a GDPR processing-activities register, while provision B requires reporting serious incidents and taking immediate risk-mitigation, suspension, or termination measures during real-world testing. One might argue that a small provider exempt from the register could lack documented processing information relevant to incident oversight, but B does not require that register or make its duties conditional on it.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different duties with different triggers: A concerns whether certain small organisations must maintain a processing-activities register, whereas B governs serious incidents during real-world testing of high-risk AI systems. A provider can comply with B's reporting, mitigation, suspension, and recall-procedure duties regardless of whether A's register exemption applies.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A can require an essential or important entity to use only products or services not supplied by a named risky party, while provision B requires a distributor to withhold a high-risk AI system from the market until it complies with Section 2. verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose distinct, simultaneously satisfiable duties triggered by different facts and addressed to different roles: A concerns national-security supplier restrictions imposed on essential or important entities, whereas B concerns a distributor's conformity check and market-placement duty for high-risk AI systems. A distributor can refrain from marketing a non-compliant system and an entity can use only permitted suppliers without contradiction.

verdict.shared_subject: Notification to a data subject after a personal-data breach by an electronic-communications provider/controller
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires the provider to notify the affected person immediately when the breach is likely to have adverse consequences for privacy. Provision B says notification is not required when one of several conditions is met, including appropriate protective measures, remedial measures, or disproportionate effort, so the same breach could appear to require notification under A but permit non-notification under B.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can be read as operating together because A's own contextual paragraph 5 contains a comparable encryption-based exception, while B's exceptions concern circumstances in which notification is unnecessary. A provider could therefore notify whenever A requires it and rely on an applicable exception where the regimes recognize one; the texts do not expressly resolve whether B's broader exceptions displace A's duty.
verdict.concrete_scenario: A public electronic-communications provider suffers a breach that is likely to have adverse consequences for a person's privacy, but the provider has taken appropriate technical and organisational measures that make the affected data unintelligible to unauthorised persons. A requires immediate notification on its face, while B says notification is not required under that condition; the shown provisions do not establish whether B's exception overrides A's duty.

verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different, sequential duties: A determines whether special-category processing is permitted, while B requires notice when lawfully obtained personal data are further processed for another purpose. A lawful exception under A can coexist with B's notice obligation, and B does not authorize processing or override A.

verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different, cumulative duties: A concerns whether a provider must notify individuals after a personal-data breach, subject to an assessment by the Dutch data-protection authority, while B concerns governance and oversight of ICT risk at a financial entity. B does not require notification, prohibit encryption, or establish a conflicting security benchmark, so both can be complied with simultaneously.

verdict.shared_subject: Retention and erasure of traffic and location data by providers of public electronic communications networks or services
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A restricts providers from processing traffic and location data retained under Article 13.2a(2) for other purposes, while Provision B gives a data subject a right to obtain erasure and requires the controller to erase personal data in specified circumstances. If the retained data are personal data and a GDPR erasure ground applies, the provider may need to erase data that A regulates, creating a possible interaction between retention-related processing restrictions and erasure duties.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different duties rather than contradictory commands: A limits the purposes for which specified retained data may be processed, whereas B requires erasure only when one of its listed conditions applies. Erasure can generally be carried out consistently with A, and B itself excludes erasure where processing is necessary to comply with a legal processing obligation or perform a public-interest task; the texts shown do not establish that the Article 13.2a retention rule requires retaining these data in the relevant scenario.

verdict.decisive_exception: Article 17(3)(b)'s exception for processing necessary to comply with a legal processing obligation, together with the content of Article 13.2a(2), is not established by the provisions shown.

verdict.shared_subject: Electronic access services and possible transfers of personal data
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: An erkende ontsluitende dienst must unlock business and organisational means and electronic authorisation statements, which could involve handling personal data. If that service also transfers such data to a third country or international organisation, Article 44 prohibits the transfer unless the GDPR Chapter V conditions are met. Thus, the service obligation could require an operation whose onward transfer is restricted by Article 44.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Article 13 requires enabling access; it does not require transferring personal data to a third country or international organisation. Article 44 merely conditions such transfers on compliance with Chapter V, so the service can perform its access duty while avoiding an unlawful transfer or satisfying the applicable transfer conditions.
verdict.evidence_span_a: Een erkende ontsluitende dienst ontsluit alle erkende bedrijfs- en organisatiemiddelen, alle door erkende machtigingsdiensten afgegeven elektronische verklaringen waaruit blijkt dat een natuurlijke persoon, onderneming of rechtspersoon gemachtigd is namens de onderneming of rechtspersoon, bedoeld in artikel 15, eerste lid, op te treden bij de toegang tot elektronische dienstverlening en alle op grond van artikel 12 aangewezen attributen.
verdict.evidence_span_b: Persoonsgegevens die worden verwerkt of die zijn bestemd om na doorgifte aan een derde land of een internationale organisatie te worden verwerkt, mogen slechts worden doorgegeven indien, onverminderd de overige bepalingen van deze verordening, de verwerkingsverantwoordelijke en de verwerker aan de in dit hoofdstuk neergelegde voorwaarden hebben voldaan; dit geldt ook voor verdere doorgiften van persoonsgegevens vanuit het derde land of een internationale organisatie aan een ander derde land of een andere internationale organisatie.

verdict.shared_subject: Uitsluitend geautomatiseerde individuele besluitvorming die iemand rechtsgevolgen heeft of anderszins in aanmerkelijke mate treft
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Artikel 22 lid 1 formuleert een recht van de betrokkene om niet aan zo’n besluit te worden onderworpen, terwijl artikel 40 een verwerkingsverantwoordelijke toestaat de besluitvorming onder voorwaarden voort te zetten mits passende beschermingsmaatregelen worden getroffen. Op het eerste gezicht kan daardoor onduidelijk lijken of maatregelen de besluitvorming zelf kunnen rechtvaardigen of alleen de gevolgen ervan moeten beperken.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: De bepalingen zijn verenigbaar omdat artikel 40 uitdrukkelijk ziet op een uitzondering op het verbod van artikel 22 en passende maatregelen als voorwaarde stelt. De context bepaalt bovendien dat artikel 22 lid 2(b) een wettelijke uitzondering toestaat wanneer de toepasselijke bepaling zelf passende maatregelen voorschrijft; artikel 40 vult juist die waarborg in, zodat het individuele recht niet wordt genegeerd maar via voorwaarden wordt beschermd.
verdict.evidence_span_a: Bij de geautomatiseerde individuele besluitvorming, bedoeld in het eerste lid, treft de verwerkingsverantwoordelijke passende maatregelen die strekken tot bescherming van de rechten en vrijheden en gerechtvaardigde belangen van de betrokkene.
verdict.evidence_span_b: De betrokkene heeft het recht niet te worden onderworpen aan een uitsluitend op geautomatiseerde verwerking, waaronder profilering, gebaseerd besluit waaraan voor hem rechtsgevolgen zijn verbonden of dat hem anderszins in aanmerkelijke mate treft.

verdict.shared_subject: Information handled by a data protection officer versus information supplied to the European Commission under the AI Act
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern disclosure of information, so a data protection officer could conceivably possess information obtained from a data subject's complaint or request that is relevant to an AI Act evaluation. Article 39 requires secrecy unless the data subject consents, while Article 112 requires the listed authorities and AI Board to provide information to the Commission without delay when requested.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions address different actors and duties: Article 39 binds the data protection officer, whereas Article 112 binds the AI Board, Member States, and national competent authorities. Article 112 therefore does not require a data protection officer to disclose anything, and the authorities can comply using information they are lawfully entitled to provide without breaching the officer's separate confidentiality duty.
verdict.evidence_span_a: De functionaris voor gegevensbescherming, bedoeld in de artikelen 37 tot en met 39 van de verordening, is verplicht tot geheimhouding van hetgeen hem op grond van een klacht of een verzoek van betrokkene is bekend geworden, tenzij de betrokkene in bekendmaking toestemt.
verdict.evidence_span_b: Voor de toepassing van de leden 1 tot en met 7 verstrekken de AI-board, de lidstaten en nationale bevoegde autoriteiten onverwijld informatie aan de Commissie op haar verzoek.

verdict.shared_subject: Access to confidential information or AI-model materials by public authorities
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A excludes confidential data from the Wet open overheid, subject to an environmental-information exception, while Provision B empowers the Commission to request access to a general-purpose AI model, potentially including source code. If the requested model materials are confidential data held by a Dutch public body, the access request could appear to collide with the exclusion in A.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision A concerns the applicability of the Dutch open-government disclosure regime, whereas Provision B concerns the Commission’s competence to request access for evaluations under the AI Act. A Commission request is not necessarily a Woo disclosure, and the texts do not establish that the requested model or source code is confidential data covered by A or that the Dutch body may refuse a binding EU-law request on that basis.
verdict.evidence_span_a: De Wet open overheid is niet van toepassing op vertrouwelijke gegevens als bedoeld in het eerste lid, behalve voor zover die gegevens milieu-informatie inhouden als bedoeld in artikel 19.1a van de Wet milieubeheer.
verdict.evidence_span_b: kan de Commissie verzoeken om toegang tot het betrokken AI-model voor algemene doeleinden via API’s of andere passende technische middelen en instrumenten, waaronder de broncode.

verdict.shared_subject: Regulatory compliance obligations concerning ICT and conformity-assessment bodies
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires detection mechanisms to support incident-response activation, while Provision B requires conformity-assessment bodies to submit an application to a notifying authority. One might argue that both concern organisational compliance processes, but the texts impose different duties with no apparent incompatibility.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions address distinct subject matters and duties: A concerns technical ICT-incident detection and response mechanisms, whereas B concerns where a conformity-assessment body must submit an application. An entity subject to both could satisfy both requirements without either affecting the other.
verdict.evidence_span_a: De in lid 1 bedoelde detectiemechanismen maken meerdere controlelagen mogelijk en bepalen waarschuwingsdrempels en criteria om processen voor respons op ICT-gerelateerde incidenten in werking te stellen, met inbegrip van automatische waarschuwingsmechanismen voor de betrokken personeelsleden die belast zijn met de respons op ICT-gerelateerde incidenten.
verdict.evidence_span_b: Conformiteitsbeoordelingsinstanties dienen een verzoek om aanmelding in bij de aanmeldende autoriteit van de lidstaat waar zij zijn gevestigd.

verdict.shared_subject: Wederzijdse bijstand tussen toezichthoudende autoriteiten
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Artikel 37 verplicht de aangezochte autoriteit in beginsel bijstand te verlenen en zegt dat zij een verzoek niet mag weigeren behalve op limitatief genoemde gronden. Artikel 61 AVG staat weigering toe wanneer het verzoek inbreuk maakt op de AVG of op toepasselijk Unierecht of nationaal recht, zodat een verzoek dat onder artikel 37 valt maar volgens de ontvangende autoriteit zulke regels schendt, tot een botsing kan leiden.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: De bepalingen kunnen worden gelezen als samenwerkende regels: artikel 37 verplicht bijstand binnen de bevoegdheid, proportionaliteit en veiligheidsgrenzen die het zelf noemt, terwijl artikel 61 een AVG-specifieke weigeringsgrond bevat. Artikel 37 kan bovendien worden toegepast zonder afbreuk te doen aan hogere of toepasselijke Unierechtelijke beperkingen, zodat niet vaststaat dat elk artikel-37-verzoek ook onder artikel 61 moet worden geweigerd.
verdict.missing_reference: De ontbrekende beslissende bepaling is de voorrangs- of verenigbaarheidsregel die bepaalt of artikel 37 van Richtlijn (EU) 2022/2555 een verzoek verplicht ondanks artikel 61, onder b, AVG, of juist toestaat dat een AVG-strijdig verzoek wordt geweigerd. Ook is de concrete inhoud van het verzoek nodig om vast te stellen of het daadwerkelijk inbreuk maakt op de AVG of ander toepasselijk recht.
verdict.evidence_span_a: b) het verzoek inbreuk maakt op deze verordening of met Unierecht of lidstatelijk recht dat van toepassing is op de toezichthoudende autoriteit die het verzoek ontvangt.
verdict.evidence_span_b: Een bevoegde autoriteit waaraan een verzoek om bijstand is gericht, mag dat verzoek niet weigeren, tenzij wordt vastgesteld dat zij niet bevoegd is om de gevraagde bijstand te verlenen, dat de gevraagde bijstand niet in verhouding staat tot de toezichthoudende taken van de bevoegde autoriteit, of dat het verzoek betrekking heeft op informatie of activiteiten inhoudt die, indien ze openbaar zouden worden gemaakt of zouden worden uitgevoerd, in strijd zouden zijn met de wezenlijke belangen van zijn nationale veiligheid, de openbare veiligheid of de defensie van die lidstaat.

verdict.shared_subject: Confidentiality of information obtained by authorities under EU digital-law regimes
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A prohibits disclosure of information covered by professional secrecy to any other person or authority unless Union or national law provides otherwise. Provision B requires notifying authorities to ensure confidentiality of information obtained under Article 78; if that information is also covered by professional secrecy, both provisions point toward non-disclosure rather than imposing incompatible conduct.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can be satisfied together: Provision B requires notifying authorities to treat Article 78 information confidentially, while Provision A independently restricts disclosure of information covered by professional secrecy and expressly allows disclosure where Union or national law provides for it. Nothing in Provision B requires disclosure or otherwise conflicts with that prohibition.
verdict.evidence_span_a: Onder het beroepsgeheim vallende informatie, waaronder de uitwisseling van informatie tussen de bevoegde autoriteiten uit hoofde van deze verordening en de overeenkomstig Richtlijn (EU) 2022/2555 aangewezen of ingestelde bevoegde autoriteiten, wordt aan geen enkele andere persoon of autoriteit verstrekt, tenzij op grond van Unierechtelijke of nationaalrechtelijke bepalingen;
verdict.evidence_span_b: Aanmeldende autoriteiten waarborgen dat de door hen verkregen informatie overeenkomstig artikel 78 vertrouwelijk wordt behandeld.

verdict.shared_subject: The timing and scope of compliance obligations for pre-existing AI systems under Article 111.
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions address AI systems already placed on the market or put into service, but they establish different conditions and deadlines for bringing certain systems into compliance. A high-risk system used by a public authority may have to comply by 2 August 2030 under A, while an AI system that is a component of a listed large-scale IT system must comply by 31 December 2030 under B, creating a possible deadline mismatch if both categories apply.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions apply to different, independently defined categories: A concerns high-risk AI systems, especially those intended for public-authority use, while B concerns components of large-scale IT systems established under the listed legal acts. If both apply, the earlier deadline can be followed without violating the later one, and the provisions do not expressly exempt compliance with one from the other.
verdict.evidence_span_a: In ieder geval ondernemen de aanbieders en gebruiksverantwoordelijken van AI-systemen met een hoog risico die bedoeld zijn om door overheidsinstanties te worden gebruikt, de nodige stappen om uiterlijk op 2 augustus 2030 aan de eisen en verplichtingen van deze verordening te voldoen.
verdict.evidence_span_b: AI-systemen die componenten zijn van de bij de in bijlage X vermelde rechtshandelingen opgezette grootschalige IT-systemen die vóór 2 augustus 2027 in de handel zijn gebracht of in gebruik zijn gesteld, uiterlijk op 31 december 2030 in overeenstemming met deze verordening gebracht.

verdict.shared_subject: Processing and international transfer of personal data, potentially including special-category data
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A states that the prohibition on processing special-category personal data does not apply in listed circumstances, while Provision B permits certain transfers of personal data to third countries without adequacy or safeguards when its transfer-specific conditions are met. If a transfer involves special-category data, B's transfer derogation might appear to permit conduct still prohibited under A unless an A exception also applies.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions regulate different legal questions: A concerns whether processing special-category data is prohibited, whereas B concerns safeguards and derogations for transferring personal data to a third country. A transfer under B must still independently comply with the special-category processing prohibition and its exceptions, so B does not purport to override A.
verdict.concrete_scenario: A controller transfers a person's health data to a third-country recipient, relying on the data subject's explicit consent to the proposed transfer under Article 49(1)(a), but the facts shown do not establish that the consent also satisfies Article 22(a)'s requirements for processing the health data for a specified purpose or that another Article 22 exception applies.
verdict.decisive_exception: Whether the Article 49 transfer derogation, particularly explicit consent to the transfer, also supplies or is accompanied by a valid Article 22/Article 9(2) exception to the prohibition on processing special-category data; that legal basis is not established by the provisions shown.

verdict.shared_subject: Protection of information and ICT-related systems
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A extends unspecified requirements concerning storing information on, or accessing information from, an end-user device to cases where that result is achieved by means other than an electronic communications network. Provision B requires financial entities to use ICT technologies and processes meeting detailed security, integrity, confidentiality, availability, and data-management objectives. If the same financial entity uses a non-network mechanism to store or access information on an end-user device, the applicable requirements from A and B could potentially impose overlapping but different operational expectations.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The texts do not establish incompatible duties or different benchmarks for the same duty. Provision A merely extends requirements from its first paragraph to a particular technical circumstance, while provision B sets ICT-security and data-protection requirements for financial entities; both can be complied with simultaneously, and A's underlying requirements are not shown.
verdict.missing_reference: Provision A's first paragraph, including the requirements that article 11.7a extends, is not shown; without it, no concrete conflict or benchmark mismatch can be established.
verdict.evidence_span_a: De in het eerste lid, onder a en b, genoemde vereisten zijn ook van toepassing in het geval op een andere wijze dan door middel van een elektronisch communicatienetwerk wordt bewerkstelligd dat via een elektronisch communicatienetwerk informatie wordt opgeslagen of toegang wordt verleend tot op het randapparaat opgeslagen informatie.

verdict.shared_subject: Notification to individuals of personal-data breaches by an electronic-communications provider/controller
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires the provider to notify the affected person immediately when the breach is likely to have adverse effects on privacy. Provision B says notification is not required when one of several conditions is met, including protective measures, remediation of high risk, or disproportionate effort; thus a breach could appear to trigger A while an exception under B permits non-notification.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can be read as compatible because A's own related context expressly contains an encryption-based exception, and B's exceptions concern cases where notification is unnecessary or replaced by equally effective information. The apparent difference between 'likely adverse effects' and 'high risk' does not by itself establish that the same breach must simultaneously be notified and not notified.
verdict.missing_reference: The operative relationship between BWBR0009950 art. 11.3a and GDPR art. 34, including whether the GDPR exceptions in art. 34(3) or the national provision's exceptions govern a provider subject to both, is not established by the provisions shown. In particular, the text does not show the full provision containing the exceptions referred to by art. 11.3a or the applicable precedence/implementation rule.

verdict.shared_subject: Regulatory oversight and confidentiality/inspection of ICT service providers
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A imposes professional secrecy on supervisory-authority members and staff, including confidentiality concerning reports of infringements. Provision B contemplates officials and other persons carrying out an inspection and communicating consequences of resistance; one might argue that inspection-related information or communications could implicate A's secrecy duty.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different duties on different subjects and address different conduct: A governs secrecy by supervisory-authority personnel, while B governs notice by authorised officials and others when a critical ICT third-party provider resists an inspection. B does not require disclosure of confidential information or otherwise prohibit compliance with A, so both can be satisfied together.

verdict.shared_subject: Incident notification obligations for providers/operators handling personal-data breaches involving high-risk AI safety components
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions can concern the same incident, but they regulate different notification questions: Provision A creates an exception to notifying affected individuals when data are adequately protected, while Provision B requires reporting specified serious incidents to a national authority. For a qualifying AI incident, the operator may therefore need to determine whether the encryption-based exception removes the individual notice while the AI Act still requires authority notification.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose duties on different recipients and have different triggers and purposes. Provision A concerns notification to the person whose personal data are affected and permits omitting that notice under specified security conditions; Provision B concerns reporting serious incidents to a designated national authority, so both duties can be performed simultaneously without contradiction.
verdict.evidence_span_a: De kennisgeving, bedoeld in het tweede lid, is niet vereist indien de aanbieder naar het oordeel van de Autoriteit persoonsgegevens gepaste technische beschermingsmaatregelen heeft genomen waardoor de persoonsgegevens die het betreft, versleuteld of anderszins onbegrijpelijk zijn voor een ieder die geen recht heeft op toegang tot die gegevens.
verdict.evidence_span_b: Voor AI-systemen met een hoog risico die veiligheidscomponenten van apparaten zijn of zelf apparaten zijn die onder de Verordeningen (EU) 2017/745 en (EU) 2017/746 vallen, wordt de melding van ernstige incidenten beperkt tot de in artikel 3, punt 49), c), van de onderhavige verordening bedoelde incidenten, en wordt het incident gemeld bij de nationale bevoegde autoriteit die daartoe is aangewezen door de lidstaten waar dat incident zich heeft voorgedaan.

verdict.shared_subject: Verplichtingen rond een hoog-risico-AI-systeem wanneer een oorspronkelijke aanbieder het systeem niet langer als aanbieder geldt en een gebruiksverantwoordelijke het systeem gebruikt.
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Artikel 25 verplicht de oorspronkelijke aanbieder tot samenwerking, informatieverstrekking en technische toegang voor naleving van onder meer de conformiteitsbeoordeling. Artikel 27 verplicht de gebruiksverantwoordelijke bij eerste gebruik tot een grondrechteneffectbeoordeling en actualisering wanneer relevante elementen wijzigen; zonder voldoende informatie of toegang van de oorspronkelijke aanbieder kan die beoordeling praktisch moeilijk worden uitgevoerd.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: De bepalingen leggen verplichtingen aan verschillende actoren op die elkaar juist kunnen ondersteunen: de oorspronkelijke aanbieder moet informatie en toegang verstrekken, terwijl de gebruiksverantwoordelijke die informatie kan benutten voor zijn eigen beoordeling. Geen van beide bepalingen verbiedt naleving van de andere of stelt onverenigbare inhoudelijke eisen.
verdict.evidence_span_a: Die ursprüngliche aanbieder werkt nauw samen met nieuwe aanbieders, stelt de nodige informatie beschikbaar en verstrekt de redelijkerwijs verwachte technische toegang en andere bijstand die nodig is om te voldoen aan de verplichtingen van deze verordening, met name wat betreft de naleving van de conformiteitsbeoordeling van AI-systemen met een hoog risico.
verdict.evidence_span_b: De gebruiksverantwoordelijke kan in soortgelijke gevallen gebruik maken van eerder uitgevoerde effectbeoordelingen op het gebied van de grondrechten of bestaande effectbeoordelingen die door de aanbieder zijn uitgevoerd.

verdict.shared_subject: A high-risk AI provider that processes personal data and is asked by a competent authority to provide information or documentation concerning the system.
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision B requires the provider to disclose all information and documentation necessary to demonstrate compliance, while provision A restricts transfers of personal data to a third country or international organisation unless the GDPR Chapter V conditions are met. If the requested material contains personal data and must be sent to an authority outside the GDPR transfer framework, complying with B could entail a transfer that A does not permit.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions regulate different immediate matters: B requires cooperation with competent authorities, whereas A permits international transfers when its Chapter V conditions are satisfied. B does not expressly require an international transfer or override GDPR safeguards, so a provider can comply by supplying non-personal information, using a lawful transfer mechanism, or otherwise responding without violating A.
verdict.concrete_scenario: A provider established in the EU operates a high-risk AI system containing identifiable personal data and receives a reasoned request from a competent authority in a third country for all documentation necessary to demonstrate compliance. Sending the requested personal-data-containing documentation to that authority would be required by B but would be prohibited by A unless the GDPR Chapter V transfer conditions are met; the shown texts do not establish that such a condition or exception applies.
verdict.decisive_exception: Whether a GDPR Chapter V transfer mechanism or other applicable exception authorises the particular disclosure to the requesting third-country authority; provision B does not establish that authorisation.
verdict.evidence_span_a: Persoonsgegevens die worden verwerkt of die zijn bestemd om na doorgifte aan een derde land of een internationale organisatie te worden verwerkt, mogen slechts worden doorgegeven indien, onverminderd de overige bepalingen van deze verordening, de verwerkingsverantwoordelijke en de verwerker aan de in dit hoofdstuk neergelegde voorwaarden hebben voldaan;
verdict.evidence_span_b: Op een met redenen omkleed verzoek van een bevoegde autoriteit, verstrekken aanbieders van AI-systemen met een hoog risico die autoriteit alle informatie en documentatie die noodzakelijk is om de overeenstemming van het AI-systeem met een hoog risico met de eisen van afdeling 2 aan te tonen, in een eenvoudig door de instantie te begrijpen en door de betrokken lidstaat gekozen officiële taal van de instellingen van de Unie.

verdict.shared_subject: Disclosure and handling of information by public authorities in connection with electronic services and high-risk AI oversight
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern information supplied to public bodies, so an authority receiving information under Provision A might also fall within Provision B's confidentiality regime. A possible tension is that A requires information to be provided as necessary for recipients' tasks or services, while B requires information obtained under its procedure to be processed under separate confidentiality obligations.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose complementary duties rather than incompatible commands: A governs when the Minister supplies information about breaches to specified recipients, while B governs how information obtained by the authorities described in Article 77(1) must subsequently be processed. Information can be supplied for the necessary task and then handled confidentially; neither provision requires disclosure that the other forbids.
verdict.evidence_span_a: Onze Minister verstrekt gegevens en inlichtingen aan bestuursorganen en aangewezen organisaties, aan de ingevolge artikel 9, tweede of derde lid, toegelaten houder van een erkenning of aan een ingevolge artikel 11 erkende middelenuitgever of dienst over de inbreuk op de veilige en betrouwbare toegang tot elektronische dienstverlening voor zover dit noodzakelijk is voor een goede uitoefening van hun taken of te verlenen diensten in het kader van deze wet.
verdict.evidence_span_b: Informatie of documentatie die op grond van dit artikel door de in lid 1 van dit artikel bedoelde overheidsinstanties of -organen wordt verkregen, wordt verwerkt overeenkomstig de in artikel 78 beschreven vertrouwelijkheidsverplichtingen.

verdict.shared_subject: Governance and enforcement concerning essential or important entities
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A extends the governance rules applicable to an essential or important entity to natural persons serving on its board on behalf of a legal person. Provision B allows authorities, after ineffective enforcement and failure to remedy deficiencies, to request that a natural person with management responsibility be temporarily barred from exercising management functions; this could affect a board member covered by A.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different, sequentially compatible rules: A determines who is subject to governance requirements, while B concerns a temporary enforcement measure triggered by unresolved deficiencies. Nothing in A requires that person to remain in office or forbids a temporary management ban, and B expressly provides procedural safeguards and applies only under specified conditions.
verdict.evidence_span_a: Indien een rechtspersoon het bestuur of een lid van het bestuur van een essentiële entiteit of belangrijke entiteit is, is het bepaalde bij of krachtens het tweede tot en met zesde lid van overeenkomstige toepassing op de natuurlijke persoon of natuurlijke personen die namens die rechtspersoon zitting heeft of hebben in het bestuur van de essentiële entiteit of belangrijke entiteit.

verdict.shared_subject: Telecommunications data disclosure and exemptions
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern the legal framework for handling a request for disclosure and an exemption, but neither text creates an incompatible command. Article 11.11 requires notifying the subscriber when the provider discloses data to a requester, while Article 11.12 merely permits an exemption to be granted subject to limitations or conditions.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can readily operate together: a provider can notify the affected subscriber under Article 11.11 while an exemption under Article 11.12 governs the conditions or limitations attached to the relevant obligation. Article 11.12 does not state that notification is prohibited or that an exemption automatically displaces Article 11.11.

verdict.shared_subject: Essential or important entities that are a vennootschap onder firma, and their significant-incident reporting obligations
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Article 24 extends the governance rules to each partner of a vennootschap onder firma, while Article 25 places the reporting duty on the essential or important entity itself. One might therefore question whether individual partners, rather than the entity, must report significant incidents. However, the texts do not state that Article 24 transfers or negates the entity-level duty in Article 25.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different, compatible obligations: Article 24 makes the governance rules applicable to each partner of a vennootschap onder firma, and Article 25 requires the essential or important entity to report every significant incident. The entity can report while its partners separately comply with the applicable governance rules; neither provision requires or forbids conduct inconsistent with the other.

verdict.evidence_span_b: De essentiële entiteit of belangrijke entiteit meldt overeenkomstig de artikelen 26 tot en met 29 ieder significant incident.

verdict.shared_subject: Incident reporting and follow-up communications involving potentially serious or criminal incidents
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern follow-up after an incident report and require official communications or guidance. In a case involving a high-risk AI system, a single incident could plausibly be both criminal in nature and a serious incident, so the CSIRT and market-surveillance authority would each have separate communication duties, potentially creating overlapping reporting channels.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The duties are directed at different actors and have different triggers and recipients: the CSIRT gives guidance to the reporting entity about reporting to law-enforcement authorities, while the market-surveillance authority notifies specified national authorities after receiving a serious-incident report. Nothing in either text requires or forbids the communication required by the other.
verdict.evidence_span_a: Wanneer wordt vermoed dat het significante incident van criminele aard is, geeft het CSIRT ook richtsnoeren aan de meldende entiteit voor het melden van het significante incident aan de rechtshandhavingsinstanties.
verdict.evidence_span_b: Na ontvangst van een melding met betrekking tot een ernstig incident als bedoeld in artikel 3, punt 49), c), stelt de betrokken markttoezichtautoriteit de in artikel 77, lid 1, bedoelde nationale overheidsinstanties of -organen in kennis.

verdict.shared_subject: The two provisions are identical copies of Article 5 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 concerning prohibited AI practices.
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: There is no honest substantive case for tension: the provisions contain the same prohibitions, exceptions, and wording. Any actor subject to Provision A is subject to exactly the same requirements under Provision B.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions are textually identical, including the prohibition of real-time remote biometric identification except where strictly necessary for specified law-enforcement objectives. Compliance with one therefore necessarily entails compliance with the other.

verdict.shared_subject: Retention and archival processing of personal data
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A removes several GDPR rights and restrictions for personal data in qualifying permanently preserved public-interest archives. Provision B requires covered supervisory personal data to be retained until supervisory tasks are completed and, in any event, for up to 15 years, so an archive holding such data might face a question whether the GDPR provisions displaced by A still constrain B’s retention-related processing.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions regulate different things: A creates exceptions from specified GDPR provisions for narrowly defined public-interest archives, while B sets a retention period for personal data processed by the ESAs or competent authorities for their regulatory tasks. B’s text does not require retention in a qualifying archive, and A does not prohibit or shorten B’s retention period; both can therefore be complied with where the data remain in the supervisory authority’s regulatory records.

verdict.shared_subject: Use and regulation of business and organizational identification means in electronic public services
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Article 11 contemplates rules governing the operation, interoperability, security, and reliability of recognized means and services, while Article 15 permits a Minister to designate a non-recognized means for access to specified electronic services. One might argue that allowing the non-recognized means undermines the security or reliability requirements associated with recognized means.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions address different legal functions: Article 11 concerns the competence to set rules for recognized services and means, whereas Article 15 concerns a time-limited designation allowing another means for a specific target group and service. Article 15 does not prohibit applying conditions or safeguards to the designated means, and Article 11 does not state that only recognized means may ever be used.

verdict.shared_subject: Independent experts and oversight functions in digital/ICT regulation
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern independent experts and oversight-related functions, but they regulate different institutional arrangements. A possible tension would require the same person or appointment to be governed simultaneously by the Dutch control-functionary requirements and the DORA oversight-forum appointment requirements; the texts do not establish that overlap.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision A requires an independent natural-person control functionary for an essential entity to monitor compliance and inform authorities and management. Provision B governs independent experts appointed by the oversight forum, requiring public and transparent selection and expertise in financial stability, digital operational resilience, and ICT security; these duties can coexist because they concern different roles and bodies.

verdict.shared_subject: Use of a public identification means or related facility by public electronic-communication providers
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: The strongest case for tension is that a communications provider might want to use a public identification means or the facility referred to in Article 5(1)(b) in operating or securing its public electronic communications network or service, while Article 8 restricts such use to access to electronic services by administrative bodies and designated organisations. If that use involved communications-related data or systems, Article 11.2a would require confidentiality, but it does not expressly resolve whether the Article 8 use is permitted.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different duties on different subject matters: Article 8 limits the permitted use of a particular public identification means and facility, whereas Article 11.2a requires providers to preserve the confidentiality of communications and related data. A provider can comply with both by using the identification means only for the access purposes allowed by Article 8 and maintaining confidentiality whenever it provides a public electronic communications network or service.

verdict.shared_subject: Information handling by public authorities
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires CSIRTs or competent authorities to provide specified incident, cyber-threat, and near-incident information to authorities competent under Directive (EU) 2022/2557. Provision B requires notifying authorities to ensure information obtained under Article 78 is treated confidentially; if the information transferred under A is information obtained under Article 78, disclosure could appear to conflict with confidentiality.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions address different authorities and duties: A concerns supplying information to authorities competent under Directive (EU) 2022/2557, while B concerns confidentiality by notifying authorities for information obtained under Article 78. The texts do not establish that the information covered by A is Article 78 information or that B prohibits the transfer required by A.
verdict.evidence_span_a: De CSIRT’s of, indien van toepassing, de bevoegde autoriteiten verstrekken de uit hoofde van Richtlijn (EU) 2022/2557 bevoegde autoriteiten informatie over significante incidenten, en cyberdreigingen en bijna-incidenten
verdict.evidence_span_b: Aanmeldende autoriteiten waarborgen dat de door hen verkregen informatie overeenkomstig artikel 78 vertrouwelijk wordt behandeld.

verdict.shared_subject: Small organisations’ GDPR records of processing and ICT-incident detection mechanisms
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A concerns whether the GDPR record-keeping obligation applies to organisations with fewer than 250 employees, while provision B requires detection mechanisms with control layers, thresholds, criteria, and automatic alerts. Nothing in the shown texts makes the detection duty require the GDPR register, prohibit it, or impose a conflicting condition.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: An organisation can comply with both provisions: where A’s exceptions apply, it can maintain the required processing register, while B can operate ICT-incident detection mechanisms with the specified alerting features. The provisions regulate different duties and do not prescribe incompatible conduct.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A imposes a concrete maximum-retention and deletion duty on a CSIRT. Provision B allows further rules to be made concerning its own article, but it does not state a retention period, deletion duty, or permission to retain these data, so no incompatible requirement is shown.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can readily coexist: A governs retention of specified personal data processed by a CSIRT, while B is merely a rule-making competence provision. Nothing in B requires retention or otherwise prevents compliance with A.

verdict.evidence_span_b: Bij of krachtens algemene maatregel van bestuur kunnen nadere regels worden gesteld ten aanzien van het bepaalde in dit artikel.

verdict.shared_subject: Use of a public identification means and ICT continuity registers
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: A possible connection is that an organisation using the public identification means might also be a financial entity subject to DORA, and its continuity or recovery activities could involve access to electronic services. Article 8 restricts the identification means to access to specified public electronic services, while Article 11 requires registers during activated ICT continuity or recovery plans; if those registers required use of the identification means for a non-permitted purpose, the duties could appear to pull in different directions.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions regulate different conduct: Article 8 limits the purposes for which a public identification means and related facility may be used, whereas Article 11 requires financial entities to keep accessible registers of activities before and during disruptions. The register duty does not require use of the public identification means, and the texts do not establish that such use is necessary or that the registers concern access to the covered public services.
verdict.evidence_span_a: Een publiek identificatiemiddel en de voorziening, bedoeld in artikel 5, eerste lid, onderdeel b, worden uitsluitend gebruikt voor de toegang tot elektronische dienstverlening door bestuursorganen en aangewezen organisaties.
verdict.evidence_span_b: Financiële entiteiten houden gemakkelijk toegankelijke registers bij van hun activiteiten vóór en tijdens storingen wanneer hun ICT-bedrijfscontinuïteitsplannen en ICT-respons- en herstelplannen worden geactiveerd.

verdict.shared_subject: An authorised representative’s handling of personal data and compliance documentation when a high-risk AI provider is established in a third country and transfers that data or documentation to the EU.
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Article 44 restricts transfers of personal data to a third country or international organisation unless the GDPR Chapter V conditions are met. Article 22 requires the representative to retain and provide documentation and logs to authorities, which could involve transferring personal data, but Article 22 itself does not state that such transfers satisfy Article 44’s conditions.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different duties rather than contradictory commands: Article 22 requires compliance-related records and information to be made available, while Article 44 permits the transfer if its separate Chapter V conditions are fulfilled. The representative can therefore perform Article 22 through a lawful transfer mechanism, or provide non-personal documentation where applicable.
verdict.concrete_scenario: A representative in the EU for a third-country provider receives automatically generated logs containing identifiable individuals’ data and transfers them to the provider or an authority in another third country to fulfil an Article 22 request, while no GDPR Chapter V transfer condition has been established. Article 22 calls for the information to be provided, whereas Article 44 prohibits the transfer absent the required conditions.
verdict.decisive_exception: The applicable GDPR Chapter V transfer condition or safeguard under Article 44 (for example, an adequacy decision, appropriate safeguards, or a relevant derogation) is not established by the texts shown.
verdict.evidence_span_a: Persoonsgegevens die worden verwerkt of die zijn bestemd om na doorgifte aan een derde land of een internationale organisatie te worden verwerkt, mogen slechts worden doorgegeven indien, onverminderd de overige bepalingen van deze verordening, de verwerkingsverantwoordelijke en de verwerker aan de in dit hoofdstuk neergelegde voorwaarden hebben voldaan

verdict.shared_subject: Disclosure of information and documentation in regulatory contexts
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern information being made available, but they impose duties toward different recipients and serve different functions: Article 15 gives the data subject a right to be informed about safeguards for a third-country transfer, while Article 34 requires notified bodies to provide documentation to a notifying authority. Nothing in either text says that complying with one duty prevents compliance with the other.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions are readily cumulative: a controller can inform the data subject about the Article 46 safeguards and a notified body can separately provide relevant documentation to the notifying authority on request. Their actors, recipients, triggers, and purposes differ, and neither provision limits the other.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: The strongest possible tension case is that a service provider might be both an entity eligible for exemption from obligations under one regime and a service requiring recognition under the other. However, Provision A concerns a ministerial power to exempt certain entities from obligations in Article 21, while Provision B concerns recognition of specified services subject to rules set by general administrative order; neither text makes compliance with one condition incompatible with the other.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions operate on different legal objects and mechanisms: A authorizes an exemption for an essential or important entity carrying out specified activities or serving a government body, whereas B requires ministerial recognition of an ontsluitende dienst or machtigingsdienst meeting separately established rules. An entity could receive an exemption and still seek or hold recognition, because nothing in either text forbids simultaneous application.

verdict.shared_subject: Recognition withdrawal and transitional-law applicability
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern recognised services or parties within an electronic-access framework. One might argue that a recognised service seeking withdrawal must submit a termination plan, while the other excludes certain private-system parties from the transitional regime, potentially affecting whether recognition-related rules apply.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Article 14 governs the voluntary withdrawal of an existing recognition and the accompanying termination plan. Article 24(3) instead states that its transitional provision does not apply to parties conducting only level-1 activities; it neither forbids withdrawal nor excuses or alters the termination-plan requirement.

verdict.shared_subject: Member States’ sanctioning rules and notification duties under the GDPR
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions require Member States to establish or apply sanctions that are effective, proportionate, and dissuasive, and both require notification to the Commission by 25 May 2018. A possible tension is that Article 83 concerns administrative fines, while Article 84 concerns other sanctions, creating a potential boundary question where an infringement might be subject to either category.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions expressly address different sanction categories: Article 83 governs administrative fines, including their judicial imposition where necessary, while Article 84 governs other sanctions, particularly infringements not subject to administrative fines under Article 83. Their common effectiveness, proportionality, dissuasiveness, and notification requirements can be satisfied simultaneously, and the contextual paragraph confirms the same notification deadline for Article 84.

verdict.shared_subject: Administrative fines for overlapping data-protection and AI-law infringements
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A prohibits the competent authority from imposing a second fine for the same conduct after a GDPR fine under Article 58(2)(i). Provision B authorizes the European Data Protection Supervisor to impose administrative fines on EU institutions and bodies, potentially creating an apparent overlap if the same conduct also falls within the AI Regulation.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions address different authorities, addressees, and legal regimes: A concerns a competent authority and duplication of fines under specified Dutch/GDPR enforcement provisions, while B concerns the EDPS fining EU institutions, bodies, and agencies under the AI Regulation. Nothing in the texts establishes that the same authority, person, conduct, or fines are covered by both provisions, so they can operate independently.
verdict.evidence_span_a: legt de bevoegde autoriteit geen bestuurlijke boete op op grond van de artikelen 80 en 87 voor een inbreuk als bedoeld in het tweede lid die voortvloeit uit dezelfde gedraging
verdict.evidence_span_b: De Europese Toezichthouder voor gegevensbescherming kan administratieve geldboeten opleggen aan instellingen, organen en instanties van de Unie die binnen het toepassingsgebied van deze verordening vallen.

verdict.shared_subject: Processing of personal data by a processor or person acting under a controller’s or processor’s authority, including special-category data in a high-risk AI system.
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires a processor or person acting under the controller’s or processor’s authority to process personal data only on the controller’s instructions, unless Union or Member State law requires the processing. Provision B exceptionally permits high-risk AI providers to process special-category personal data for bias detection and correction, so a provider or processor could face uncertainty if the AI Act permission is not itself treated as a Union-law obligation or sufficient instruction under Provision A.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can be satisfied together: the provider can process the special-category data only on the controller’s documented instructions, while complying with all of Provision B’s necessity, security, access-control, deletion, and documentation conditions. Provision B expressly operates alongside Regulation 2016/679, and its permission need not displace Provision A’s instruction requirement.
verdict.concrete_scenario: A provider operating a high-risk AI system uses identifiable health data to detect and correct bias after determining that anonymised or synthetic data cannot work effectively. The provider is acting as a processor under a controller’s authority, but the controller has not instructed or authorised this special-category-data processing; the provider must therefore determine whether Provision B’s exceptional permission and Union-law status allow it to proceed despite Provision A’s instruction-only rule.
verdict.decisive_exception: Whether the exceptional permission in Provision B constitutes a Union-law obligation or otherwise satisfies the instruction/authorisation requirement in Provision A, and whether the GDPR special-category-data exception applicable to the processing is established. The texts shown do not resolve that legal-basis and instruction link.
verdict.evidence_span_a: verwerkt deze uitsluitend in opdracht van de verwerkingsverantwoordelijke, tenzij hij Unierechtelijk of lidstaatrechtelijk tot de verwerking gehouden is.
verdict.evidence_span_b: mogen de aanbieders van dergelijke systemen uitzonderlijk bijzondere categorieën persoonsgegevens verwerken, mits passende waarborgen worden geboden voor de grondrechten en fundamentele vrijheden van natuurlijke personen.

verdict.shared_subject: Cybersecurity and serious-incident governance involving a national cyber-crisis authority and an AI-system market-surveillance authority
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern incident-related governance, but they assign functions to different authorities and do not state how those functions interact. A possible operational overlap exists if a serious incident involving a high-risk AI system is also a large-scale cybersecurity incident covered by the national plan, potentially creating uncertainty about coordination or responsibility.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision A merely designates the Minister and assigns the tasks contained in the national plan, while Provision B requires the market-surveillance authority to take measures within seven days after receiving a notification and follow Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 procedures. The provisions impose no incompatible command, deadline, or prohibition, and their different authorities and triggers can operate concurrently.
verdict.evidence_span_a: Onze Minister is de cybercrisisbeheerautoriteit, bedoeld in artikel 9, eerste lid, van de NIS2-richtlijn, en heeft in die hoedanigheid de taken die zijn opgenomen in het nationaal plan voor grootschalige cyberbeveiligingsincidenten en crisisrespons, genoemd in artikel 20.
verdict.evidence_span_b: De markttoezichtautoriteit neemt passende maatregelen, zoals bedoeld in artikel 19 van Verordening (EU) 2019/1020, binnen zeven dagen na de datum waarop zij de in lid 1 van dit artikel bedoelde kennisgeving heeft ontvangen, en volgt de kennisgevingsprocedures waarin die verordening voorziet.

verdict.shared_subject: Organisations that may be subject to both incident-reporting and records-of-processing obligations
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions can apply to the same organisation, but they regulate different duties: Provision A concerns submitting an incident progress or final report, while Provision B concerns the applicability of a register-of-processing-activities obligation. Nothing in either text requires or forbids conduct that would prevent compliance with the other.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: An organisation can submit the required incident report within the applicable timeframe while also maintaining a processing-activities register, or qualify for the Article 30(5) exception without affecting its incident-reporting duty. The provisions have different subject matters, triggers, and consequences, so they are readily satisfied together.

verdict.evidence_span_b: De in de leden 1 en 2 bedoelde verplichtingen zijn niet van toepassing op ondernemingen of organisaties die minder dan 250 personen in dienst hebben, tenzij het waarschijnlijk is dat de verwerking die zij verrichten een risico inhoudt voor de rechten en vrijheden van de betrokkenen, de verwerking niet incidenteel is, of de verwerking bijzondere categorieën van gegevens, als bedoeld in artikel 9, lid 1, of persoonsgegevens in verband met strafrechtelijke veroordelingen en strafbare feiten als bedoeld in artikel 10 betreft.

verdict.shared_subject: Whether an organization remains registered or designated under the two regimes
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions allow a ministerial status to be changed or withdrawn when the organization no longer satisfies a condition. One refers to the changed, expired, or absent basis for registration, while the other specifically refers to no longer providing electronic services requiring substantial or high authentication; the texts do not establish that these triggers coincide.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can operate independently because they concern different legal statuses and triggers: A concerns registration in a national register of specified entities, while B concerns withdrawal of an organization's designation based on its electronic services. An organization can therefore comply with both by meeting each regime's separate conditions.
verdict.concrete_scenario: A medical-device manufacturer is registered in A's national register and designated under B, but it stops providing electronic services requiring substantial or high authentication while the factual basis for its registration under A remains unchanged. B would support withdrawing its designation, whereas A's quoted rule would not require changing or ending its registration on that fact alone.

verdict.shared_subject: Public disclosure and publication/reporting duties of organs or regulated entities
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A delays publication of a decision for ten working days unless an exception applies. Provision B permits rules requiring organs to publish an up-to-date statement on their website and potentially report an auditor’s statement, which could create a publication or reporting obligation during that period.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision B only authorizes further rules; it does not itself require immediate publication of the decision or its contents. Its possible website statement and auditor-report duties can concern the application of a standard rather than the prohibited early disclosure addressed by Provision A, and any implementing rules could be framed consistently with the ten-day restriction.

verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can operate cumulatively: A's permission is expressly conditional on the competent authority making the relevant declaration or judicial necessity, while B adds a prior-consultation requirement for a narrower category of information and circumstances. Nothing in the texts expressly says that A's disclosure exception overrides B's consultation requirement, and B's opening wording preserves other paragraphs' rules.

verdict.shared_subject: Processing special-category or criminal-offence personal data by a committee or advisory body where consent is the legal basis.
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A creates an exception to the prohibition when consent is impossible or disproportionately burdensome, while provision B requires the controller to be able to demonstrate that the data subject gave consent whenever processing is based on consent. In a case where consent is impossible, A may permit processing but B's consent-based evidentiary duty cannot be met if the processing is nevertheless characterized as consent-based.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can operate cumulatively: if processing actually relies on consent, the controller must demonstrate that consent under B; A's exception is relevant only where consent is impossible or disproportionately burdensome and other conditions are met. Thus A need not authorize consent-based processing without proof, and B does not itself prohibit A's public-interest exception.

verdict.shared_subject: Incident reporting by an essential or important entity
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions require an entity to submit a final incident report containing substantially the same information within one month, but A measures that month from the Article 27 notification, whereas B measures it from submission of the incident notification under point b). For an entity subject to both, those reference points could differ, creating potentially different final-report deadlines.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can be complied with together if the Article 27 notification in A is the same incident notification as B's point-b notification, in which case both impose the same one-month deadline and substantially identical content. B also expressly requires the same final-report information listed in A, so there is no content conflict.
verdict.concrete_scenario: A medical-device manufacturer classified as an essential or important entity reports a significant incident through an Article 27 notification before submitting B's 72-hour incident notification. A's one-month period then starts with the earlier Article 27 notification, while B's one-month period starts with the later point-b incident notification, leaving two potentially different deadlines for the same final report.

verdict.shared_subject: Information supplied by a critical third-country ICT-service provider that may involve personal data transferred to an international organisation or third country.
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Article 37 requires the critical third-country ICT-service provider to provide requested information, while Article 44 permits personal-data transfers to a third country or international organisation only after the GDPR Chapter V conditions are met. If the requested information contains personal data and supplying it entails a transfer lacking those conditions, compliance with the request could expose the provider to violating Article 44.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different duties and can ordinarily be satisfied together: the provider can supply the requested information while ensuring that any personal-data transfer complies with Chapter V, for example by removing personal data or using an applicable transfer mechanism. Article 37 does not expressly require an unlawful transfer or override Article 44.
verdict.concrete_scenario: A critical third-country ICT-service provider receives an Article 37 request for an incident file containing identifiable EU customer data and would have to send that file to an international organisation, but no Article 44-compliant Chapter V transfer condition is established in the texts shown.
verdict.decisive_exception: Whether an Article 44 Chapter V condition or other applicable GDPR basis permits this particular transfer in response to the Article 37 request is not established by the provisions shown.

verdict.shared_subject: An organisation using a high-risk AI system that experiences a personal-data breach
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions may apply to the same organisation, but they impose different obligations triggered by different events: Article 34 concerns notifying affected data subjects after a high-risk personal-data breach, while Article 27 concerns conducting and updating a fundamental-rights impact assessment for certain high-risk AI uses. Compliance with the impact-assessment duty does not determine whether breach notification is required, and the notification duty does not satisfy the assessment duty.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions regulate distinct duties and can be performed cumulatively without contradiction. An organisation can conduct and update the required AI impact assessment while also notifying data subjects of a qualifying personal-data breach, or rely on Article 34's stated exceptions where applicable.

verdict.shared_subject: Responsibilities and conformity assessment for substantially modified high-risk AI systems
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Article 25 requires the original provider to cooperate and provide information and technical access needed for conformity-assessment compliance when another actor becomes the provider after a substantial modification. Article 43 separately requires a new conformity assessment whenever a high-risk AI system is substantially modified, so the original provider’s cooperation duty and the modified system’s reassessment duty may create practical coordination burdens, especially where the original provider has disclaimed modification into a high-risk system.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose complementary duties rather than incompatible ones: Article 25 governs cooperation and assistance in the value chain, while Article 43 governs when a new conformity assessment must occur. Article 25’s express exception also aligns with the situation in which the original provider clearly stated that the system may not be modified into a high-risk system and therefore need not provide the documentation.

verdict.shared_subject: Processing special-category personal data in automated individual decision-making
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A restricts processing of special-category personal data unless one of its listed exceptions applies. Provision B requires safeguards, including human intervention and the opportunity to state a view and challenge the decision, when an automated individual decision falls within the referenced exceptions. If implementing those safeguards requires processing special-category data about the person, A may restrict that processing while B requires measures that could involve it.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision B does not itself require processing special-category personal data; it requires protective measures for certain automated decisions. Those measures can generally be implemented without such processing, and Provision A expressly permits processing where one of its listed exceptions applies, so the texts do not establish an actual prohibition-versus-permission conflict.

If a controller instructs processing of special-category data for a purpose not covered by A's listed exceptions, B could appear to require conduct that A does not permit.

A processor can comply with B by following only lawful instructions, and B's statutory-obligation exception does not itself authorize processing contrary to A.

verdict.shared_subject: AI-based automated decision-making and prohibited AI practices
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions can apply to an AI system used to make a significant automated decision about a person, while Article 22 prohibits the person from being subjected to that decision and Article 5 prohibits only specified AI practices, not every such decision. The provisions therefore do not establish a general conflict: Article 5 may prohibit the system for an independent reason, but it does not clearly regulate the same conduct as Article 22 in most cases.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose distinct prohibitions with different triggers. Article 22 concerns a person being subjected to a solely automated decision with legal or similarly significant effects, whereas Article 5 concerns enumerated practices such as manipulative systems, social scoring, certain biometric categorisation, and real-time remote biometric identification; an operator can comply with both by avoiding each applicable practice and ensuring that significant decisions are not solely automated unless an Article 22 exception applies.

verdict.shared_subject: Decisions concerning recognition and business/organizational identification means under BWBR0048156
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern ministerial decisions in the recognition regime, but they impose different kinds of rules: Article 14 requires publication of a decision in the Staatscourant, while Article 15 prohibits taking a particular acceptance decision for a means that fails specified security and reliability requirements. One might argue that publication of an Article 14 decision could disclose or formalize a decision concerning a means that Article 15 says may not be taken.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions regulate different acts and triggers. Article 14 concerns notification of a decision to withdraw or transfer recognition, whereas Article 15 bars a decision under its fifth paragraph concerning a means that fails the applicable requirements; nothing in Article 14 requires the prohibited Article 15 decision, and publication can occur for a lawful withdrawal or transfer decision. They can therefore both be obeyed without contradiction.

verdict.shared_subject: Automated decision-making by a high-risk AI system and the information supplied to its deployer
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Article 22 gives the data subject a right not to be subjected to a solely automated decision with legal or similarly significant effects. Article 13 requires instructions to describe the system’s capabilities, limitations, human-oversight measures, and output-interpretation mechanisms, but those system-level disclosures do not themselves prevent such a decision or ensure that the affected person can invoke the Article 22 protection.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different, potentially complementary duties: Article 22 governs whether an individual may be subjected to a qualifying solely automated decision, while Article 13 governs what a provider must tell a deployer about a high-risk AI system. Supplying the required instructions can support compliant human oversight without requiring any prohibited automated decision.
verdict.concrete_scenario: A provider supplies a high-risk AI system to a lender, with instructions fully documenting its intended purpose, limitations, human-oversight measures, and output-interpretation mechanisms. The lender nevertheless uses the system’s output to automatically reject a person’s loan application, producing a legal or similarly significant effect, without providing that person an effective way to prevent or challenge the solely automated decision under Article 22.
verdict.decisive_exception: Article 22(2) exceptions are supplied only as contextual text and could alter the prohibition; whether any such exception applies to the concrete decision would need to be assessed separately.

verdict.shared_subject: Protection of personal data and notification after a personal-data breach

A controller can comply with A and still notify under B, or qualify for B's non-notification exception while continuing to maintain A's required safeguards.

verdict.evidence_span_a: Bij onderhandelingen over contractuele overeenkomsten houden financiële entiteiten en derde aanbieders van ICT-diensten rekening met het gebruik van modelcontractbepalingen die door overheidsinstanties zijn ontwikkeld voor specifieke diensten.
verdict.evidence_span_b: Deze uitzondering is niet van toepassing op AI-modellen voor algemene doeleinden met systeemrisico's.

verdict.shared_subject: Withdrawal of an institutional designation by a minister
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern withdrawing an organisation's designation, but they appear to use different substantive conditions: provision A withdraws the higher-education essential-entity designation when its basis no longer exists, while provision B permits withdrawal when the organisation no longer provides electronic services requiring substantial or high authentication. If the same organisation is subject to both, those conditions might not coincide.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can operate independently because they concern different designations, different ministers, and potentially different statutory regimes. Provision A concerns designation as an essential entity in higher education, whereas provision B concerns an organisation providing specified electronic services; neither text says that the two designations or withdrawal conditions are legally identical or mutually exclusive.

verdict.shared_subject: Ministerial regulations concerning identification and access-related communications rules
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions delegate rulemaking to ministerial regulations concerning identification-related matters. In a broad sense, rules on access authentication under Provision A could coexist with rules on caller-number identification and blocking under Provision B, but the texts do not establish any incompatible requirement.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision A concerns authentication of a person seeking access to electronic services, including required assurance levels and authentication factors. Provision B concerns telephone-number identification, blocking or refusal, and information duties for providers, users, and subscribers; these are different subject matters and can be regulated simultaneously without contradiction.
