verdict.evidence_span_b: volgt de aanbieder de relevante conformiteitsbeoordelingsprocedure zoals vereist volgens die rechtshandelingen

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions appear in the same instrument, but they regulate entirely different matters: Article 5 concerns consent by a legal representative for services to protected persons, while Article 21b concerns suspending publication of an administrative decision during interim-relief proceedings. No actor is required by one provision to do something that the other prohibits or makes impossible.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can operate simultaneously without interaction. A service provider can comply with Article 5's scope rule, while the relevant authority separately suspends publication under Article 21b when an interim-relief request is made.
verdict.evidence_span_a: Dit artikel is niet van toepassing op hulp- en adviesdiensten die rechtstreeks en kosteloos aan een minderjarige of een onder curatele gestelde of een persoon ten behoeve van wie een bewind of mentorschap is ingesteld worden aangeboden.
verdict.evidence_span_b: Indien wordt verzocht om een voorlopige voorziening als bedoeld in artikel 8:81 van de Algemene wet bestuursrecht, wordt de openbaarmaking van de beschikking opgeschort totdat de voorzieningenrechter uitspraak heeft gedaan of het verzoek is ingetrokken.

verdict.shared_subject: Information and communications-network services
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions may concern an entity operating communications or network-related services, but Article 47 requires supplying registration information to a central contact point, while Article 11.10a regulates misleading information about network-termination points or users. One might argue that information supplied under Article 47 could include identifying network information and therefore raise a concern under the prohibition.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different duties on different subject matter: Article 47 requires specified entity and IP-range information to be provided to the central contact point, whereas Article 11.10a prohibits using a number-provision facility to give a called user incorrect information about a network termination point or individual user. An entity can provide the required registration information accurately while complying fully with the prohibition; neither provision requires the misleading conduct prohibited by the other.

verdict.evidence_span_b: wordt niet gebruikt om de opgeroepen gebruiker onjuiste informatie te verstrekken met betrekking tot dat netwerkaansluitpunt of die individuele gebruiker.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern institutional oversight or preparedness in the broad area of cybersecurity and regulatory compliance. One might argue that a national crisis-response plan could involve measures affecting accredited code-monitoring bodies, while the GDPR requires withdrawal of accreditation when those bodies breach the Regulation.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision A requires the Minister to establish a national plan for large-scale cybersecurity incidents and crisis response; it does not regulate accreditation or the conduct of GDPR code-monitoring bodies. Provision B requires the competent supervisory authority to withdraw accreditation when accreditation conditions fail or the body's measures infringe the GDPR. The duties concern different actors, triggers, and subject matter and can plainly be performed together.
verdict.evidence_span_a: Onze Minister stelt een nationaal plan voor grootschalige cyberbeveiligingsincidenten en crisisrespons als bedoeld in artikel 9, vierde lid, van de NIS2-richtlijn vast.
verdict.evidence_span_b: De bevoegde toezichthoudende autoriteit trekt de accreditatie van een in lid 1 bedoeld orgaan in indien de voorwaarden voor accreditatie niet of niet meer worden vervuld of indien de door het orgaan genomen maatregelen inbreuk maken op deze verordening.

verdict.shared_subject: Administrative handling of requests under the GDPR, including possible judicial proceedings concerning a transfer decision
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A permits the Council of State to stay a request when a related validity question is pending before the Court of Justice. Provision B requires a written decision on requests under Articles 15–22 of the GDPR to be made within the GDPR's specified time limits, which could appear to leave no room for waiting beyond those deadlines.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions address different procedural actors and functions: A concerns the Council of State's judicial handling of a request, while B concerns a written decision by an administrative authority. Nothing in B expressly governs or prohibits a judicial stay under A, and nothing in A says that an administrative authority may disregard the applicable decision deadline.
verdict.evidence_span_a: De Afdeling bestuursrechtspraak van de Raad van State kan besluiten het verzoek aan te houden als er bij het Hof van Justitie van de Europese Unie al een prejudiciële vraag omtrent de geldigheid van het desbetreffende besluit aanhangig is.
verdict.evidence_span_b: Een schriftelijke beslissing op een verzoek als bedoeld in de artikelen 15 tot en met 22 van de verordening wordt genomen binnen de in artikel 12, derde lid, van de verordening genoemde termijnen en geldt, voor zover deze is genomen door een bestuursorgaan, als een besluit in de zin van de Algemene wet bestuursrecht.

verdict.shared_subject: Processing of personal data, including possible special-category data, under an approved code of conduct
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A prohibits processing of special-category personal data unless one of the listed Article 9(2) exceptions applies. Provision B requires participating controllers or processors to make binding commitments concerning safeguards and data-subject rights, potentially in connection with transfers, but it does not itself establish that processing special-category data is permitted under any of A’s exceptions; this creates a possible sensitive-data permission gap rather than a demonstrated contradiction.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision B does not require processing special-category data at all: it concerns joining an approved code of conduct and applying appropriate safeguards for transfers, including commitments regarding data-subject rights. An actor can comply with both by refraining from prohibited processing or ensuring that any special-category processing independently satisfies one of A’s listed exceptions.
verdict.concrete_scenario: A controller joins an approved code of conduct and transfers a dataset containing health data to a third-country organisation under the code’s safeguards, while relying only on the code and its contractual commitments—not on any identified Article 9(2) exception—to justify the health-data processing. Provision B requires the safeguards and commitments, whereas Provision A still prohibits the processing unless one of its listed exceptions applies; the text shown does not establish that participation in the code supplies such an exception.
verdict.decisive_exception: Whether the processing of the special-category data is covered by an applicable Article 9(2) exception—such as explicit consent, vital interests, manifestly public data, or legal claims—is not established by Provision B. In particular, the code-of-conduct mechanism and contractual commitments in Article 40 do not, on the text shown, establish an Article 9(2) legal basis.
verdict.evidence_span_a: Overeenkomstig artikel 9, tweede lid, onderdelen a, c, d, e en f, van de verordening is het verbod om bijzondere categorieën van persoonsgegevens te verwerken niet van toepassing, indien:
verdict.evidence_span_b: Die verwerkingsverantwoordelijken of verwerkers doen, via contractuele of andere juridisch bindende instrumenten, bindende en afdwingbare toezeggingen om die passende waarborgen toe te passen, ook wat betreft de rechten van de betrokkenen.

verdict.shared_subject: Verplichtingen van nationale bevoegde autoriteiten rond AI-testomgevingen voor regelgeving onder artikel 57 van Verordening (EU) 2024/1689.
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Beide bepalingen leggen verplichtingen op aan nationale bevoegde autoriteiten in verband met dezelfde testomgeving. Men zou kunnen denken dat de kennisgeving en openbare lijst uit bepaling A overlappen met de jaarlijkse verslaglegging en online beschikbaarstelling uit bepaling B, waardoor onduidelijkheid ontstaat over welke informatie openbaar moet worden gemaakt.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: De bepalingen regelen duidelijk verschillende, cumulatieve handelingen: A vereist kennisgeving van de oprichting aan het AI-bureau en de AI-board en een openbare lijst door het AI-bureau, terwijl B periodieke en afsluitende inhoudelijke verslagen door de nationale autoriteiten vereist, met onlinepublicatie van die verslagen of samenvattingen. Een autoriteit kan beide verplichtingen zonder tegenstrijdigheid nakomen.
verdict.evidence_span_a: De nationale bevoegde autoriteiten stellen het AI-bureau en de AI-board in kennis van de oprichting van een testomgeving en kunnen hen om ondersteuning en begeleiding verzoeken.
verdict.evidence_span_b: De nationale bevoegde autoriteiten dienen vanaf één jaar na de oprichting van de AI-testomgeving voor regelgeving en vervolgens elk jaar tot de beëindiging ervan, bij het AI-bureau en de AI-board jaarverslagen in, alsook een afsluitend verslag.

verdict.shared_subject: Administrative enforcement and fines for entities subject to the two instruments
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions authorize administrative fines, so an entity could face enforcement by different authorities for overlapping conduct. However, the provisions do not prohibit either authority from acting, prescribe incompatible sanctions, or establish mutually exclusive competence; they concern different statutory violations and authorities.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can be satisfied cumulatively: the competent authority under BWBR0052872 may fine an important entity for violating Article 5:20(1) of the General Administrative Law Act, while the Dutch Data Protection Authority may impose a fine for the separately listed provisions concerning personal-data processing. Different enforcement powers and potentially concurrent sanctions are not, without an exclusivity rule, a legal conflict.
verdict.evidence_span_a: De bevoegde autoriteit kan tevens aan een belangrijke entiteit een bestuurlijke boete opleggen in geval van overtreding van artikel 5:20, eerste lid, van de Algemene wet bestuursrecht.
verdict.evidence_span_b: De Autoriteit persoonsgegevens is ter handhaving van de artikelen 4, twaalfde lid, 5, zevende en achtste lid, 6, eerste lid, voor zover het de verwerking van persoonsgegevens betreft, en tweede lid, onderdeel b, 14, 17, tweede lid, derde lid, eerste volzin, en vierde lid, laatste twee volzinnen, 18, eerste en vierde lid, 19, 21, tweede, derde, vierde en vijfde lid, en 22, tweede lid, bevoegd tot oplegging van:

verdict.shared_subject: Security and personal-data breach compliance by entities that may be subject to both regimes
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A creates an exception to notifying affected persons where appropriate technical measures make the data unintelligible to unauthorised persons. Provision B requires substantial administrative fines for essential entities that infringe NIS2 Articles 21 or 23, so an entity might face a fine under B for a security or incident-management infringement even though A removes the notification requirement in the stated circumstances.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different consequences and address different duties: A concerns whether a personal-data breach notification is required, while B concerns fines for infringement of Articles 21 or 23 by essential entities. An entity can comply with both by applying A's notification exception where its conditions are met and separately complying with Articles 21 and 23; nothing in either text makes the notification exception a defence to, or incompatible with, the NIS2 fine regime.
verdict.evidence_span_a: De kennisgeving, bedoeld in het tweede lid, is niet vereist indien de aanbieder naar het oordeel van de Autoriteit persoonsgegevens gepaste technische beschermingsmaatregelen heeft genomen waardoor de persoonsgegevens die het betreft, versleuteld of anderszins onbegrijpelijk zijn voor een ieder die geen recht heeft op toegang tot die gegevens.
verdict.evidence_span_b: De lidstaten zorgen ervoor dat essentiële entiteiten die inbreuk maken op artikel 21 of 23 overeenkomstig de leden 2 en 3 van dit artikel onderworpen worden aan administratieve geldboeten met een maximumbedrag van ten minste 10 000 000 EUR of ten minste 2 % van de totale wereldwijde jaaromzet in het voorgaande boekjaar van de onderneming waartoe de essentiële entiteit behoort, afhankelijk van welk bedrag hoger is.

verdict.shared_subject: Regulatory enforcement involving ICT or data-protection breaches
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A prohibits the competent authority from imposing a second administrative fine for the same conduct once an GDPR Article 58(2)(i) fine has been imposed. Provision B requires the lead overseer to impose a coercive penalty for non-compliance with measures after the specified period, which could superficially appear to require another monetary sanction for related conduct.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions address different sanctions, authorities, legal bases, and triggers. Provision A concerns duplication of administrative fines for the same conduct, whereas Provision B concerns a coercive penalty intended to compel compliance with oversight measures after non-compliance; nothing in the texts states that the coercive penalty is an administrative fine under Articles 80 or 87 or that it is imposed for the same conduct.
verdict.evidence_span_a: legt de bevoegde autoriteit geen bestuurlijke boete op op grond van de artikelen 80 en 87 voor een inbreuk als bedoeld in het tweede lid die voortvloeit uit dezelfde gedraging als die waarvoor de bestuurlijke boete op grond van artikel 58, tweede lid, onderdeel i, van de Algemene verordening gegevensbescherming is opgelegd.
verdict.evidence_span_b: neemt de lead overseer een besluit aan waarmee een dwangsom wordt opgelegd om de kritieke derde aanbieder van ICT-diensten tot nakoming van die maatregelen te dwingen.

verdict.shared_subject: Notification duties concerning cyber threats or personal-data breaches
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires an essential or important entity to promptly inform service recipients about measures they can take in response to a significant cyber threat, and, if necessary, about the threat itself. Provision B removes a personal-data-breach notification requirement where the provider has taken appropriate technical measures making the data unintelligible to unauthorised persons; if the same incident is both a significant cyber threat and a qualifying personal-data breach, the provisions could appear to point in different directions about whether notification is required.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions address different notification duties, triggers, and recipients: A concerns recipients of services affected by a significant cyber threat, while B concerns notification under article 11.3a(2) to the person whose personal data were affected by a breach. B's exception only removes the notification duty referred to in its second paragraph and does not prohibit A's separate cyber-threat communication. Both duties can therefore be performed cumulatively, or B can exempt only its own notification duty.
verdict.evidence_span_a: De essentiële entiteit of belangrijke entiteit deelt de ontvangers van haar diensten, die mogelijkerwijs door een significante cyberdreiging in relatie tot het ontvangen van die diensten worden getroffen, onverwijld mee welke maatregelen die ontvangers kunnen nemen in reactie op die dreiging.
verdict.evidence_span_b: De kennisgeving, bedoeld in het tweede lid, is niet vereist indien de aanbieder naar het oordeel van de Autoriteit persoonsgegevens gepaste technische beschermingsmaatregelen heeft genomen waardoor de persoonsgegevens die het betreft, versleuteld of anderszins onbegrijpelijk zijn voor een ieder die geen recht heeft op toegang tot die gegevens.

verdict.shared_subject: Delegated authority to make further rules by or under a general administrative measure
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions authorize further rules by or under an algemene maatregel van bestuur, but they concern different underlying provisions and apparently different legislative instruments. One could argue that subordinate rules made under the two delegations might overlap, creating uncertainty about which delegation governs a particular rule.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions are parallel competence clauses, not contradictory commands. Article 62 concerns implementation of Article 29(3) of the NIS2 Directive, while Article 11a.3 concerns further rules regarding Article 11a; both delegations can be exercised cumulatively within their respective scopes.
verdict.evidence_span_a: Bij of krachtens algemene maatregel van bestuur kunnen regels worden gesteld ter uitvoering van het bepaalde in artikel 29, derde lid, van de NIS2-richtlijn.
verdict.evidence_span_b: Bij of krachtens algemene maatregel van bestuur kunnen nadere regels worden gesteld ten aanzien van het bepaalde in dit artikel.

verdict.shared_subject: Disclosure of personal information obtained during conformity-assessment activities pursuant to a third-country judicial or administrative demand
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Article 48 restricts recognition or enforceability of a third-country demand to disclose personal data unless it is based on an international agreement or another GDPR Chapter V transfer ground. Article 31 requires notified bodies to keep information confidential except where disclosure is legally required, so a third-country demand might appear to make disclosure mandatory while Article 48 withholds recognition or enforceability.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Article 31 does not require disclosure whenever any third-country authority demands it; it expressly preserves confidentiality except where disclosure is legally required. Article 48 supplies a condition for recognising or enforcing a third-country demand for personal-data disclosure, so a notified body can comply with both by refusing or not treating an unsupported demand as legally requiring disclosure, while disclosing where Article 48 and any other applicable requirements are satisfied.
verdict.evidence_span_a: Elke rechterlijke uitspraak en elk besluit van een administratieve autoriteit van een derde land op grond waarvan een verwerkingsverantwoordelijke of een verwerker persoonsgegevens moet doorgeven of verstrekken, mag alleen op enigerlei wijze worden erkend of afdwingbaar zijn indien zij gebaseerd zijn op een internationale overeenkomst
verdict.evidence_span_b: behalve wanneer de openbaarmaking ervan wettelijk vereist is

verdict.shared_subject: Public disclosure of administrative sanctions or coercive fines by supervisory authorities
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions impose publication duties concerning sanctions, but they use different exceptions. Provision A incorporates the access-to-information exemptions in article 5.1 of the Wet open overheid, while Provision B permits withholding publication where disclosure would seriously endanger financial markets or cause disproportionate harm to the parties concerned. If the same disclosure is covered by both regimes, the provisions do not themselves explain how these exceptions interact.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The duties can be applied cumulatively: each authority can publish the relevant sanction unless its own statutory exception applies. The provisions may also concern different authorities, sanctions, and legal regimes, and nothing in the texts expressly requires publication despite the other provision's exception or states that one exception overrides the other.
verdict.evidence_span_a: De Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens maakt een door haar genomen beschikking tot het opleggen van een bestuurlijke sanctie openbaar, behoudens voor zover artikel 5.1, eerste, tweede en vijfde lid van de Wet open overheid, aan openbaarmaking in de weg staan.
verdict.evidence_span_b: De lead overseer maakt alle opgelegde dwangsommen openbaar, tenzij die openbaarmaking de financiële markten ernstig in gevaar zou brengen of onevenredige schade zou toebrengen aan de betrokken partijen.

verdict.shared_subject: Possible information and consent requirements involving providers of trust services and public-law information-society services
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions contain exceptions or limits concerning information-related obligations, so one might initially suspect that a trust-service provider could be exempt from one obligation while a public-law service provider is barred from conditioning access on consent. However, neither provision regulates the same concrete act or imposes incompatible commands on the same actor.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision A concerns when the first paragraph's national-register information obligation does not apply to a trust-service provider, depending on whether its services are used exclusively in legally or contractually closed systems. Provision B concerns access to an information-society service supplied by or for a public-law legal person and prohibits making that access conditional on consent under paragraph 1; the provisions have different actors, triggers, and duties and can readily both be obeyed.
verdict.evidence_span_a: Het eerste lid is niet van toepassing wanneer en voor zover een entiteit optreedt als verlener van vertrouwensdiensten die niet uitsluitend worden gebruikt binnen systemen die gesloten zijn als gevolg van een wettelijke regeling of een overeenkomst tussen een bepaalde groep deelnemers.
verdict.evidence_span_b: De toegang van de gebruiker tot een dienst van de informatiemaatschappij die wordt geleverd door of namens een krachtens publiekrecht ingestelde rechtspersoon wordt niet afhankelijk gemaakt van het verlenen van toestemming als bedoeld in het eerste lid.

verdict.shared_subject: Use of personal contact data for unsolicited communications, potentially including data revealing religious or philosophical beliefs
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A prohibits disclosure of the relevant personal data to third parties without the data subject’s consent. Provision B requires a sender using certain means to send unsolicited communications to give the recipient an easy, cost-free opportunity to object, which could involve using or disclosing contact data. If the contact data also reveals religious or philosophical beliefs, B’s communication duty might appear to require conduct that A restricts.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions regulate different conduct and triggers: A concerns disclosure of data revealing religious or philosophical beliefs in the context of spiritual care, while B concerns unsolicited communications and an objection mechanism. B does not require disclosure of special-category data, and its consent/objection rules can be complied with without disclosing such data to a third party; therefore both can be satisfied cumulatively.
verdict.evidence_span_a: In de gevallen, bedoeld in het eerste lid, worden geen persoonsgegevens aan derden verstrekt zonder toestemming van de betrokkene.
verdict.evidence_span_b: Bij het gebruik van andere dan de in het eerste lid bedoelde middelen voor het met toestemming overbrengen van deze ongevraagde communicatie aan natuurlijke personen, geeft de verzender de desbetreffende natuurlijke persoon bij iedere boodschap duidelijk en expliciet de gelegenheid om kosteloos en op gemakkelijke wijze verzet aan te tekenen tegen het gebruik van zijn contactgegevens.

verdict.shared_subject: Internal allocation and performance of duties within an organisational body
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires the members to establish a division of tasks, while Provision B requires the secretariat to perform its tasks exclusively according to the chair's instructions. One might argue that a task allocated by the members could conflict with a contrary instruction from the chair.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions regulate different actors and complementary organisational matters: the members allocate tasks, whereas the secretariat performs its tasks under the chair's instructions. Nothing in either text says that the members' allocation overrides the chair's instructions or that the secretariat must disregard them; both duties can therefore be complied with.
verdict.evidence_span_a: De leden stellen een verdeling van taken vast en betrekken hierbij zoveel mogelijk de buitengewone leden.
verdict.evidence_span_b: Het secretariaat verricht zijn taken uitsluitend volgens de instructies van de voorzitter van het Comité.

verdict.shared_subject: BWBR0048156: erkende diensten versus bestuursorganen of aangewezen organisaties
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Artikel 13 imposes a delivery duty on an erkende dienst, while article 29 delays acceptance duties for a bestuursorgaan or aangewezen organisatie until infrastructure is available under the connection schedule. If the recognised service must deliver before the recipient organisation can yet accept the relevant service, this could create a practical mismatch in timing or operational readiness.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose duties on different actors and address different matters: article 13 governs the recognised service's compliance with its recognition conditions, including a delivery duty, whereas article 29 governs when acceptance duties apply to a public body or designated organisation. The acceptance-duty commencement rule does not prohibit delivery or make compliance with article 13 impossible; both can be obeyed independently.
verdict.evidence_span_a: Een krachtens artikel 11 erkende dienst voldoet aan de voor de betrokken dienst bij of krachtens algemene maatregel van bestuur gestelde regels en aan de aan de erkenning of aanwijzing verbonden voorschriften en beperkingen.
verdict.evidence_span_b: De in de artikelen 7 en 15 opgenomen acceptatieplichten zijn voor een bestuursorgaan of aangewezen organisatie niet eerder van toepassing dan nadat dat bestuursorgaan of die aangewezen organisatie kan worden aangesloten op de in artikel 5, eerste lid, onderdelen a tot en met e, en tweede lid bedoelde infrastructuur en voorzieningen overeenkomstig het bij regeling van Onze Minister, gehoord Onze Ministers die het mede aangaat, op te stellen aansluitschema.

verdict.shared_subject: Processing biometric and other special-category personal data in connection with public-space real-time remote biometric identification for law enforcement.
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A permits a commission or advisory body to process special-category and criminal-offence data when its own conditions are met, while Provision B makes a particular use of biometric identification in public spaces conditional on prior judicial or independent-administrative authorisation and strict necessity and proportionality. If the commission or advisory body itself conducts that biometric identification, A's permission does not on its face establish compliance with B's separate authorisation regime.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions regulate different actors and mechanisms: A is a data-processing exception for a commission or advisory body, whereas B regulates real-time remote biometric identification for law-enforcement purposes. They can be complied with cumulatively: the actor can satisfy A's safeguards and also obtain B's required authorisation, and A does not purport to override B.
verdict.concrete_scenario: A temporary commission or advisory body performs real-time remote facial identification in a public space on behalf of law enforcement, processing biometric data and criminal-offence-related data under an important-public-interest task in its establishing instrument, with consent impossible and specified safeguards included. The commission may satisfy Article 47a, but Article 5 still requires the separate prior authorisation (or the narrowly limited emergency procedure); the shown texts do not establish that Article 47a is a legal basis satisfying or displacing that requirement.
verdict.decisive_exception: The unresolved link is whether the Article 47a exception for processing special-category and criminal-offence data constitutes a sufficient legal basis or exception under the AI Act's prohibition and authorisation regime, including the requirement that the use be strictly necessary and proportionate for an Article 5(1)(h) objective and be authorised by the specified judicial or independent administrative authority. The texts shown do not answer that question.

verdict.shared_subject: An entity that is both subject to GDPR Article 30 record-keeping rules and NIS2 Article 23 significant-incident reporting rules
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Article 30 can exempt a small organisation from the referenced records-of-processing obligations, while Article 23 requires essential and important entities to report significant incidents. One might argue that an incident report could require information about processing activities that the small organisation is not required to maintain under Article 30, creating an apparent documentation mismatch.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different, independently satisfiable duties: Article 30 concerns whether certain organisations must maintain a register of processing activities, whereas Article 23 concerns prompt reporting of significant incidents by essential and important entities. Article 23 does not require the entity to maintain an Article 30 register, and the Article 30 exemption does not prohibit incident reporting or prevent an entity from collecting the information needed for it.
verdict.evidence_span_a: De in de leden 1 en 2 bedoelde verplichtingen zijn niet van toepassing op ondernemingen of organisaties die minder dan 250 personen in dienst hebben, tenzij het waarschijnlijk is dat de verwerking die zij verrichten een risico inhoudt voor de rechten en vrijheden van de betrokkenen, de verwerking niet incidenteel is, of de verwerking bijzondere categorieën van gegevens, als bedoeld in artikel 9, lid 1, of persoonsgegevens in verband met strafrechtelijke veroordelingen en strafbare feiten als bedoeld in artikel 10 betreft.
verdict.evidence_span_b: Elke lidstaat zorgt ervoor dat essentiële en belangrijke entiteiten elk incident dat aanzienlijke gevolgen heeft voor de verlening van hun diensten als bedoeld in lid 3 (significant incident) onverwijld meldt bij zijn CSIRT of, indien van toepassing, zijn bevoegde autoriteit overeenkomstig lid 4.

verdict.shared_subject: Regulatory oversight and cybersecurity-related monitoring
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions involve institutional oversight functions, so one might initially suspect that CSIRT monitoring or incident analysis could overlap with a supervisory authority’s oversight of an accredited code-monitoring body. However, Article 16 assigns cybersecurity-support and threat-monitoring tasks to the CSIRT, while Article 41 governs withdrawal of accreditation by a data-protection supervisory authority; neither requires or forbids the other’s action.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose duties on different actors for different purposes: the CSIRT monitors cyber threats, vulnerabilities and incidents and assists entities, whereas the competent supervisory authority withdraws accreditation when a code-monitoring body no longer meets accreditation conditions or breaches the GDPR. Both can be fully performed together without incompatible commands, and the texts do not establish that CSIRT activity affects accreditation.
verdict.evidence_span_a: het monitoren en analyseren van cyberdreigingen, kwetsbaarheden en incidenten op nationaal niveau
verdict.evidence_span_b: De bevoegde toezichthoudende autoriteit trekt de accreditatie van een in lid 1 bedoeld orgaan in indien de voorwaarden voor accreditatie niet of niet meer worden vervuld of indien de door het orgaan genomen maatregelen inbreuk maken op deze verordening.

verdict.shared_subject: A system involving personal-data processing that is also an AI system listed in Annex III of the AI Act
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires the controller to conduct a data-protection impact assessment before processing where the processing is likely to create a high risk to natural persons’ rights and freedoms. Provision B separately addresses an Annex III AI system that the provider considers not to be high-risk, requiring that provider to document that assessment before placing the system on the market or putting it into service; the different assessments and classifications could leave uncertainty about whether one assessment satisfies the other.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose cumulative duties with different triggers and purposes: a GDPR controller must perform a DPIA when the processing is likely to pose a high risk, while an AI Act provider must document its contrary assessment for an Annex III system and register it. An actor can comply with both by conducting and documenting each required assessment; neither provision says that one assessment substitutes for or overrides the other.
verdict.concrete_scenario: A company provides an Annex III AI system used by a customer to process personal data. The provider concludes that the AI system itself does not constitute a high-risk AI system and documents that conclusion under Article 6, while the customer, as controller, determines that the intended personal-data processing is likely to pose a high risk to individuals’ rights and freedoms and must conduct a GDPR DPIA. Conversely, an Annex III classification and Article 6 documentation do not by themselves establish whether the customer’s processing meets Article 35’s separate high-risk trigger.
verdict.evidence_span_a: Wanneer een soort verwerking, in het bijzonder een verwerking waarbij nieuwe technologieën worden gebruikt, gelet op de aard, de omvang, de context en de doeleinden daarvan waarschijnlijk een hoog risico inhoudt voor de rechten en vrijheden van natuurlijke personen voert de verwerkingsverantwoordelijke vóór de verwerking een beoordeling uit van het effect van de beoogde verwerkingsactiviteiten op de bescherming van persoonsgegevens.
verdict.evidence_span_b: Een aanbieder die van mening is dat een in bijlage III bedoeld AI-systeem geen hoog risico inhoudt, documenteert zijn beoordeling voordat dat systeem in de handel wordt gebracht of in gebruik wordt gesteld.

verdict.shared_subject: Processing of personal data by a temporary commission or advisory body and the data subject’s right to object
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A permits an otherwise prohibited processing of special-category or criminal-offence data when its listed conditions are met. Provision B gives the data subject a right to object to processing based on Article 6(1)(e) or (f), requiring the controller to stop unless overriding compelling legitimate grounds or legal-claim grounds exist. If the processing relies on Article 6(1)(e) or (f), the permission in A does not by itself establish that the Article 21 exception is satisfied.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can operate cumulatively: A addresses whether the special-category or criminal-offence processing prohibition is lifted, while B addresses an individual objection to processing based on Article 6(1)(e) or (f). A commission can comply with both by stopping after an objection unless it can establish the overriding grounds specified in Article 21; A’s conditions do not purport to override that right.
verdict.concrete_scenario: A temporary advisory commission processes a person’s criminal-conviction data under Article 6(1)(e) in performing a task of substantial public interest, after satisfying Article 47a’s conditions. The person objects for reasons relating to their specific situation, but the commission cannot establish compelling legitimate grounds outweighing the person’s interests, rights and freedoms; A permits the sensitive-data processing while B requires it to cease.
verdict.decisive_exception: Whether the Article 21 exception—compelling legitimate grounds that outweigh the data subject’s interests, rights and freedoms, or grounds connected with legal claims—applies to the processing authorised under Article 47a is not established by the texts shown. In particular, Article 47a’s conditions do not state that they satisfy or override Article 21.

verdict.shared_subject: Public disclosure of official administrative decisions or measures
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions require publication of an official governmental act, so an authority could conceivably have to publish under both regimes. However, they concern different acts and impose compatible publication duties: Provision A concerns a decision designating attributes, while Provision B concerns final administrative sanctions and adds its own notice and website conditions.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The Minister can publish a designation decision in the Staatscourant under Provision A, while the competent authority can publish a non-appealable administrative-sanction decision on its official website under Provision B. Nothing in either text prohibits the other publication, and the provisions do not prescribe incompatible timing, content, or retention requirements.
verdict.evidence_span_a: Van een besluit tot aanwijzing doet Onze Minister mededeling in de Staatscourant.
verdict.evidence_span_b: De bevoegde autoriteiten maken op hun officiële website onverwijld alle niet voor beroep vatbare besluiten tot het nemen van administratieve strafmaatregelen bekend, nadat de natuurlijke of rechtspersoon op wie een dergelijke maatregel van toepassing is, van deze maatregel in kennis is gesteld.

verdict.shared_subject: Processing and publication of subscriber personal data
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A prohibits processing special-category personal data unless one of its listed exceptions applies. Provision B requires that subscriber data be included in publicly available directories or subscriber-information databases when the subscriber has consented, which could include special-category data. If such data were included on consent alone, B might appear to require processing that A permits only if the consent satisfies A's specific exception.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision B concerns ordinary subscriber personal data and requires the subscriber's consent; it does not require processing special-category data. If special-category data are involved, B can be complied with only alongside A, including its requirement that consent be explicit and tied to specified purposes. Thus the provisions can operate cumulatively without contradiction.
verdict.concrete_scenario: A telecommunications provider receives a subscriber's explicit request to publish a directory entry containing a special-category datum about that subscriber, such as a health-related designation. Provision B requires inclusion of the subscriber's indicated data after consent, while Provision A prohibits processing special-category data unless the consent meets its specific exception; the excerpts do not establish whether the consent required by B is sufficiently explicit and purpose-specific for A.
verdict.decisive_exception: Whether the subscriber's consent under Provision B qualifies as the explicit, purpose-specific consent required by Article 9(2)(a) of the GDPR as incorporated by Provision A, and whether any other applicable exception permits the directory processing.

verdict.shared_subject: Public notice of official decisions
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions require public disclosure of official decisions, so one might initially suspect overlapping publication duties. However, they concern different decisions and different publication mechanisms: Provision A concerns an AP decision imposing an administrative sanction and publication subject to Woo exceptions, while Provision B concerns a decision designating or withdrawing a designation and publication in the Staatscourant.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The duties can readily be performed cumulatively because they have different triggers and addressees: the AP publishes sanction decisions unless the specified Woo provisions prevent disclosure, whereas the relevant authority gives notice of designation or withdrawal decisions through the Staatscourant. Nothing in either text forbids the other form of publication or makes one publication substitute for the other.
verdict.evidence_span_a: De Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens maakt een door haar genomen beschikking tot het opleggen van een bestuurlijke sanctie openbaar, behoudens voor zover artikel 5.1, eerste, tweede en vijfde lid van de Wet open overheid, aan openbaarmaking in de weg staan.
verdict.evidence_span_b: Van een besluit tot aanwijzing of intrekking wordt mededeling gedaan door plaatsing in de Staatscourant.

verdict.shared_subject: Telecommunications investigation and exemptions
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions are in the same statutory context, but they regulate different matters: Article 11.11 requires an operator to cooperate with an investigation and provide available subscriber-identifying data on request, while Article 11.12 concerns conditions and requirements attached to an exemption. No text indicates that an exemption can relieve the cooperation duty or that cooperation is prohibited.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can plainly operate cumulatively: an operator may have to cooperate under Article 11.11, while any exemption under Article 11.12 may be granted subject to limitations or conditions. Article 11.12 does not address the investigation duty or create an incompatible refusal right.
verdict.evidence_span_a: verstrekt, indien het onderzoek daartoe aanleiding geeft, de beschikbare op het oproepende nummer betrekking hebbende naam-, adres-, postcode- en woonplaatsgegevens
verdict.evidence_span_b: Een ontheffing kan onder beperkingen worden verleend. Aan een ontheffing kunnen voorschriften worden verbonden.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions are in the same legislative instrument, but they regulate entirely different matters: withdrawal of an accreditation and parliamentary involvement in delegated regulation. No actor is required by one provision to do something that the other forbids or makes impossible.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Article 14 governs an accredited service's request to withdraw its accreditation and the accompanying termination plan. Article 25 governs the parliamentary laying-before and possible withdrawal of a general administrative measure made under Article 5(6); these obligations can operate independently without contradiction.

verdict.evidence_span_b: Een krachtens artikel 5, zesde lid, vastgestelde algemene maatregel van bestuur wordt aan beide Kamers der Staten-Generaal overgelegd.

verdict.shared_subject: Processing of personal data, including special-category personal data, and the controller’s information duties
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A prohibits processing special-category personal data unless one of the listed Article 9(2) exceptions applies. Provision B requires a controller, where personal data were not obtained from the data subject, to provide extensive information, including the source and certain rights, but it does not itself authorise processing or create an exception to the prohibition. Thus, the strongest tension case is that B’s disclosure duty may accompany processing that A prohibits, but B does not require that prohibited processing.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different, cumulative obligations: A determines whether processing special-category data is lawful, while B requires transparency information when the data were obtained indirectly. A controller can comply with both by processing only where an Article 9(2) exception applies and then providing the information required by Article 14. Nothing in B overrides or substitutes for A’s prohibition.

verdict.shared_subject: Processing special-category personal data and facilitating data-subject rights
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A prohibits processing special-category personal data unless one of the listed Article 9(2) exceptions applies. Provision B requires the controller to facilitate the data subject’s rights, which may in practice require handling or communicating personal data, potentially including special-category data; if that handling lacks an applicable Article 9(2) exception, the duties could point in opposite directions.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision B does not itself require processing special-category data: rights can be facilitated through identification, access procedures, redaction, or other means that comply with Article 9. If processing such data is necessary, Provision A expressly permits it where one of its exceptions applies, so both provisions can be satisfied cumulatively.
verdict.concrete_scenario: A controller receives an access request under Article 15 concerning a file containing the person’s health data. Facilitating the request may require processing and disclosing that health data, but the facts do not establish that the data subject gave explicit consent, that another listed Article 9(2) exception applies, or that the controller can comply without processing the special-category data.
verdict.decisive_exception: It is not established whether the processing needed to facilitate the Article 15–22 right is covered by one of Provision A’s Article 9(2) exceptions, such as explicit consent, vital interests, manifestly public data, or legal claims.

verdict.evidence_span_b: De verwerkingsverantwoordelijke faciliteert de uitoefening van de rechten van de betrokkene uit hoofde van de artikelen 15 tot en met 22.

verdict.shared_subject: Confidentiality and disclosure of personal information during conformity-assessment activities
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A removes a notification duty when technical measures make the affected personal data unintelligible to unauthorised persons, while Provision B requires notified bodies to keep information confidential but permits disclosure when legally required. One might argue that a legally required disclosure could concern information protected under A, creating an apparent conflict between confidentiality and disclosure obligations.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions regulate different duties and actors: A concerns a provider's notification to the affected person after a personal-data breach, whereas B concerns notified bodies' confidentiality procedures and professional secrecy during conformity assessment. B's legal-disclosure exception can be complied with alongside A, and A does not prohibit disclosure or require notification where its stated encryption condition applies.
verdict.evidence_span_a: De kennisgeving, bedoeld in het tweede lid, is niet vereist indien de aanbieder naar het oordeel van de Autoriteit persoonsgegevens gepaste technische beschermingsmaatregelen heeft genomen waardoor de persoonsgegevens die het betreft, versleuteld of anderszins onbegrijpelijk zijn voor een ieder die geen recht heeft op toegang tot die gegevens.
verdict.evidence_span_b: Aangemelde instanties beschikken over gedocumenteerde procedures die waarborgen dat hun personeel, comités, dochterondernemingen, onderaannemers, geassocieerde instanties of personeel van externe instanties overeenkomstig artikel 78 de informatie die zij tijdens conformiteitsbeoordelingsactiviteiten in hun bezit krijgen vertrouwelijk houden, behalve wanneer de openbaarmaking ervan wettelijk vereist is.

verdict.shared_subject: Public authorities and regulated electronic/AI services
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern regulated public-sector or organisational activity and could involve an authority overseeing or approving a transfer. One provision restricts ministerial approval of transferring an accreditation, while the other requires national competent authorities to comply with confidentiality duties. In a broad factual setting, confidentiality could make it harder to disclose information relevant to the transfer decision, but neither text requires disclosure or makes confidentiality incompatible with the transfer rule.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision A governs when the Minister may approve transferring an accreditation and requires refusal where competition or continuity of reliable electronic access is endangered. Provision B imposes confidentiality duties on national competent authorities under a separate EU AI-law framework; the duties can be complied with while the Minister applies the transfer criteria, and the provisions address different actors, decisions, and subject matter.
verdict.evidence_span_a: Onze Minister verleent geen toestemming voor overdracht indien daarmee naar zijn oordeel de daadwerkelijke mededinging wordt of dreigt te worden verstoord of indien de continuïteit van een betrouwbare toegang tot elektronische dienstverlening met erkende bedrijfs- en organisatiemiddelen als gevolg van die overdracht in het geding dreigt te komen.
verdict.evidence_span_b: Bij de uitvoering van hun taken voldoen de nationale bevoegde autoriteiten aan de in artikel 78 vastgelegde vertrouwelijkheidsverplichtingen.

verdict.shared_subject: A high-risk AI system involving processing of personal data, where the provider and deployer may also be subject to GDPR duties.
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions can concern the same high-risk AI system, but they impose different obligations on potentially different actors: GDPR Article 35 requires the controller to conduct a data-protection impact assessment before processing where the processing is likely to create a high risk, while Article 13 requires the provider's instructions to contain specified information. The strongest tension case is therefore that the AI Act's documentation duty might be mistaken for, or treated as sufficient to replace, the GDPR's prior impact assessment, although neither text says that it does.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose cumulative and independently satisfiable duties, not incompatible commands. A controller can conduct the GDPR assessment before processing, while the provider supplies the required instructions and information; Article 13 does not prohibit or displace the assessment, and Article 35 does not prohibit the instructions.

verdict.shared_subject: Organisational obligations concerning financial entities’ ICT and personal-data processing
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A concerns an exemption from the GDPR records-of-processing obligations for certain organisations with fewer than 250 employees, subject to stated exceptions. Provision B requires a financial entity to designate a communications spokesperson; nothing in B requires or prohibits maintaining a GDPR processing record, so the provisions regulate different duties.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: A financial entity can comply with B by appointing a spokesperson and can independently comply with A by keeping a processing record where an exception applies, or by relying on the small-organisation exemption where it does not. The spokesperson duty does not require processing personal data in a way that would conflict with A’s record-keeping rule.
verdict.evidence_span_a: De in de leden 1 en 2 bedoelde verplichtingen zijn niet van toepassing op ondernemingen of organisaties die minder dan 250 personen in dienst hebben, tenzij het waarschijnlijk is dat de verwerking die zij verrichten een risico inhoudt voor de rechten en vrijheden van de betrokkenen, de verwerking niet incidenteel is, of de verwerking bijzondere categorieën van gegevens, als bedoeld in artikel 9, lid 1, of persoonsgegevens in verband met strafrechtelijke veroordelingen en strafbare feiten als bedoeld in artikel 10 betreft.
verdict.evidence_span_b: Ten minste één persoon in de financiële entiteit wordt belast met de uitvoering van de communicatiestrategie voor ICT-gerelateerde incidenten en vervult daartoe de rol van woordvoerder bij het publiek en de media.

verdict.shared_subject: Disclosure and exchange of confidential information with authorities under NIS2 and DORA
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A permits confidential information to be exchanged with the Commission and other competent authorities when necessary for applying the directive, whereas Provision B states that information covered by professional secrecy is not to be provided to any other person or authority unless Union or national law provides a basis. If an exchange under A is necessary but no separate Union or national-law basis under B is established, the provisions could appear to point in opposite directions.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision A itself limits exchange to information necessary, relevant and proportionate to applying the directive and requires confidentiality safeguards. Provision B contains an express exception for disclosure based on Union or national law, and A is a Union-law provision; therefore the exchange can be understood as falling within B's exception, subject to the stated necessity and proportionality conditions.
verdict.decisive_exception: Provision B's exception for disclosure 'op grond van Unierechtelijke of nationaalrechtelijke bepalingen' (on the basis of provisions of Union or national law) is the relevant legal basis; Provision A supplies a Union-law framework for the specified exchange, while also limiting it by necessity, relevance and proportionality.
verdict.evidence_span_a: informatie die krachtens Unie- of nationale voorschriften vertrouwelijk is, zoals de voorschriften inzake de vertrouwelijkheid van bedrijfsinformatie, alleen met de Commissie en andere bevoegde autoriteiten overeenkomstig deze richtlijn uitgewisseld wanneer die uitwisseling noodzakelijk is voor de toepassing van deze richtlijn
verdict.evidence_span_b: wordt aan geen enkele andere persoon of autoriteit verstrekt, tenzij op grond van Unierechtelijke of nationaalrechtelijke bepalingen;

verdict.shared_subject: Cybersecurity and personal-data incident handling
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern consequences of security incidents, and a financial entity could face an incident involving personal data while also having to classify a cyberthreat. However, neither provision prescribes an incompatible action, deadline, or classification consequence for the other.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision A creates an exception to notifying affected individuals where appropriate technical measures make the data unintelligible to unauthorised persons. Provision B requires financial entities to classify cyberthreats as significant using factors concerning critical services, affected clients or counterparties, and geographic spread; the entity can perform that classification while separately applying the notification exception.
verdict.evidence_span_a: De kennisgeving, bedoeld in het tweede lid, is niet vereist indien de aanbieder naar het oordeel van de Autoriteit persoonsgegevens gepaste technische beschermingsmaatregelen heeft genomen waardoor de persoonsgegevens die het betreft, versleuteld of anderszins onbegrijpelijk zijn voor een ieder die geen recht heeft op toegang tot die gegevens.
verdict.evidence_span_b: Financiële entiteiten classificeren cyberdreigingen als significant op basis van de mate waarin de risicovolle diensten, waaronder de transacties en verrichtingen van de financiële entiteit, als cruciaal kunnen worden aangemerkt, het aantal en/of de relevantie van de beoogde cliënten of financiële tegenpartijen en de geografische spreiding van de risicogebieden.

verdict.shared_subject: Access to and disclosure of confidential information in the context of public authorities and AI expertise
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A excludes confidential data from the Wet open overheid, subject to an environmental-information exception. Provision B requires the Commission to facilitate Member States’ timely access to experts, which could in practice involve sharing information, but it does not expressly require disclosure of confidential data or public access to it.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision B concerns organising Member States’ access to experts, not access to or disclosure of the confidential data covered by Provision A. The Commission and Member States can comply with B while preserving confidentiality and using lawful, restricted channels for any necessary information exchange.

Provision B prohibits providers from processing traffic and location data retained under Article 13.2a(2) for other purposes unless the processing is permitted under Articles 11.5 and 11.5a and complies with those articles; this could appear to restrict disclosure if the requested data are within that retained dataset and the investigation purpose is not covered.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can be satisfied cumulatively: Article 11.11 concerns disclosure of specified subscriber-identification data in response to an investigation, while Article 11.13 concerns traffic and location data retained under Article 13.2a(2). Article 11.11 does not expressly require disclosure of traffic or location data, and its disclosure can be made subject to Article 11.13 where the requested information falls within that category.
verdict.decisive_exception: If the requested name, address, postcode and residence data are themselves traffic or location data retained under Article 13.2a(2), their disclosure would additionally need to fall within the permission in Articles 11.5 or 11.5a; the shown provisions do not establish that factual or legal overlap. This does not establish a conflict because Article 11.11 can be complied with using data outside that restricted category, or subject to the stated exception.

verdict.shared_subject: Continuation or termination of services affecting reliable electronic access and ICT-service use

verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions address different legal mechanisms and actors: provision A concerns the Minister’s possible continuation order after withdrawal of an acknowledgement, whereas provision B concerns competent authorities’ measures against a financial entity using a critical third-party ICT provider. They can be complied with cumulatively, including by continuing the service for other users while the financial entity stops using it; neither text expressly makes one order override the other.

verdict.shared_subject: An AI system involving personal-data processing that may be high-risk under the AI Act
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions may apply to the same AI-related activity, but they impose different obligations: GDPR Article 35 requires a data-protection impact assessment before processing where the processing is likely to create a high risk to individuals’ rights and freedoms, while AI Act Article 25 requires cooperation, information, technical access and assistance from the original provider in specified high-risk-system supply-chain circumstances. One obligation does not prevent compliance with the other, and the provisions do not establish incompatible benchmarks or substitute one duty for the other.

verdict.shared_subject: Whether obligations under Directive (EU) 2022/2555 displace or coexist with requirements applicable to data-reporting service providers under Regulation (EU) 2022/2554.
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Article 4 of the Directive says its relevant provisions are not applicable where sector-specific Union legislation imposes at-least-equivalent cybersecurity-risk-management or significant-incident-reporting requirements. Article 10 of the Regulation imposes a systems obligation on data-reporting service providers, so one might argue that this sector-specific obligation displaces the Directive’s corresponding requirements for those providers.

verdict.shared_subject: Processing and erasure of special-category personal data
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A prohibits processing of listed special-category data, while provision B can require a controller to erase personal data, including such data, without undue delay. In a case where the data is already being processed, however, erasure is a cessation or removal of processing rather than a permission to continue it, so the provisions do not impose incompatible conduct.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The prohibition in A can be obeyed by not processing the listed data, and B can be obeyed by erasing personal data when one of its conditions applies. If special-category data was unlawfully processed, B's erasure duty reinforces A's prohibition; if an exception or lawful basis permits processing, B's erasure rule still operates independently and does not require continued processing.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A permits the Minister to exempt certain entities from information-provision obligations, while Provision B requires recognition of an issuer when the service and means satisfy the applicable rules. However, the provisions concern different duties and do not state that exemption affects recognition.

An entity can be exempt from Article 44 obligations and still satisfy the independent recognition conditions in Article 11; neither provision forbids compliance with the other.

verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can be satisfied cumulatively: A removes the notification duty under its own conditions, while B specifies the content only if an Article 34(1) notification is otherwise required. Article 27(2) instead defines exceptions to the separate obligation to appoint an EU representative; the provisions have different duties, triggers, and subject matter, and neither requires nor forbids conduct required by the other.

verdict.shared_subject: Regulatory authorities’ handling of information and personal-data incidents
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions impose duties on authorities concerning information, so one might initially ask whether notifying a data-protection authority under Provision A could conflict with the confidentiality guarantee in Provision B. However, Provision A concerns notification of a potential personal-data breach, while Provision B concerns information obtained by notifying authorities under a different provision and does not prohibit the notification required by A.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The duties apply to different authorities and different triggers: Provision A requires the competent authority to notify the Dutch Data Protection Authority or other GDPR supervisory authorities when it learns of a possible reportable personal-data breach, whereas Provision B requires notifying authorities to keep information obtained under Article 78 confidential. The authorities can notify the competent data-protection authority and ensure that the information is handled confidentially, so both duties can be fulfilled.

verdict.shared_subject: Publication of administrative decisions in the Staatscourant
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions require publication in the Staatscourant, but they concern different decisions and different statutory schemes. Nothing in either text prohibits or makes incompatible the publication required by the other.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The duties are cumulative and can plainly be performed together: each relevant decision can be published in the Staatscourant under its respective legal basis. Provision A applies to decisions referred to in several paragraphs of its own article, while provision B specifically concerns designation decisions under article 11.10.

verdict.shared_subject: Public authorities’ conduct in relation to inspections and their legal duties
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions regulate official conduct, and an inspection notice could theoretically disclose confidential information or undermine an inspection’s effectiveness. However, Provision A expressly allows withholding notice where notice would make the inspection ineffective, while Provision B only imposes confidentiality obligations and does not prohibit the inspection notice required by A.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different, cumulatively satisfiable duties: the lead overseer must normally give reasonable advance notice, subject to A’s exceptions, and national competent authorities must comply with the separate confidentiality obligations in Article 78. Confidentiality can be maintained when giving notice, and A already permits non-notification where disclosure would defeat the inspection.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions confer regulatory competence, so one might argue that rules made under Provision A could overlap with ministerial prescriptions under Provision B concerning continuity planning. However, neither provision requires or forbids conduct that the other requires or forbids, and they concern different legal bases and subject matters.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision A authorises rules by or under a general administrative measure to implement NIS2 implementing acts, delegated acts and guidelines. Provision B authorises the Minister to prescribe how a joint continuity plan is established only when the specified providers cannot agree; both competences can operate cumulatively within their respective scopes.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires covered public bodies and designated organisations to obtain an auditor’s statement about compliance with electronic-service access rules. Provision B independently prohibits transfers of personal data to third countries or international organisations unless the GDPR Chapter V conditions are met; an audit under A does not establish those transfer conditions, so an organisation might mistakenly treat A compliance as sufficient for a transfer.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different, cumulative duties: A concerns an auditor’s statement about compliance with access-system rules, while B governs the legality of international personal-data transfers. An organisation can obtain the required audit statement and separately ensure that every transfer satisfies Chapter V, so nothing in the texts makes simultaneous compliance impossible.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern the Minister’s handling of recognised authentication services, but they impose different kinds of obligations: Article 11 requires recognition when the service meets the applicable rules, while Article 17 requires publication of certain decisions. One might argue that publication could expose or complicate the recognition process, but neither text makes publication incompatible with recognition.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Article 11 governs the substantive conditions for recognising an authentication service. Article 17 governs publicity of specified decisions through the Staatscourant; publication can occur alongside a recognition decision and does not alter or prevent the substantive recognition duty.

Provision B allows an exemption to be granted subject to limitations and conditions, so an exemption could theoretically impose a condition concerning those blocking facilities; however, B does not itself say that an exemption may authorise conduct prohibited by A.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions perform different functions: A imposes a specific prohibition on the sender, while B merely gives the competent authority power to grant a conditional exemption. An exemption granted under B can be framed consistently with A, and the text shown does not establish that B overrides or permits breach of A.

verdict.shared_subject: Processing and erasure of personal data, potentially including special-category data
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A permits processing of special-category personal data in specified circumstances, while provision B requires a controller to notify other controllers to erase publicly disclosed personal data when the erasure duty in Article 17(1) applies. If the data are special-category data and an Article 17(1) erasure ground applies, continued dissemination could appear permitted by A but inconsistent with B's erasure-related duty.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision A concerns when the prohibition on processing special-category data does not apply; it does not require retention or prohibit erasure. Provision B concerns the procedure for communicating an already-applicable erasure obligation, and the two can be satisfied cumulatively: a controller may erase or seek erasure of the data while relying on A for any separate processing that remains legally permitted.

Provision B requires domain-name registries and registration-service entities to provide specific registration data to legitimate access-requesting parties within 72 hours, which could involve data connected with communications or users and therefore create a disclosure pressure.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision B expressly limits access to lawful, duly reasoned requests and requires compliance with EU data-protection law; it does not require disclosure of communications or communications-related data contrary to Provision A. The provisions also principally address different data and actors, and both duties can be satisfied by disclosing only lawfully accessible registration data while preserving confidential communications.

verdict.shared_subject: Automated decision-making and human oversight of high-risk AI systems
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Article 22 gives the individual a right not to be subjected to a solely automated decision with significant effects, while Article 14 requires high-risk AI to be designed so that natural persons can exercise effective oversight. Effective oversight could be understood as requiring intervention capability, but Article 14 does not expressly require that every significant decision actually receive human involvement or prevent solely automated decisions.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose cumulative and compatible safeguards: Article 14 requires a system-level capability for effective human oversight, while Article 22 separately protects individuals against specified solely automated decisions, subject to its own exceptions. A high-risk AI operator can comply with both by designing effective oversight and ensuring that Article 22 decisions are not made solely automatically unless an Article 22(2) exception applies.

If the forwarding duty were itself an infringement covered by the sanctioning provision, one might ask whether the duty is enforceable in the same way.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires an essential or important entity to promptly inform service recipients about measures responding to a significant cyber threat. Provision B, however, is not a prohibition on that communication; it merely provides that the Article 30(1) and (2) record-keeping obligations do not apply to certain organisations with fewer than 250 employees, subject to listed exceptions. The provisions regulate different duties and can operate cumulatively without contradiction.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: An entity can notify service recipients under A while separately determining whether it must maintain a GDPR processing-activities register under B. Even where B exempts a small organisation from the register duty, that exemption does not forbid cyber-threat communications, and where an exception removes the exemption the entity can comply with both duties.

A sender/controller can comply with both by providing the objection opportunity clearly and accessibly, without either provision requiring what the other forbids.
