verdict.shared_subject: Processing of traffic/location data and special-category personal data by providers of public electronic communications networks or services
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Article 11.13 prohibits providers from processing traffic and location data retained under Article 13.2a for other purposes, unless processing is permitted under Articles 11.5 and 11.5a and complies with those articles. Article 10 permits, under stated conditions, exceptional processing of special-category personal data for bias detection and correction in high-risk AI systems; if the retained traffic or location data include special-category personal data and the AI bias-detection purpose is not covered by Articles 11.5 or 11.5a, the Article 10 permission would appear to authorize processing that Article 11.13 prohibits.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Article 10 is not a general authorization to process all data: it concerns only strictly necessary special-category data used for bias detection or correction in specified high-risk AI systems and requires extensive safeguards. Article 11.13 itself preserves processing permitted under Articles 11.5 and 11.5a, so both provisions can be complied with if the Article 10 processing also satisfies those provisions; the text shown does not establish that the relevant traffic or location data are special-category data or that the Article 10 permission falls outside those exceptions.
verdict.concrete_scenario: A provider of a public electronic communications service retains traffic or location data under Article 13.2a, including data revealing a person's health or another Article 9 GDPR special category, and uses those data in a high-risk AI system to detect or correct bias because other data cannot do so effectively. The provider satisfies Article 10's listed safeguards, but Articles 11.5 and 11.5a do not permit that purpose; Article 10 would then permit the sensitive-data processing while Article 11.13 prohibits it.
verdict.decisive_exception: Whether the processing is permitted under Articles 11.5 and 11.5a, as required by Article 11.13. The provisions shown do not establish that Article 10's exceptional permission for bias detection satisfies those exceptions or overrides Article 11.13.
verdict.evidence_span_a: De verkeers- en locatiegegevens die de aanbieders van openbare elektronische communicatienetwerken of openbare elektronische communicatiediensten bewaren op grond van artikel 13.2a, tweede lid, worden door de aanbieders niet voor andere doelen verwerkt, tenzij het gegevens betreft waarvan de verwerking op grond van de artikelen 11.5 en 11.5a is toegestaan en de verwerking plaatsvindt met inachtneming van die artikelen.
verdict.evidence_span_b: Voor zover dit strikt noodzakelijk is om de opsporing en correctie van vertekeningen te waarborgen in verband met de AI-systemen met een hoog risico overeenkomstig lid 2, punten f) en g), van dit artikel, mogen de aanbieders van dergelijke systemen uitzonderlijk bijzondere categorieën persoonsgegevens verwerken, mits passende waarborgen worden geboden voor de grondrechten en fundamentele vrijheden van natuurlijke personen.

verdict.shared_subject: Handling vulnerability reports and personal-data breach notifications
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires the coordinator to preserve the anonymity of the person or entity reporting a vulnerability. Provision B gives a supervisory authority competence to order a controller to communicate a personal-data breach to the data subject, which might appear to require disclosure connected with a vulnerability report.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different functions on different actors: A governs the coordinator's follow-up to a voluntary vulnerability report, while B concerns a supervisory authority's corrective power over a controller. B orders communication of a personal-data breach to the data subject, not disclosure of the reporter's identity, so both duties can be performed together while preserving anonymity.

verdict.shared_subject: Processing and international transfer of personal data, potentially including special-category data
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A removes the prohibition on processing special-category personal data only in listed circumstances, while provision B permits a third-country transfer in listed situations and requires informing the data subject in a fallback case. A transfer under B could involve special-category data, but B does not itself establish that one of A’s exceptions applies to that processing.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions regulate different legal questions: A concerns whether processing special-category data is prohibited, whereas B concerns safeguards and derogations for transferring personal data to a third country. They can be complied with cumulatively: a controller must both satisfy an applicable Article 9 exception for any special-category processing and satisfy Article 49’s transfer conditions and information duty.
verdict.concrete_scenario: A controller transfers a person’s health data to a third-country organisation under Article 49(1)(a), relying on the person’s explicit, risk-informed consent to the proposed transfer, but the text shown does not establish that the processing of the health data itself falls within Article 22’s listed exceptions. The controller therefore faces an unresolved question whether the transfer-related permission also satisfies the separate special-category processing prohibition.
verdict.decisive_exception: The missing link is whether the Article 49 transfer derogation—particularly explicit consent to the transfer, or another Article 49 ground—also constitutes an applicable Article 9(2) exception to the prohibition on processing the special-category data under Article 22. The provisions shown do not establish that it does.

verdict.shared_subject: Verboden AI-praktijken onder artikel 5, lid 1, punten c en f, van Verordening (EU) 2024/1689
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Beide bepalingen verbieden het gebruik van AI-systemen, maar zij zien op verschillende praktijken: sociale scoring enerzijds en emotie-inferentie op de werkplek of in het onderwijs anderzijds. Een systeem kan feitelijk beide functies hebben, zodat dezelfde inzet onder twee afzonderlijke verboden valt; dat maakt naleving echter niet onmogelijk, omdat de exploitant het gebruik kan staken.

verdict.shared_subject: Contractual obligations concerning third-party ICT/AI service providers and providers of high-risk AI systems
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires a third-party ICT provider to provide details about the scope, procedures and frequency of inspections and audits. Provision B requires the parties in a high-risk AI supply chain to specify the information, technical access and assistance needed for full compliance with the AI Act. If the same contract covers both services, these obligations could be viewed as imposing different or potentially overlapping contractual specifications.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose cumulative contractual requirements with different purposes: A concerns audit and inspection arrangements for ICT services supporting critical or important functions, while B concerns information, access and assistance enabling compliance with the AI Act for high-risk AI systems. A contract can specify both sets of details; neither provision forbids or substitutes for the other.

verdict.shared_subject: Operational continuity and information handling by regulated entities
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires a public electronic communications provider to disclose location data simultaneously during an emergency call, even when the user has temporarily blocked processing of those data. Provision B requires a central securities depository to maintain a secondary processing site immediately accessible to staff for continuity of critical or important functions; one might loosely see both as imposing operational obligations involving data and continuity, but they regulate different actors and conduct.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose distinct duties on different regulated entities and concern different actions: emergency location-data disclosure under A versus secondary-site accessibility and business continuity under B. An entity subject to both, if that were possible, could provide the required location data during an emergency while also maintaining an immediately accessible secondary site; neither provision prohibits compliance with the other.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires a domain-name registry or registrar to provide specific registration data to a legitimate party on a lawful, properly reasoned request. Provision B prohibits special-category personal data from being transmitted, transferred, or otherwise accessed by other parties, so a request could theoretically seek data falling within that category.

verdict.shared_subject: Wederzijdse bijstand tussen bevoegde/toezichthoudende autoriteiten
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision B requires the requested authority not to refuse assistance except on three specified grounds, while Provision A permits refusal where the request violates the GDPR or other applicable EU or national law. If a request under B violates applicable law, A appears to permit refusal even though B's listed refusal grounds do not expressly include every such legal violation.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can operate cumulatively: B governs cooperation under the NIS2 framework, while A governs GDPR mutual assistance by GDPR supervisory authorities. Moreover, B itself permits refusal where the requested assistance would conflict with fundamental national-security, public-security or defence interests, and A's legal-compliance ground may concern a request that is outside B's scope or otherwise unlawful under the receiving authority's applicable law.
verdict.concrete_scenario: A GDPR supervisory authority that is also the NIS2 authority receives a motivated request under Article 37(1)(c) to conduct an inspection or targeted security audit. The authority is competent, the request is proportionate, and none of Article 37's national-security, public-security or defence grounds applies, but carrying out the requested measure would violate an applicable GDPR or national-law restriction; Article 61 permits refusal, whereas Article 37 says the request may not be refused on the stated facts.
verdict.decisive_exception: Whether Article 37's phrase allowing refusal when the requested information or activity would conflict with the receiving authority's applicable law, or another applicable EU-law rule, incorporates Article 61(b)'s broader legal-compliance ground. The shown text does not establish that exception or reconciliation.

verdict.shared_subject: The authorised representative’s obligations under Article 22(e) for a high-risk AI system

verdict.shared_subject: Notification to individuals after a personal-data breach
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires the provider to notify the affected person immediately when the breach is likely to have adverse effects on privacy. Provision B says notification is not required when appropriate technical and organisational measures were taken and applied, particularly measures making the data unintelligible to unauthorised persons; thus, for an encrypted breach, A's trigger could appear to require notification while B removes that requirement.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can be read cumulatively: A imposes the general notification duty, while B supplies an applicable exception where its stated conditions are met. The apparent conflict is resolved by the exception in B, so an actor can comply by notifying in cases covered by A unless B's non-notification condition applies.
verdict.concrete_scenario: A provider suffers a breach involving encrypted personal data. The provider has taken and applied appropriate technical and organisational measures making the data unintelligible to unauthorised persons, but the breach is nevertheless likely to have adverse effects on the affected person's privacy. Provision A points toward immediate notification, while Provision B permits withholding that notification under its stated condition.
verdict.decisive_exception: Whether Provision B's exception allowing non-notification for appropriately protected and unintelligible data overrides or qualifies Provision A's notification duty, including whether the two provisions are legally coordinated for this provider and breach, is not established by the two isolated provisions. The supplied context suggests parallel encryption-based exceptions, but it is not itself the norm being compared.

verdict.shared_subject: Information supplied to the Minister under Dutch electronic-services access rules and the handling of special-category personal data by high-risk AI providers.
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A can require a covered organisation to provide the Minister with data and information needed to prevent or end breaches of secure and reliable access. Provision B prohibits transmitting, transferring, or otherwise consulting special-category personal data by other parties, even though the same paragraph exceptionally permits strictly necessary processing for bias detection subject to safeguards; if the information needed by the Minister included such data, supplying it could conflict with B's prohibition.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision A requires only the data and information necessary for the specified security measures, not necessarily special-category personal data. Provision B's prohibition applies within its own high-risk-AI processing context and may be complied with by supplying non-sensitive information, anonymised information, or information without transmitting the special-category data; the texts do not establish that A requires the prohibited disclosure.
verdict.concrete_scenario: A covered recognised means issuer that is also a provider of a high-risk AI system holds special-category personal data used under Article 10 to detect bias. The Minister requests information under Article 19 that, on the facts, requires the issuer to transmit those special-category data to the Minister so that the Minister can prevent or end a breach of secure and reliable electronic access; Article 10(4)(d) says those data are not to be transmitted, transferred, or otherwise consulted by other parties.
verdict.decisive_exception: It is not established whether Article 19's statutory information duty, or another applicable legal basis and safeguard, qualifies as an exception to Article 10(4)(d)'s prohibition on transmission or consultation by other parties. It is also not shown that the requested information can be supplied without transmitting the special-category data.

The texts shown do not establish whether B’s non-requirement exception displaces A’s duty.

Artikel 32, lid 5, onder b, voorziet daarnaast in een tijdelijk verbod voor een natuurlijke persoon met leidinggevende verantwoordelijkheden; bij een bestuurder die onder beide bepalingen valt, kan dat lijken op een botsing tussen toepasselijkheid van de governance-regels en het bestuursverbod.

Bovendien is artikel 32 volgens de gegeven normselectie alleen een uitsluiting voor overheidsinstanties, niet een algemeen verbod op toepassing van artikel 24.

verdict.shared_subject: Independent experts and oversight-related governance

verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions regulate different roles, actors, and functions. A control officer can report NIS2 compliance under Provision A while DORA's oversight forum separately appoints experts based on expertise and requires them to act independently and without instructions; both duties can be performed simultaneously.

verdict.shared_subject: Processing and access to personal data, including special categories of personal data, by persons acting under a controller or processor’s authority.
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires persons with access to personal data who act under a controller’s or processor’s authority to process it only on instructions, unless Union or Member State law requires the processing. Provision B prohibits other parties from transmitting, transferring, or otherwise accessing the special-category data, so a person acting under the controller or processor’s authority might be instructed to access such data while B forbids that access as access by another party.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can be complied with cumulatively: the controller or processor can instruct only authorised persons who are not “other parties” for purposes of B, and any access can be limited to the exceptional, strictly necessary bias-detection context and the safeguards listed in B. A’s instruction rule does not itself authorise access or override B’s prohibition.
verdict.concrete_scenario: A high-risk AI provider processes special-category data to detect bias and instructs an external analytics company, acting under the provider’s authority and having access to the data, to process it. A permits that company to process the data on the provider’s instructions, but B prohibits the data from being transmitted, transferred, or otherwise accessed by other parties; the shown text does not establish whether the analytics company is excluded from “other parties” or whether another exception permits its access.
verdict.decisive_exception: Whether a person or entity acting under the controller’s or processor’s authority is nevertheless an “other party” under Provision B, and whether B’s exceptional permission to process special-category data permits the specific transmission, transfer, or access prohibited by the separately stated rule in paragraph 10(5)(d).

verdict.shared_subject: The transfer of personal data to a third country or international organisation while an authorised representative supplies AI-system documentation to authorities.
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Article 44 prohibits transferring personal data unless the GDPR Chapter V conditions are met. Article 22 obliges the authorised representative, on a reasoned request, to provide all necessary documentation, including logs, which could contain personal data and could be held or accessed outside the EU; if supplying that material entails a third-country transfer without a Chapter V condition, the duties may point in opposite directions.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Article 22 requires supplying information to a competent authority, but it does not require transferring personal data to a third country or international organisation. The representative can comply using non-personal, redacted, or lawfully transferred material, while Article 44 remains fully applicable to any personal-data transfer.
verdict.concrete_scenario: A representative established outside the EU receives a reasoned request from an EU authority for logs under its control; the logs contain identifiable individuals’ personal data, and sending them to the representative or another recipient in the representative’s third country would be necessary to fulfil Article 22, but no Chapter V transfer condition under Article 44 has been established.
verdict.decisive_exception: Whether a Chapter V transfer mechanism or other applicable GDPR exception authorises the particular transfer required to provide the requested logs; Article 22 itself does not establish that exception.

verdict.shared_subject: Automated or biometric AI-based decision-making affecting natural persons
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Article 22 prohibits subjecting a person to a solely automated decision with legal or similarly significant effects, while Article 5(h) prohibits real-time remote biometric identification for law enforcement only subject to narrowly defined necessity exceptions. A law-enforcement biometric-identification use could therefore be permitted under Article 5(h) yet produce a prohibited solely automated significant decision under Article 22.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions regulate different acts and can be obeyed cumulatively: Article 5(h) governs whether a particular real-time remote biometric-identification use may occur, whereas Article 22 governs whether a resulting decision may be made solely by automated processing. A permitted identification operation can be followed by human review or another compliant decision process, so permission under Article 5(h) does not require violating Article 22.

verdict.shared_subject: ICT/cybersecurity business-continuity duties
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions require continuity and recovery planning, but they formulate the protected subject differently: Provision A covers network and information systems and their physical environment against incidents, while Provision B requires continuity specifically for critical or important functions of certain exempt financial entities. verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The duties are cumulative and can be satisfied together: an entity can protect its network and information systems through continuity, backup, recovery and crisis measures under A while separately ensuring continuity of its critical or important functions under B. Provision B expressly requires plans and response/recovery measures that include at least backup and recovery, which is consistent with, rather than incompatible with, A's continuity requirement.

verdict.shared_subject: Communication to the data subject after a personal-data breach
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A states that the notification to the person concerned must include specified information, apparently requiring such notification. Provision B states that notification to the data subject is not required where, for example, appropriate protective measures were applied and made the data unintelligible to unauthorised persons.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision B is an express exception to the notification duty and therefore can qualify the apparent general duty in Provision A. The provisions can be read together: notification is made with the required contents unless one of the conditions in Provision B removes the obligation to notify; no incompatible content, deadline, or action is otherwise prescribed.
verdict.concrete_scenario: An operator subject to both provisions suffers a breach involving personal data that was encrypted and remained unintelligible to unauthorised persons. Provision A appears to require notifying the affected person, while Provision B says that such communication is not required. Whether Provision B legally overrides the duty in Provision A, including whether its exception applies to this operator and incident, is not established by the text shown.
verdict.decisive_exception: The decisive issue is whether the exception in Provision B—particularly the condition that appropriate technical and organisational measures were taken and applied so that the data was unintelligible to unauthorised persons—legally qualifies or overrides Provision A's notification duty. The texts do not expressly establish the relationship between the two instruments.

verdict.shared_subject: Processing special-category personal data for bias detection and correction in high-risk AI systems
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A states that processing special-category personal data is prohibited, while Provision B expressly permits providers of certain high-risk AI systems to process such data exceptionally for bias detection and correction. Thus, absent an applicable exception under Article 9(2) GDPR, the same processing appears both prohibited and permitted/required subject to safeguards.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can be read cumulatively: Article 10 permits the processing only where it is strictly necessary, alternative data cannot achieve the purpose, extensive safeguards are applied, and the processing also complies with GDPR. Article 9(2) GDPR may provide the legal basis that removes the prohibition, but the text shown does not establish that the AI Act permission itself satisfies any particular Article 9(2) condition.
verdict.concrete_scenario: A provider of a high-risk AI system uses users’ ethnic-origin data to detect and correct discriminatory performance because anonymised or synthetic data cannot do so effectively, applies pseudonymisation and strict access controls, and deletes the data after correction. The processing satisfies the stated Article 10 conditions, but it remains prohibited under Article 9(1) unless a separate Article 9(2) GDPR exception—such as a sufficiently grounded substantial-public-interest basis—also applies.
verdict.decisive_exception: Whether the processing falls within an applicable exception to Article 9(1), especially Article 9(2)(g) GDPR or another Article 9(2) condition, and whether that exception has the required Union or Member State legal basis and safeguards. Article 10 itself says the processing must comply with Regulation (EU) 2016/679 but does not establish that legal basis.

The provisions can therefore generally be complied with cumulatively, and B may simply be irrelevant unless the same disclosure obligation and security interest are engaged.

verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision B concerns contractual audit transparency for ICT services supporting critical or important functions, while Provision A imposes confidentiality on communications and related data. The audit-information duty can be fulfilled without disclosing confidential communications—for example, by describing audit scope, procedures and frequency at a sufficiently general level—so the texts do not require incompatible conduct.

Provision A requires an essential or important entity offering a trust service to report a significant incident to public authorities; Provision B concerns whether a controller must communicate a personal-data breach to the affected individuals, and expressly makes that communication unnecessary under specified conditions. verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern cybersecurity monitoring or incident management, so the Cooperation Group’s assessment of the state of cyber threats or incidents could inform how incident-management processes are designed. verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The Cooperation Group may regularly assess the state of cyber threats or incidents, while the ICT incident-management process must introduce early-warning indicators. verdict.shared_subject: Processing and access to information or personal data in electronic communications and AI systems
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A extends the requirements in Article 11.7(1)(a) and (b) to information stored on, or accessed from, an end device even where the mechanism is not an electronic communications network. Provision B prohibits other parties from transmitting, transferring, or otherwise consulting special-category personal data in the specified high-risk-AI context; if A's incorporated requirements required such access or disclosure, the duties could point in opposite directions.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision A does not itself state what the incorporated requirements require, and it does not expressly concern special-category personal data or the transmission, transfer, or consultation of such data by other parties. verdict.shared_subject: Processing personal data in connection with AI systems, particularly facial-recognition databases
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A permits further processing for a different purpose when the controller assesses compatibility using the listed factors, potentially allowing processing of facial images for a new purpose. Provision B categorically prohibits placing on the market, putting into service for that purpose, or using AI systems that build or supplement facial-recognition databases through untargeted scraping of internet or CCTV facial images, so a GDPR compatibility assessment cannot authorize that specifically prohibited AI practice.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can be satisfied cumulatively: Article 6 governs the lawfulness and purpose compatibility of personal-data processing, while Article 5 independently prohibits a specified AI practice. Article 6 does not expressly grant permission to conduct processing that another EU rule prohibits; therefore, a controller can comply by refraining from the prohibited scraping practice and applying Article 6 to any lawful, non-prohibited further processing.

verdict.shared_subject: Gebruik van hoog-risico-AI-systemen die geautomatiseerde individuele besluiten nemen met aanzienlijke gevolgen voor natuurlijke personen.
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Artikel 22 geeft de betrokkene een individueel recht om niet aan zo’n uitsluitend geautomatiseerd besluit te worden onderworpen. Artikel 27 verplicht bepaalde gebruiksverantwoordelijken slechts tot een voorafgaande grondrechteneffectbeoordeling, inclusief een beschrijving van menselijk toezicht; die beoordeling kan risico’s en toezicht beschrijven zonder het concrete geautomatiseerde besluit te verhinderen.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: De bepalingen leggen verschillende, cumulatieve verplichtingen op: artikel 27 vereist een voorafgaande systeem- en contextbeoordeling, terwijl artikel 22 het concrete besluit aan een afzonderlijke beperking onderwerpt. Een gebruiksverantwoordelijke kan beide naleven door de beoordeling uit te voeren én geen uitsluitend geautomatiseerd besluit met de bedoelde gevolgen te nemen, tenzij een toepasselijke uitzondering op artikel 22 geldt.
verdict.decisive_exception: Niet nodig voor de compatibiliteitsbeoordeling; artikel 22, lid 2, bevat wel uitzonderingen op het recht, maar artikel 27 zelf heft dat recht niet op of vervangt het niet.
verdict.evidence_span_a: De betrokkene heeft het recht niet te worden onderworpen aan een uitsluitend op geautomatiseerde verwerking, waaronder profilering, gebaseerd besluit waaraan voor hem rechtsgevolgen zijn verbonden of dat hem anderszins in aanmerkelijke mate treft.
verdict.evidence_span_b: Voordat een AI-systeem met een hoog risico als bedoeld in artikel 6, lid 2, in gebruik wordt gesteld, met uitzondering van AI-systemen met een hoog risico die bedoeld zijn om te worden gebruikt op het in punt 2 van bijlage III vermelde gebied, voeren gebruiksverantwoordelijken die publiekrechtelijke organen zijn of particuliere entiteiten zijn die openbare diensten verlenen, en gebruiksverantwoordelijken van AI-systemen met een hoog risico als bedoeld in bijlage III, punt 5, b) en c), een beoordeling uit van de gevolgen voor de grondrechten die het gebruik van een dergelijk systeem kan opleveren.

verdict.shared_subject: The competent authorities’ powers to impose or require corrective/enforcement measures
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A prohibits the competent authority from imposing a fine under articles 80 and 87 for the same conduct once the GDPR fine has been imposed. Provision B gives competent authorities at least the power to require corrective measures for infringements, so one might ask whether that power remains available after the prohibition in A.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions address different measures: A bars a duplicate administrative fine for the same conduct, whereas B concerns the competence to require corrective measures under DORA. A does not prohibit corrective measures, and B does not require imposing a fine or require measures for conduct covered by A’s specific prohibition.

verdict.shared_subject: Regulatory competence concerning authorisations, certification, and continuity of electronic services
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A allows the Minister, when approving a transfer, to impose a continuing-service obligation on the requesting service. Provision B gives a supervisory authority competence to order a certification body not to issue certification when certification requirements are no longer met; in a concrete case, that order could affect an organisation whose continued service is required under A, creating an apparent conflict between continuity and withholding certification.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions confer different powers on different authorities and regulate different objects: A concerns conditions attached to the transfer of an authorisation and continuity of electronic services, while B concerns corrective supervision of certification under the GDPR. Neither provision requires certification to be issued or makes continuity prevail over a lawful certification decision; both authorities can exercise their respective powers cumulatively.

verdict.shared_subject: Regulatory compliance by an organisation involved in high-risk AI processing
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions impose compliance-related obligations involving authorities, but they regulate different duties: GDPR Article 36 requires prior consultation where a DPIA identifies an unmitigated high risk, while AI Act Article 22(2)(e) concerns ensuring the accuracy of registration information when the provider performs the registration itself. Nothing in either text makes one duty replace, obstruct, or contradict the other.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: An organisation can comply with both by consulting the supervisory authority before processing where Article 36 is triggered and, separately, ensuring accurate Annex VIII registration information if the provider performs the registration. The provisions have different triggers, actors and subject matter, and simultaneous compliance is straightforward.

verdict.shared_subject: Use of network-connection-number facilities and ICT-risk management
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A prohibits using a caller-identification facility to provide the called user with incorrect information about the network endpoint or individual user. Provision B requires certain financial entities to use robust, resilient and up-to-date ICT systems and tools to minimise ICT risks and protect data. One might argue that a security or resilience measure could involve presenting altered caller-identification information, potentially creating a conflict with A.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision A regulates the truthfulness of information supplied through a specific caller-identification facility, whereas B imposes a general ICT-risk-management and data-protection duty. An entity can use robust and resilient systems while ensuring that any information supplied through that facility remains accurate; B does not require misleading information or prescribe any incompatible implementation.

verdict.shared_subject: Processing of special-category personal data for AI bias detection and correction
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A states that processing special-category personal data is prohibited unless one of the listed GDPR Article 9(2) grounds applies. Provision B requires that, in a narrowly defined high-risk-AI bias-detection context, providers may exceptionally process such data subject to safeguards; the text shown does not establish that this AI Act permission itself satisfies one of A’s exceptions.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can operate cumulatively: a provider may process the data only where Provision B’s strict necessity and safeguards are met and where an applicable exception under Provision A also applies. Provision B expressly preserves the requirements of Regulations (EU) 2016/679 and related instruments, so it need not displace Provision A.
verdict.concrete_scenario: A provider of a high-risk AI system processes identifiable health or ethnic-origin data because it is strictly necessary to detect and correct bias, cannot be replaced by synthetic or anonymised data, and all of Provision B’s listed safeguards are met. However, the facts do not establish that the data subject gave explicit consent, that the data were manifestly made public, or that another exception listed in Provision A applies; the provider therefore has B’s permission but may still be prohibited by A.
verdict.decisive_exception: Whether the processing permitted by Provision B is covered by an applicable exception to the special-category-data prohibition under Article 9(2) GDPR, as implemented or otherwise addressed by Provision A. Provision B’s reference to compliance with Regulations (EU) 2016/679 and related instruments does not, in the text shown, establish that its specific bias-detection permission independently satisfies that exception.

verdict.shared_subject: Processing and handling of data and results in regulated testing environments
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires financial entities to ensure that processing TLPT results—including generating, storing, aggregating, reporting, communicating, or destroying them—does not create risks for the financial entity. Provision B prohibits personal-data processing in an AI regulatory sandbox from leading to measures or decisions affecting data subjects or the exercise of their data-protection rights; if TLPT results contained personal data and their processing affected individuals' rights, the duties could point in different directions, with A requiring result handling and B prohibiting such effects.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions regulate different activities and actors: A concerns financial entities' contracts with external TLPT testers and risks to the financial entity, while B concerns further processing of personal data in a specific AI regulatory testing environment and effects on data subjects. A can be satisfied through secure, rights-compliant handling of TLPT results, and B does not prohibit processing that merely avoids measures or decisions affecting individuals or their rights.

verdict.shared_subject: Governance of a financial entity’s internal ICT audits versus access to special-category personal data in a high-risk AI system
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A obliges the governing body to approve and periodically evaluate internal ICT-audit plans and audits. Provision B prohibits special-category personal data from being transmitted, disclosed, or otherwise consulted by other parties, which could appear to restrict an audit involving such data. However, A does not expressly require auditors to access that data, and B’s prohibition is part of a conditional exception framework for processing such data.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The financial entity can approve and evaluate its ICT-audit plans without giving auditors access to special-category personal data; it can use appropriate access controls, anonymisation, documentation, or other audit evidence. Provision B’s prohibition can therefore be obeyed while the governance duty in A is fulfilled.

verdict.shared_subject: Public-authority access to or provision of information and documentation concerning personal-data protection and high-risk AI systems
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A empowers a supervisory authority to provide advice to public bodies and the public on matters related to personal-data protection, while provision B requires information or documentation obtained by certain fundamental-rights authorities under Article 77 to be processed according to confidentiality obligations. If advice under A involved information obtained under B, disclosure or use might appear constrained by B's confidentiality rule.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different, compatible norms on different activities: A grants an advisory competence, subject to applicable national law, whereas B governs how information or documentation obtained by the authorities referred to in Article 77(1) must be processed. Advice under A can be given while respecting the confidentiality obligations in B; neither text requires disclosure of protected information or forbids all advice about data protection.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A excludes confidential data from the Wet open overheid, subject to an environmental-information exception. Provision B obliges EU supervisory authorities to establish administrative-cooperation arrangements that may facilitate inspections and information exchange with a third-country authority; if those arrangements involved disclosure or public-access treatment of confidential data, A could appear to restrict what B facilitates.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision B requires cooperation arrangements and specifies information-sharing mechanisms, but it does not itself require disclosure of information that is confidential under Dutch law or require application of the Wet open overheid. The arrangements can therefore be designed and operated consistently with A's confidentiality restriction and its applicable exceptions.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern supervisory decisions, but neither imposes an incompatible substantive requirement. verdict.shared_subject: Financial entities' ICT technologies and processes under DORA Article 9
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions impose obligations concerning ICT security and data protection, but they address different aspects: provision A concerns securing data-transfer means, while provision B concerns preventing availability failures, loss of authenticity or integrity, confidentiality breaches, and data loss. One might argue that the breadth of B creates overlapping or potentially different security benchmarks.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The obligations are cumulative and can readily be satisfied together: a financial entity can secure its data-transfer means while also preventing the separately listed availability, integrity, confidentiality, and loss risks. Neither provision requires conduct that would prevent compliance with the other, and both appear in the same Article 9 as complementary norms.

verdict.shared_subject: Communicating significant incidents or personal-data breaches to service recipients/data subjects
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires an essential or important entity to promptly inform recipients when a significant incident adversely affects service provision. Provision B says communication to the data subject is not required where appropriate protective measures were applied to the affected personal data, so the same event could appear to require communication under A while permitting non-communication under B.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions address different duties, actors and triggers: A concerns significant incidents affecting service provision and recipients generally, while B concerns a GDPR personal-data breach and an exception to communication to the data subject. Even if the same event qualifies under both, B's exception only removes the GDPR communication duty; it does not state that communication required by A is prohibited or dispensed with.

verdict.shared_subject: Cybercrisisbeheerautoriteit and the CSIRT designated to coordinate vulnerability disclosure
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern public cyber-security functions, but Provision A assigns the Minister the role and tasks of the cybercrisisbeheerautoriteit, while Provision B requires a Member State to designate one of its CSIRTs as vulnerability-disclosure coordinator. If the Minister and the designated CSIRT are treated as competing holders of the same coordination function, their institutional assignments could appear misaligned. The texts, however, do not say that the Minister must personally perform the CSIRT coordinator's tasks or that the two roles are mutually exclusive.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision A concerns the Minister's competence and tasks under the national plan for large-scale cyber incidents and crisis response. Nothing in the shown text expressly says that A’s considerations automatically suspend or override B, and A’s reference to informing the data subject is itself compatible with disclosure under B.
verdict.missing_reference: The exact content of BWBR0040940 art. 41(1), including how its restriction mechanism applies to the GDPR information duty in art. 14, would be needed to determine whether a particular restriction lawfully displaces that duty; the text shown does not establish such displacement.

verdict.shared_subject: Wederzijdse bijstand tussen toezichthoudende/bevoegde autoriteiten
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Beide provisions impose cooperation and mutual-assistance duties on authorities, so a request under one regime could overlap with a request under the other. The strongest possible tension would be if one regime required assistance while the other prohibited refusal subject to different conditions, but the texts shown do not make those conditions incompatible.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can be satisfied cumulatively: Article 61 GDPR requires supervisory authorities to exchange relevant information and cooperate effectively, while Article 37 NIS2 requires competent authorities to cooperate for entities operating across Member States and expressly limits assistance to what is proportionate to the requested authority’s resources and tasks. Neither provision forbids compliance with the other; they concern parallel cooperation duties with compatible scopes and safeguards.
verdict.evidence_span_a: De toezichthoudende autoriteiten verstrekken elkaar relevante informatie en wederzijdse bijstand om deze verordening op een consequente manier ten uitvoer te leggen en toe te passen, en nemen maatregelen om doeltreffend met elkaar samen te werken.

verdict.shared_subject: Processing special-category personal data in connection with AI systems
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Article 5 prohibits workplace or education emotion-inference AI, while Article 10 permits—and in the stated circumstances requires compliance conditions for—processing special-category personal data to detect and correct bias in certain high-risk systems. If emotion inference in the workplace or education uses such data for bias detection, Article 10 could appear to authorise processing connected with an activity Article 5 prohibits.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Article 10 does not authorise emotion inference or override Article 5; it concerns exceptional processing of special-category data for bias detection in specified high-risk systems. An operator can comply with both by not using a prohibited emotion-inference system and, where a lawful non-prohibited high-risk system requires bias detection, processing the data only under Article 10’s safeguards.
verdict.concrete_scenario: A provider operates a high-risk AI system in a workplace that infers employees’ emotions and processes biometric or health-related data to detect and correct bias in that inference. Article 5 prohibits the workplace emotion-inference use, while Article 10 appears to permit the exceptional processing for bias detection if its conditions are met; the provisions shown do not establish whether Article 10 can supply a legal basis for processing connected with the prohibited use.
verdict.decisive_exception: Whether Article 10’s exceptional permission to process special-category personal data for bias detection can apply when the underlying workplace or education emotion-inference use is prohibited by Article 5, or whether another applicable exception/legal basis permits that processing. Article 10 itself does not state that it overrides Article 5.

verdict.shared_subject: Public authorities and their statutory duties
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions impose duties on public bodies, but they concern entirely different functions: GDPR supervisory authorities must issue a final decision within one month after an EDPB notification, while CSIRTs must monitor and analyse national cyber threats, vulnerabilities and incidents and assist entities on request. No text indicates that performing one duty prevents or delays performance of the other.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The duties have different actors, subject matters, triggers and procedures. A supervisory authority can issue the required GDPR decision while a CSIRT performs cyber-threat monitoring and, if requested, provides assistance; neither provision regulates the other's deadline or content.

verdict.shared_subject: Processing and disclosure of personal data by a controller
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A removes the prohibition on processing special-category personal data only in specified circumstances, while Provision B requires the controller to provide information when personal data are first disclosed to another recipient. If the data are special-category data and the disclosure is not covered by one of A's listed exceptions, the disclosure-related processing may be prohibited even though B requires the information to be provided.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision B concerns transparency information when disclosure to another recipient is contemplated; it does not itself authorise disclosure or processing of the data. A controller can comply with both by disclosing only where an applicable exception to the special-category processing prohibition exists, and then providing the required information at the prescribed time.
verdict.decisive_exception: Not needed for the compatibility verdict; whether a particular disclosure is lawful depends on the applicable legal basis and exceptions, but Provision B does not purport to override Provision A.

verdict.shared_subject: Regulatory compliance and dealings with authorities concerning high-risk AI systems and potentially high-risk personal-data processing
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions can involve a high-risk activity and require engagement with authorities, so an operator may need to satisfy both GDPR prior consultation and the AI Act representative's documentation and cooperation duties. However, neither provision requires an action that prevents compliance with the other: consultation under Article 36 and retaining or supplying conformity documents under Article 22 are distinct obligations.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Article 36 requires the controller to consult the supervisory authority before processing where a DPIA shows an unmitigated high risk. Article 22(b) requires an authorised representative to keep specified AI-compliance documents available for ten years; the duties concern different actors, triggers, and subject matter and can be performed cumulatively without contradiction.

verdict.shared_subject: Notification to data subjects after a personal-data breach
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires the provider to notify the affected person immediately when the breach is likely to have adverse consequences for that person's privacy. Provision B says notification is not required in specified circumstances, including appropriate protective measures, effective remedial measures, or disproportionate effort, so the same breach could appear to trigger A while being exempt under B.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can be read as cumulative rules: A establishes a notification duty for breaches likely to have adverse privacy consequences, while B supplies exceptions or alternative measures governing when that notification is unnecessary. In particular, B's exceptions may be understood as qualifying the notification obligation rather than creating an unavoidable contradiction.
verdict.concrete_scenario: A provider suffers a breach involving a person's personal data that is likely to have adverse consequences for that person's privacy, so A requires immediate notification, but the controller has taken appropriate technical and organisational measures that make the affected data unintelligible to unauthorised persons, so B says the notification is not required.
verdict.decisive_exception: Whether the exceptions in Article 34(3), especially the condition that appropriate protective measures made the data unintelligible, legally qualify or override the separate notification duty in Article 11.3a, and whether the Article 34 exception is satisfied on the facts.

verdict.shared_subject: ICT and personal-data security practices
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A makes notification to the data subject unnecessary when appropriate technical and organisational measures, such as encryption, were applied to the affected personal data. Provision B requires an ICT test programme containing appropriate tests, including vulnerability assessments and penetration tests; one might argue that testing could expose or otherwise affect the protected data or security measures relevant to A.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different, independently satisfiable requirements: A concerns whether a personal-data-breach notification to the data subject is required after protective measures were applied, while B concerns testing ICT tools and systems. Conducting the required tests does not require withholding notification, and applying protective measures does not prevent conducting the tests.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions impose obligations connected with regulated digital or data-governance activities and refer to competent authorities. One might therefore initially suspect that an entity’s post-incident evaluation could overlap with certification-related reporting.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different duties on different actors and concern different subject matters: certification bodies must notify authorities of certification decisions, while financial entities must conduct post-incident ICT evaluations. Compliance with one does not prevent compliance with the other, and neither provision limits or overrides the other.
verdict.evidence_span_a: De in lid 1 bedoelde certificeringsorganen stellen de bevoegde toezichthoudende autoriteiten op de hoogte van de redenen voor het afgeven of het intrekken van het aangevraagde certificaat.

verdict.shared_subject: Processing special-category personal data in connection with AI systems that infer emotions at work or in education
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A prohibits processing data revealing, among other things, health data and biometric data, while provision B prohibits using an AI system to infer emotions at work or in education, subject to a medical or safety-related exception. An emotion-inference system could process health or biometric data, so both prohibitions may apply to the same deployment; however, B's exception does not itself establish that the processing satisfies an exception to A.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions regulate different conduct: A concerns processing specified categories of personal data, whereas B concerns placing on the market, putting into service, or using an AI system for emotion inference. A system could be prohibited under B without processing special-category data, and any processing covered by A may independently need to satisfy A's exceptions. The rules can therefore be complied with cumulatively, unless the medical or safety purpose is shown to provide a valid legal basis under A.
verdict.concrete_scenario: A hospital deploys at a workplace or school an AI system that infers a person's emotions from biometric or health-related data for a medical or safety-related purpose. The deployment falls within B's stated exception to its emotion-inference prohibition, but the processing remains within A's prohibition unless a separate Article 9(2) exception and any applicable safeguards are established.
verdict.decisive_exception: Whether the medical or safety-related purpose in provision B satisfies one of provision A's exceptions to its prohibition, such as the necessity and legal-basis requirements in Article 9(2), points h or i, is not established by the provisions shown.

verdict.shared_subject: Incident and personal-data-breach notification obligations
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires an essential or important entity to give its CSIRT and competent authority an early warning within 24 hours of learning of a significant incident. Provision B says communication to affected data subjects is not required where appropriate protective measures, such as encryption, were applied, so the same security event may trigger an authority warning while exempting communication to individuals.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different duties on different recipients: A concerns an early warning to a CSIRT and competent authority, whereas B concerns communication to data subjects. The encryption-based exception in B removes only the data-subject communication duty and does not prohibit or excuse the authority-facing warning required by A; both can therefore be complied with cumulatively.

verdict.shared_subject: Enforcement powers and sanctions for regulatory non-compliance
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern enforcement consequences, but they regulate different authorities, addressees, and legal regimes. One permits the Dutch data-protection authority to impose an administrative fine for specified financial-supervision violations, while the other obliges the lead overseer to consult within the JON when determining a coercive-fine amount; neither text says that one sanction excludes or limits the other.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can plainly operate cumulatively: the AP's competence to impose an administrative fine under the financial-supervision legislation is distinct from the lead overseer's obligation to consult concerning a coercive fine imposed on a critical ICT third-party provider under DORA. They have different actors, triggers, sanction types, and scopes, so compliance with both presents no contradiction.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A gives a Dutch court broad competence to regulate the consequences of suspending board members, while provision B obliges a notifying authority to take appropriate measures against possible risks to health, safety or fundamental rights. One might argue that court-ordered consequences could affect an authority’s ability to take those measures, but neither text makes the court’s competence or the authority’s duty exclusive or incompatible.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions concern different actors, subject matters and triggers: A concerns a court’s ancillary arrangements following suspension of board members, whereas B concerns measures by a notifying authority after a designation is restricted, suspended or withdrawn. Both can be complied with independently, and A does not prohibit the measures required by B.

verdict.shared_subject: Handling and communicating cybersecurity-related information
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: CSIRTs must disseminate warnings, notifications and information about cyber threats, vulnerabilities and incidents to entities, authorities and other stakeholders, potentially in near real time. Separately, notifying authorities must ensure that information obtained under Article 78 is kept confidential; if the information to be disseminated is information obtained under Article 78, disclosure could appear to conflict with confidentiality.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose duties on different actors and do not establish that the CSIRT’s information is information obtained under Article 78. The CSIRT duty can therefore be performed while notifying authorities preserve the confidentiality of Article 78 information, for example by sharing only information not covered by that confidentiality obligation or by applying any applicable confidentiality-preserving procedures.
verdict.missing_reference: The provision establishing what information is obtained under Article 78 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, including whether it covers the cybersecurity warnings, notifications or information that a CSIRT must disseminate and whether an exception permits that disclosure.
verdict.decisive_exception: Whether Article 78 information may be disclosed or disseminated despite the confidentiality duty in Article 45.

verdict.shared_subject: Processing special-category personal data to detect and correct bias in high-risk AI systems that may also make solely automated decisions significantly affecting individuals.
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision B expressly permits exceptional processing of special-category personal data for bias detection and correction, while Provision A protects individuals against solely automated decisions with legal or similarly significant effects. If the bias-detection processing is part of making such a decision, it could appear to facilitate a practice that Provision A prohibits. However, the texts do not establish that the permitted data processing itself constitutes, or necessarily leads to, a prohibited automated decision.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions regulate different acts: A concerns subjecting a person to a solely automated significant decision, whereas B concerns exceptional processing of special-category data for bias detection in certain high-risk AI systems. The processing in B can be used to improve or monitor a system without making a prohibited decision, and A's own exceptions and Article 9 safeguards may also be relevant.
verdict.concrete_scenario: A provider of a high-risk AI system processes health or ethnic-origin data under Article 10 to detect and correct bias, while the system is used to make solely automated decisions that have significant effects on individuals. Article 10 permits the sensitive-data processing subject to its safeguards, but Article 22 prohibits subjecting affected individuals to the automated decisions unless an Article 22(2) exception applies; the shown texts do not establish whether that exception applies to this use.
verdict.decisive_exception: Whether the Article 22(2) exceptions apply—particularly whether the automated decision is authorised by Union or Member State law with appropriate safeguards, necessary for a contract, or based on explicit consent—and, for special-category data, whether GDPR Article 9(2)(a) or (g) applies with appropriate safeguards. Provision B itself does not establish that these exceptions are satisfied.

verdict.shared_subject: Processing personal data in AI-based biometric categorisation
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A regulates further processing of personal data by requiring a compatibility assessment, including consideration of the data’s nature and safeguards. Provision B prohibits a particular AI use—biometric categorisation to infer highly sensitive traits—so a processing operation might satisfy A’s compatibility factors yet still be prohibited by B.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different, cumulative requirements rather than contradictory commands: GDPR Article 6 may govern the lawfulness assessment for a further purpose, while Article 5 independently prohibits the specified AI practice. Compliance with Article 6 does not authorise conduct prohibited by Article 5, and Article 5 does not prevent compliance with Article 6 for processing outside its defined prohibition.
verdict.decisive_exception: None is needed to classify the provisions as compatible. Whether a particular processing operation is lawful under GDPR also depends on the applicable Article 6(1) legal basis and potentially other provisions, while Article 5 independently determines whether the specified AI practice is prohibited.

verdict.shared_subject: Access to a public-sector information-society service and ICT/data security
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A prohibits making access to a public-law entity’s service conditional on consent, while Provision B requires financial entities to use ICT processes that prevent loss, unauthorised access, and confidentiality breaches. One might argue that requiring consent for certain access-related data processing could support security or confidentiality, but B does not expressly require consent and applies to a different class of actor.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions regulate different matters and actors: A concerns consent as a condition for user access to a service supplied by or on behalf of a public-law legal person, whereas B imposes ICT-security duties on financial entities. A financial entity can comply with B through technical and organisational safeguards that do not make service access dependent on consent, and the texts do not establish that the same actor or processing activity is covered by both.

verdict.shared_subject: Processing special-category personal data in connection with prohibited AI practices
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A prohibits processing data revealing, among other things, racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religious or philosophical beliefs, trade-union membership, genetic or biometric data for unique identification, health data, and sexual-behaviour or sexual-orientation data. Provision B prohibits a particular AI practice—criminal-risk assessment based exclusively on profiling or personality assessment—but does not itself regulate whether special-category data may be processed; therefore, an AI system could fall within B while A independently prohibits its data processing.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different prohibitions with different objects: A concerns processing specified categories of personal data, while B concerns placing on the market, putting into service, or using a specified AI system for criminal-risk assessment. An operator can comply with both by not processing the data prohibited by A and not using the AI practice prohibited by B; neither provision requires conduct forbidden by the other.

verdict.shared_subject: Processing of personal data, including special categories of personal data, in high-risk processing or AI systems
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires a controller to conduct a data-protection impact assessment before processing that is likely to create a high risk to natural persons’ rights and freedoms. Provision B, while permitting exceptional processing of special-category data for bias detection and correction under stated conditions, prohibits sending, transferring, or otherwise making that data accessible to other parties; a bias-detection arrangement involving another party could therefore make the permitted processing operationally difficult or impossible.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different, cumulative requirements rather than contradictory commands: the controller can perform the required impact assessment while complying with the restrictions on special-category data. Provision A does not require disclosure or transfer of data, and Provision B expressly frames its permission as subject to the GDPR and additional safeguards, so the impact-assessment duty does not override the prohibition.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires Member States’ authorities to notify the DORA oversight forum when exercising supervisory and enforcement powers concerning a critical ICT third-party provider. Provision B requires financial entities, before contracting for ICT services, to identify and assess conflicts of interest. One might argue that supervisory involvement under A could affect or constrain the entity’s contracting assessment under B, but A does not regulate that assessment or prescribe a conflicting outcome.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different, cumulative duties on different actors and at different stages: A concerns cooperation and notification by national competent authorities during supervision or enforcement, while B concerns a financial entity’s pre-contractual identification and assessment of conflicts of interest. verdict.shared_subject: Cross-border mutual assistance between competent authorities concerning regulated entities

Provision B imposes mutual-assistance cooperation where an entity operates across Member States and requires the requested authority to provide assistance proportionate to its resources, so one might initially see a discretionary request mechanism in A alongside a mandatory assistance regime in B.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can operate cumulatively: A identifies a national-law competence to request assistance for specified categories of entities, while B supplies the EU-wide cooperation framework and duties when its cross-border conditions are met. A's 'kan ... verzoeken' concerns whether and for whom a request may be made; it does not prohibit or displace B's obligation to provide proportionate assistance, and B itself preserves refusal grounds where the requested authority is not competent, the request is disproportionate, or essential national interests are implicated.

verdict.shared_subject: Regulatory compliance and oversight of high-risk AI systems involving personal-data processing
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern oversight of potentially high-risk processing or AI systems, so an operator may need to engage with authorities under both regimes. However, Article 36 requires the controller to consult a supervisory authority before processing only when the DPIA indicates high residual risk absent mitigation, while Article 22 requires an authorised representative to perform mandate-specific compliance and authority-cooperation tasks; neither duty prevents compliance with the other.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different, cumulative duties on different actors and at different triggers. The controller can conduct the GDPR prior consultation, while the authorised representative performs the AI Act mandate tasks and cooperates with market-surveillance authorities; nothing in either text makes one duty substitute for or prohibit the other.

verdict.shared_subject: Regulatory compliance and information supplied to authorities for high-risk AI systems involving personal-data processing
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions can involve the same high-risk AI deployment and contacts with public authorities. One requires the controller to consult the data-protection supervisory authority before processing where a DPIA indicates unmitigated high risk, while the other requires an authorised representative, on a reasoned request, to provide documentation demonstrating compliance with the AI Act; this could create parallel regulatory interactions, but neither text makes the duties incompatible.

An actor can comply with both by consulting the supervisory authority when Article 36 is triggered and providing the requested AI documentation under Article 22.

verdict.shared_subject: Processing activities involving special-category personal data and their documentation

Provision B obliges a processor to maintain a register covering all processing activities, which could include such processing, but the registration duty does not itself authorise or require the underlying processing.

Registering an activity is documentation, not permission to conduct it, so compliance with B does not displace A.

verdict.shared_subject: ICT-risk-management duties for certain exempt financial entities and instructions for users of high-risk AI systems
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A removes Articles 5–15 of DORA from applying to specified small or exempt financial entities, while Provision B requires high-risk AI systems to be accompanied by clear and accessible instructions for deployers. One might argue that an exempt financial entity using a high-risk AI system is relieved from the broader DORA requirements that could otherwise support or document ICT-risk management, while still facing the AI Act instruction duty.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different duties on different subjects and concern different matters: A is a scope exclusion plus a simplified ICT-risk-management framework for specified financial entities, whereas B requires providers of high-risk AI systems to supply instructions to deployers. Nothing in A prohibits, disapplies, or substitutes for the AI Act duty, and the duties can be complied with cumulatively where applicable.

verdict.shared_subject: Cooperation and information handling by public cybersecurity authorities
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires competent authorities handling personal-data-breach incidents to exchange all necessary data, including personal data, with the Dutch data-protection authority. Provision B requires the coordinating CSIRT to guarantee the anonymity of a person or legal entity reporting a vulnerability; if the same report is both a vulnerability report and a personal-data-breach incident, disclosure of the reporter’s identity could appear inconsistent with that anonymity duty.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions address different functions and can be complied with cumulatively: authorities may exchange necessary incident data under A while the coordinating CSIRT preserves the reporter’s anonymity under B, for example by sharing the incident details without identifying the reporter. Neither text expressly requires A’s data exchange to include the reporter’s identity or states that B’s anonymity guarantee is overridden.

verdict.shared_subject: ICT-risk governance and supervision involving financial entities, ICT third-party providers, and potentially critical entities
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires Member States and their competent authorities to cooperate with DORA authorities and notify the oversight forum when exercising supervisory and enforcement powers concerning a critical ICT third-party provider. Provision B requires financial entities to manage third-party ICT risk within their ICT-risk-management framework and remain fully responsible for compliance. One might argue that overlapping supervision and responsibility could create coordination or accountability friction.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different, cumulative duties on different actors: A concerns Member States and competent authorities exercising supervision, while B concerns financial entities managing their own third-party ICT risk. A's cooperation and notification duty does not prohibit or displace the financial entity's continuing responsibility, and B does not restrict supervisory cooperation under A; both can therefore be complied with simultaneously.

verdict.shared_subject: Protection and security of personal/data systems
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A allows the provider to avoid notifying a personal-data breach when appropriate technical safeguards make the data unintelligible to unauthorised persons. Provision B requires certain financial entities to use resilient, up-to-date ICT systems and adequately protect data confidentiality, so one might argue that the security measures relevant to A overlap with B's ICT-protection duty.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different, cumulative rules rather than incompatible commands. A concerns an exception to a breach-notification duty, conditioned on the data being encrypted or otherwise unintelligible; B requires an entity-level ICT-risk-management and data-protection standard, but does not require notification or prohibit reliance on A's exception. Compliance with B therefore does not itself establish that A's notification exception is satisfied, and failure to satisfy A's condition does not conflict with B.

verdict.shared_subject: The handling of information by critical third-party ICT service providers and the processing/access of special-category personal data by providers of high-risk AI systems.
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires representatives of critical third-party ICT service providers to provide requested information, while provision B prohibits special-category personal data from being transmitted, transferred, or otherwise accessed by other parties. If the requested information includes such data and must be supplied to another party, A could appear to require conduct that B prohibits. However, A does not expressly require disclosure of special-category personal data, and the provisions apply to differently defined actors and contexts.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision A can be complied with by providing the requested information without disclosing special-category personal data, or by applying any applicable legal basis and safeguards outside the text shown. Provision B concerns a specific prohibition within the exceptional processing regime for high-risk AI systems, whereas A concerns information requests to critical third-party ICT service providers; the texts do not establish that the requested information must contain the protected data or that the same actor is subject to both rules in the relevant capacity.
verdict.concrete_scenario: A critical third-party ICT service provider that is also acting as a provider of a high-risk AI system receives an information request requiring it to transmit a report containing identifiable health or biometric data to another party. A requires the requested information to be provided, while B states that the special-category data must not be transmitted, transferred, or otherwise accessed by other parties.

verdict.shared_subject: High-risk AI-system processing of personal data and the associated compliance duties
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions may apply to the same high-risk AI system: the GDPR controller must conduct a data-protection impact assessment before processing where the processing is likely to create a high risk, while the AI Act authorised representative must perform the mandate tasks concerning conformity documentation and cooperation with authorities. One might argue that the AI Act’s conformity-focused mandate does not expressly require the representative to ensure that a GDPR impact assessment is performed, creating uncertainty about whether the AI Act compliance process covers that assessment.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different, cumulative duties on different actors and do not require incompatible conduct. The controller can perform the GDPR impact assessment, while the authorised representative carries out the mandate tasks and supplies or checks the AI Act documentation; neither provision says that compliance with one substitutes for or prevents compliance with the other.
