verdict.shared_subject: Conformiteitscontrole van hoog-risico-AI-systemen door aangemelde instanties
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Artikel 34 verwijst naar de conformiteitsbeoordelingsprocedures van artikel 43, terwijl artikel 43 de controlebevoegdheid van bepaalde aangemelde instanties conditioneert op een beoordeling van naleving van artikel 31, leden 4, 10 en 11. Men zou daarom kunnen aanvoeren dat artikel 34 een algemene controleplicht formuleert zonder die aanvullende voorwaarde.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: De bepalingen vullen elkaar aan: artikel 34 legt de operationele controleplicht vast, en artikel 43 bepaalt welke procedure en, voor de daarin bedoelde aangemelde instanties, welke voorwaarden voor die controle gelden. De verwijzing in artikel 34 naar artikel 43 maakt het mogelijk beide bepalingen cumulatief toe te passen; er is geen onverenigbare verplichting of verbod.
verdict.evidence_span_a: Aangemelde instanties controleren de conformiteit van AI-systemen met een hoog risico overeenkomstig de conformiteitsbeoordelingsprocedures van artikel 43.
verdict.evidence_span_b: Voor die beoordeling hebben aangemelde instanties die volgens die rechtshandelingen zijn aangemeld het recht de conformiteit van de AI-systemen met een hoog risico met de in afdeling 2 beschreven voorschriften te controleren, mits de overeenstemming van die aangemelde instanties met voorschriften van artikel 31, leden 4, 10 en 11, in de context van de aanmeldingsprocedure volgens die rechtshandelingen is beoordeeld.

verdict.shared_subject: The controller’s duty to adopt appropriate technical and organisational measures for GDPR-compliant processing and protection of data subjects’ rights.
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions impose a closely related measures duty, but Article 25 adds design/default-setting requirements and expressly directs that measures implement principles such as data minimisation and safeguards. One might therefore argue that Article 24’s general, risk-based accountability benchmark and Article 25’s technology- and design-oriented benchmark leave uncertainty about which measures are sufficient.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The duties are cumulative and expressly compatible: Article 24 requires measures that ensure and demonstrate compliance, while Article 25 specifies that appropriate measures must be taken both when determining processing means and during processing, to implement GDPR principles and safeguards. A controller can satisfy both by adopting and documenting measures that meet both provisions; neither text says that compliance with one substitutes for the other.

verdict.evidence_span_b: treft de verwerkingsverantwoordelijke, zowel bij de bepaling van de verwerkingsmiddelen als bij de verwerking zelf, passende technische en organisatorische maatregelen, zoals pseudonimisering, die zijn opgesteld met als doel de gegevensbeschermingsbeginselen, zoals minimale gegevensverwerking, op een doeltreffende manier uit te voeren en de nodige waarborgen in de verwerking in te bouwen ter naleving van de voorschriften van deze verordening en ter bescherming van de rechten van de betrokkenen.

verdict.shared_subject: AI-systemen met een hoog risico en beoordeling van risico’s voor grondrechten
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires a data-protection impact assessment before processing where the processing is likely to create a high risk to natural persons’ rights and freedoms. Provision B requires another notified body to assume immediate responsibility and complete its assessment within twelve months after withdrawal of the designation, while the certificate remains valid only under specified confirmations; these are different assessment duties and do not state how they interact.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose cumulative duties on different actors and for different regulatory purposes: A concerns the controller’s GDPR data-protection impact assessment before processing, whereas B concerns a notified body’s certification assessment and the continued validity of an AI-system certificate. Compliance with B does not purport to replace A, and compliance with A does not prevent the notified body from performing B’s assessment.
verdict.evidence_span_a: voert de verwerkingsverantwoordelijke vóór de verwerking een beoordeling uit van het effect van de beoogde verwerkingsactiviteiten op de bescherming van persoonsgegevens
verdict.evidence_span_b: een andere aangemelde instantie schriftelijk heeft bevestigd dat zij de onmiddellijke verantwoordelijkheid voor deze AI-systemen op zich neemt en haar beoordeling binnen twaalf maanden na intrekking van de aanwijzing afrondt

verdict.shared_subject: Significante cyberdreigingen en de daaropvolgende informatieverstrekking
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A concerns forwarding a voluntary notification of a significant cyber threat to another competent authority, while Provision B requires the essential or important entity itself to inform potentially affected service recipients. If the same threat triggers both duties, they involve different recipients and separate communications, so forwarding the authority notification would not inform the service recipients.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The duties can readily be performed cumulatively: the entity may voluntarily report the threat to the competent authority and, where necessary, separately inform affected service recipients about protective measures and the threat. Moreover, A is expressly voluntary, so an entity that does not make that optional notification faces no conflict with B.
verdict.evidence_span_a: De lidstaten kunnen bepalen dat de financiële entiteiten die overeenkomstig de eerste alinea op vrijwillige basis kennisgeving doen, die kennisgeving ook kunnen doorsturen naar de overeenkomstig Richtlijn (EU) 2022/2555 aangewezen of ingestelde CSIRT’s.
verdict.evidence_span_b: De essentiële entiteit of belangrijke entiteit deelt de ontvangers van haar diensten, die mogelijkerwijs door een significante cyberdreiging in relatie tot het ontvangen van die diensten worden getroffen, onverwijld mee welke maatregelen die ontvangers kunnen nemen in reactie op die dreiging.

verdict.shared_subject: Cybersecurity information and ICT-incident analysis
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A facilitates voluntary information exchange about cyber threats, incidents and vulnerabilities, while Provision B obliges financial entities to analyse the frequency, types, scale and evolution of ICT-related incidents. One might argue that sharing incident information could create confidentiality or operational burdens while the entity is carrying out its analysis, or that the provisions point toward different information-handling practices.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision A requires Member States to enable voluntary inter-entity cybersecurity information exchange, subject to specified purposes; it does not require any particular entity to disclose information. Provision B independently requires financial entities to analyse ICT-related incidents and their patterns. An entity can perform that analysis and, if it chooses to participate in an exchange, share relevant information in a manner consistent with both provisions; the texts contain no incompatible deadline, content requirement, prohibition, or substitute benchmark.
verdict.evidence_span_a: op vrijwillige basis onderling relevante informatie over cyberbeveiliging kunnen uitwisselen
verdict.evidence_span_b: Zij inventariseren de ontwikkeling van ICT-risico’s in de tijd, analyseren de frequentie, de types, de omvang en de evolutie van ICT-gerelateerde incidenten

verdict.shared_subject: Incident reporting by entities subject to both DORA and the Dutch NIS2 implementation rules
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions require incident-related reporting by an entity that may fall within both regimes, but they identify different reporting recipients and potentially different clocks. A single incident could therefore require a DORA updated notification to the relevant competent authority and a separate NIS2 final report to both the CSIRT and the competent authority; filing one does not, on the text shown, discharge the other.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The duties can be performed cumulatively: the entity can submit the DORA updated notification within the Article 20 deadlines and submit the NIS2 final report within one month after the Article 27 notification. Nothing in either provision forbids the other filing or states that the reports are mutually exclusive, and the reports concern different stages and content.
verdict.concrete_scenario: A financial entity is also an essential or important entity and suffers one incident that triggers both regimes. After its initial DORA notification, the incident status materially changes, requiring an updated notification to “de relevante bevoegde autoriteit” within the Article 20 deadlines, while the same incident also requires a final report no later than one month after the Article 27 notification, submitted “bij haar CSIRT en haar bevoegde autoriteit.” The entity must make both filings; the DORA filing to the competent authority does not, on the text shown, satisfy the separate CSIRT filing or the distinct final-report duty.
verdict.decisive_exception: None is established in the provisions shown. The decisive point is whether the two regimes contain an unshown coordination rule treating one report as sufficient or harmonising the triggers and deadlines; absent such a rule, the different recipients and report stages support cumulative reporting.

verdict.shared_subject: ICT- and personal-data incidents involving financial entities
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires notification of a qualifying personal-data breach to the competent supervisory authority within 72 hours where possible. Provision B requires financial entities to register all ICT-related incidents and establish processes for monitoring, treatment, follow-up, and documenting and removing root causes; a single incident may therefore trigger both notification and internal registration/remediation duties.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different, cumulative duties rather than conflicting ones: A is an external notification duty to a specified supervisory authority, while B is an internal incident-management and documentation duty with no reporting recipient or deadline. Registering and investigating an incident does not purport to replace the notification required by A, and notifying the authority does not prevent compliance with B.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions impose obligations within EU digital regulation, but they govern different actors and actions: Provision A concerns the ESAs’ technical standards and consideration of SME resources, while Provision B concerns conformity-assessment bodies submitting an application to a notifying authority. Nothing in the shown text makes compliance with one obligation prevent compliance with the other.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The obligations are fully compatible because they apply to different actors and regulate different conduct. The ESAs can account for SMEs’ ability to mobilise resources while conformity-assessment bodies independently submit their notification applications to the competent authority.
verdict.evidence_span_a: Voor de toepassing van de criteria van artikel 4, lid 2, houden de ETA’s er terdege rekening mee dat micro-ondernemingen en kleine en middelgrote ondernemingen voldoende middelen en capaciteit moeten kunnen mobiliseren om ICT-gerelateerde incidenten snel onder controle te krijgen.

verdict.shared_subject: Informing service recipients about significant incidents affecting service provision
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions impose an immediate notification duty on the same type of essential or important entity and refer to notifying the entity’s service recipients. One might argue that they create two separately sourced notification obligations, potentially requiring duplicate notices. However, neither text identifies different recipients, content, or reporting channels.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions are substantively identical: both require the entity, where appropriate, to inform its service recipients without delay of significant incidents that may adversely affect service provision. A single notification to those recipients satisfies both duties; the texts do not require separate filings or distinguish the obligations by recipient or deadline.
verdict.evidence_span_a: In voorkomend geval stellen de betrokken entiteiten de ontvangers van hun diensten onverwijld in kennis van significante incidenten die een nadelige invloed kunnen hebben op de verlening van die diensten.

verdict.shared_subject: Incident-reporting obligations for entities operating high-risk AI systems
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: A significant incident involving a high-risk AI system may trigger both provisions. Provision A requires reporting to the CSIRT or competent authority within specified deadlines, while provision B requires immediate sequential notification to the provider, importer or distributor, and market-surveillance authorities; the duties therefore impose cumulative reporting to different recipients and on different clocks.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can both be obeyed: the operator can make the NIS2 early warning and incident report to the CSIRT or competent authority while separately notifying the AI Act recipients. Neither provision forbids the other notification, and the different reporting channels make the obligations complementary rather than mutually impossible.
verdict.concrete_scenario: A company operating a high-risk AI system discovers a significant incident that is also a serious incident under Article 26. Within 24 hours it must give the NIS2 early warning to “het CSIRT of, indien van toepassing, de bevoegde autoriteit” and submit the required incident report within 72 hours, while Article 26 requires it to notify “eerst de aanbieder hiervan, en vervolgens de importeur of distributeur en de betreffende markttoezichtautoriteiten” immediately. Reporting to the CSIRT or competent authority does not itself notify the provider, importer/distributor, or market-surveillance authorities, so both reporting tracks must be completed.

verdict.evidence_span_b: Wanneer de gebruiksverantwoordelijke een ernstig incident vaststellen, stellen zij ook onmiddellijk eerst de aanbieder hiervan in kennis, en vervolgens de importeur of distributeur en de betreffende markttoezichtautoriteiten van dat incident.

verdict.shared_subject: Compliance obligations for high-risk AI systems and processing that presents a high data-protection risk
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions can apply to the same project, but they impose different obligations triggered by different assessments: Article 36 requires prior consultation only where a DPIA identifies high residual risk absent mitigation, while Article 16 requires providers to ensure compliance with the AI Act’s high-risk-system requirements. The texts do not state that satisfying the AI Act obligations removes the GDPR consultation duty or that consultation substitutes for AI Act compliance.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The obligations are cumulative and readily satisfiable: an operator can ensure that its high-risk AI system complies with the AI Act and, if its DPIA shows the specified high risk, consult the supervisory authority before processing. They concern different duties, triggers, and regulatory regimes, with no incompatible command or prohibition.

verdict.shared_subject: Reporting incidents involving a financial entity and potentially affected individuals
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions can be triggered by the same underlying event, but they require separate notifications to different recipients: the competent authority under A and the affected person under B. The financial entity therefore cannot satisfy B by filing A, or satisfy A by notifying the individual; it must make both notifications, potentially on different clocks.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The duties are individually satisfiable and concern different recipients and purposes: regulatory incident reporting versus informing the person whose privacy is likely adversely affected. Nothing in either text prohibits the other notification or makes one substitute for the other.
verdict.concrete_scenario: A financial entity suffers a serious ICT-related incident that is also a personal-data breach likely to have adverse effects on an identifiable person's privacy. It must submit the updated notification to “bij de relevante bevoegde autoriteit” within the Article 20 deadlines and separately notify “degene wiens persoonsgegevens het betreft” “onverwijld”; filing with the authority does not notify the affected person, and notifying that person does not discharge the regulatory filing.

verdict.shared_subject: Reporting incidents that may involve both a personal-data breach and a significant incident affecting services
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: A personal-data breach that is also a significant incident triggers two reporting duties for the same entity. Article 33 requires reporting to the competent data-protection supervisory authority, while Article 23 requires reporting to the entity’s CSIRT or, where applicable, competent authority; these are distinct regimes and recipients, so one filing does not necessarily discharge the other.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The duties can be complied with cumulatively: the entity can report the same incident to both designated recipients, without any textual impossibility. Article 23 also provides for forwarding from the competent authority to the CSIRT, which could reduce duplication within that regime, although it does not state that such reporting replaces the Article 33 notification.
verdict.concrete_scenario: An essential entity suffers a cyberattack that both constitutes a personal-data breach posing a likely risk to individuals and causes a serious operational disruption to its services. The entity must notify the Article 55 competent supervisory authority within 72 hours where possible and, separately, report the significant incident without delay to its CSIRT or applicable competent authority; reporting to one recipient does not, on the text shown, discharge the other duty.
verdict.decisive_exception: Whether the same national authority or an implementing or transposing rule treats one notification as satisfying both regimes is not established, but Article 33 and Article 23 as shown prescribe different reporting regimes and do not contain such a substitution rule.
verdict.evidence_span_a: meldt de verwerkingsverantwoordelijke deze zonder onredelijke vertraging en, indien mogelijk, uiterlijk 72 uur nadat hij er kennis van heeft genomen, aan de overeenkomstig artikel 55 bevoegde toezichthoudende autoriteit

verdict.shared_subject: Bevoegdheid van bevoegde autoriteiten om waarschuwingen te geven over inbreuken op Richtlijn (EU) 2022/2555
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Beide bepalingen formuleren een bevoegdheid om waarschuwingen te geven, maar koppelen die aan verschillende categorieën entiteiten: essentiële entiteiten in artikel 32 en belangrijke entiteiten in artikel 33. Men zou kunnen aanvoeren dat een entiteit die onder beide categorieën valt, of waarvan de classificatie onzeker is, onder twee regimes met verschillende reikwijdte valt.

Dat is een verschil in toepassingsgebied en geen onverenigbare verplichting; dezelfde autoriteit kan beide bevoegdheden cumulatief uitoefenen wanneer de respectieve voorwaarden zijn vervuld.

verdict.shared_subject: High-risk AI systems involving personal-data processing
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions impose an assessment-related obligation on an operator or provider of a high-risk system, but they concern different assessments with different triggers and purposes. A system may require a GDPR data-protection impact assessment because its processing is likely to create a high risk to natural persons, while also requiring the AI Act conformity-assessment procedure; neither text says that one assessment substitutes for the other.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The obligations are cumulative and can be performed independently: the GDPR assessment addresses risks to personal-data protection, whereas the AI Act provision requires the relevant conformity-assessment procedure for specified high-risk AI systems under listed Union harmonisation legislation. Compliance with both is possible, and the texts do not establish incompatible deadlines, contents, or a rule that one assessment discharges the other.

verdict.shared_subject: Incident reporting and notification following a security or personal-data incident
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: A significant incident may also be a personal-data breach with likely adverse privacy effects. In that case, the entity must submit an incident report to the CSIRT or competent authority within 72 hours, while the provider must separately notify the affected person without delay; the recipients and communications differ, so one notification cannot discharge the other.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The duties can be performed cumulatively without contradiction: the actor can report the significant incident to the CSIRT or competent authority and simultaneously notify the affected data subject. Neither provision forbids the other notification or makes compliance with one a substitute for the other.
verdict.concrete_scenario: A covered provider discovers a significant cyber incident that exposes a customer's personal data and is likely to have adverse effects on that customer's privacy. The provider must submit the incident report to the CSIRT or competent authority within 72 hours and must separately notify the affected customer without delay; notifying the customer does not satisfy the authority-reporting duty, and reporting to the authority does not satisfy the individual notification duty.

verdict.shared_subject: Melding van significante cyberdreigingen of significante incidenten door financiële/essentiële of belangrijke entiteiten
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A concerns a voluntary onward transmission of a cyber-threat notification, ultimately to the ECB for certain significant credit institutions, whereas Provision B imposes a mandatory notification of every significant incident. If the same event is both a voluntarily reported cyber-threat and a significant incident, the texts could appear to involve separate reporting channels and different legal triggers.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: A's norm is expressly voluntary: the financial entity may choose whether to make the initial cyber-threat notification and, for certain institutions, may have it forwarded to the ECB. Provision B independently requires an essential or important entity to report every significant incident under Articles 26–29. The texts therefore impose cumulative but avoidable/independent duties, not incompatible duties; an entity can comply with both, and A does not state that its voluntary notification substitutes for B's mandatory report.
verdict.decisive_exception: None. The decisive point is that A is voluntary and concerns forwarding a notification, while B is a separate mandatory incident-reporting duty; no conflict follows merely because both may concern the same event.

verdict.shared_subject: Reporting a serious incident or security breach involving an AI system or electronic communications service
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions impose notification duties that could be triggered by the same underlying event, but they direct the actor to different recipients: provision A requires notification to the relevant market-surveillance authorities and subsequently to the importer or distributor, while provision B requires immediate notification to the Dutch data-protection authority. The texts do not say that notifying one recipient satisfies the other duty.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can be complied with cumulatively: an actor can notify the data-protection authority immediately under provision B and notify the market-surveillance authorities and importer or distributor under provision A. Moreover, the triggers and actors are not identical, since A concerns users of high-risk AI systems and a serious incident, whereas B concerns providers of public electronic communications services and a security breach affecting personal-data protection.
verdict.concrete_scenario: A provider of a public electronic communications service uses a high-risk AI system and is also its user. A security breach involving that service causes a serious incident affecting the protection of personal data. The actor must notify the Autoriteit persoonsgegevens 'onverwijld' under B, while also notifying the relevant market-surveillance authorities and then the importer or distributor under A; filing with the data-protection authority does not, on the texts shown, discharge the separate notifications required by A.

Men zou kunnen aanvoeren dat onduidelijk is welke bepaling geldt wanneer een entiteit of activiteit aan beide categorieën raakt.

verdict.shared_subject: Supervision and mitigation of risks in regulated entities or AI regulatory sandboxes
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions impose duties involving regulatory oversight and risk mitigation, and both use open-ended standards: authorities must consider the duration of an infringement, while significant health, safety and fundamental-rights risks in an AI sandbox must be adequately mitigated. One might argue that an authority could regard continued testing as justified while mitigation remains incomplete, creating uncertainty about how enforcement considerations interact with the sandbox duty.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions regulate different duties and actors in different contexts. Provision A governs how competent authorities determine enforcement measures against essential entities, including consideration of the duration of an infringement; Provision B requires risks identified during development and testing in AI regulatory sandboxes to be adequately mitigated and permits suspension where effective mitigation is impossible. Both can be complied with cumulatively, and neither exempts an actor from the other duty or establishes competing benchmarks for the same obligation.

verdict.shared_subject: Human oversight of high-risk AI and an individual's right to object to certain personal-data processing
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A gives the data subject an individual right to object and requires the controller to stop processing unless overriding legitimate grounds exist. Provision B requires responsible persons to remain aware of automation bias when relying on high-risk AI output; if that output supports processing based on Article 6(1)(e) or (f), insufficient awareness could undermine proper handling of an objection, creating a possible practical tension between continued AI-supported processing and the individual's objection right.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different, cumulatively satisfiable duties: Article 21 governs the controller's response to an objection, while Article 14(b) concerns human overseers' awareness of automation bias, where appropriate and proportionate. A controller can maintain that awareness and still stop processing when Article 21 requires it, or continue only where it establishes overriding legitimate grounds.
verdict.decisive_exception: Article 21 itself supplies the relevant exception: processing may continue where the controller demonstrates compelling legitimate grounds outweighing the data subject's interests, rights and freedoms, or where processing is needed for legal claims. Nothing in Article 14(b) overrides or substitutes for that assessment.

Provision B requires the CSIRT to monitor and analyse cyber threats, vulnerabilities and incidents nationally; both concern cybersecurity incidents, but they impose different functions on different actors and do not prescribe incompatible conduct.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions are readily cumulative: the competent authority can assess infringement duration during enforcement while the CSIRT independently performs national monitoring and analysis. Neither provision requires an actor to refrain from, or alter, the conduct required by the other.

verdict.shared_subject: Public-authority decision-making and CSIRT incident response
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern governmental action in a telecommunications/cybersecurity context, and an incident could conceivably arise while the Minister is deciding whether to prohibit a transaction. One might therefore ask whether the Minister's decision timetable constrains incident-response activity, or vice versa.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different norms on different actors and address different actions: provision A gives the Minister a procedural competence and timetable for deciding whether to impose a prohibition after a notification, while provision B assigns the CSIRT conditional incident-response tasks. Nothing in either text requires the Minister to refrain from deciding, or the CSIRT to refrain from responding, and the CSIRT duty is not a deadline or content rule incompatible with the Minister's timetable.

verdict.shared_subject: Regulatory powers and the ACM’s number register
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A empowers competent authorities to order cessation of conduct that infringes the regulation, while Provision B requires the ACM to maintain a register containing identifying details of number assignees. In an unusual case, maintaining or disclosing such register information might be viewed as conduct subject to a cessation order, but the texts do not establish that the register duty itself infringes Regulation 2022/2554.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different kinds of rules on different subjects: A grants competent authorities an enforcement power concerning infringements of Regulation 2022/2554, whereas B obliges the ACM to maintain a statutory number register and include specified information. The register duty does not require the ACM to engage in conduct that infringes the Regulation, and A is only a competence to order cessation, not an operative prohibition on maintaining the register.

verdict.shared_subject: Human oversight of high-risk AI processing personal data
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Article 21 GDPR gives the data subject an individual right to object and requires the controller to stop processing unless overriding legitimate grounds or legal-claim grounds exist. Article 14(d) AI Act requires the system to enable human overseers, where appropriate and proportionate, to decide not to use or to override the system’s output; one might argue that this operational intervention could conflict with continuing processing based on an asserted legitimate ground, or that the AI Act’s system-level capability does not itself ensure the GDPR right is honoured.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose cumulative and compatible requirements: a controller must respect an applicable objection and stop processing unless the GDPR exception applies, while the AI system must provide human overseers with the capability to disregard or stop using its output where appropriate and proportionate. Article 14 does not require continued processing or prohibit stopping it, and Article 21 does not prohibit human oversight or intervention.

verdict.shared_subject: Reporting or notifying authorities about legally relevant events
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A concerns a voluntary notification by financial entities of significant cyber threats, with onward transmission by the competent authority; provision B concerns advance notification of cable-maintenance works on public land and, where applicable, onward notification to the mayor. If the same actor and event somehow fell within both regimes, the notifications would concern different subject matters and authorities, so one would not discharge the other.

verdict.shared_subject: Incident reporting by entities subject to both provisions
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires the provider to notify the Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens immediately of a qualifying security breach. Provision B requires an essential or important entity to submit a progress report when an incident is still ongoing at the end-report deadline; if the same incident qualifies under both regimes, the texts could impose an immediate notification and a later progress report, with no stated rule that one filing replaces the other.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can both be obeyed because they concern different reporting duties and triggers: A concerns a security breach affecting personal-data protection and requires notification to a named authority, while B concerns an ongoing incident and requires a progress report in place of the end report. Nothing in B says that its progress report is the same filing as A's notification, nor that it discharges A's duty.

It must notify the Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens onverwijld under A and, when the end report would otherwise be due while the incident continues, submit a progress report op dat moment under B; the texts identify no common recipient or substitution rule, so both filings may be required.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions involve competent authorities and protective oversight, but they impose different functions: A requires acknowledgment of a financial entity’s notification, while B requires adequate mitigation of significant health, safety, and fundamental-rights risks in AI regulatory sandboxes. Article 19 requires reporting to the relevant competent authority, while Article 26 requires immediate notification first to the provider and then to the importer or distributor and the relevant market-surveillance authorities.

verdict.shared_subject: Transparency about automated decision-making and human oversight of high-risk AI
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires the controller to inform the data subject about automated decision-making, including useful information about the underlying logic and expected consequences. Provision B requires the high-risk AI system to enable responsible natural persons to understand its capabilities and limitations, monitor its operation, and address irregularities, failures, and unexpected performance; one might argue that these impose different transparency and oversight expectations around the same AI system.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose complementary duties on different aspects of operation: A is an individual information duty owed by a controller to a data subject, while B is a system-design and human-oversight duty concerning users responsible for supervising a high-risk AI system. The texts do not make compliance with one substitute for the other, and both can be satisfied cumulatively by providing the required individual information while also enabling effective human oversight.
verdict.evidence_span_a: g) het bestaan van geautomatiseerde besluitvorming, met inbegrip van de in artikel 22, leden 1 en 4, bedoelde profilering, en, ten minste in die gevallen, nuttige informatie over de onderliggende logica, alsmede het belang en de verwachte gevolgen van die verwerking voor de betrokkene.
verdict.evidence_span_b: a) de relevante capaciteiten en beperkingen van het AI-systeem met een hoog risico goed te begrijpen en de werking ervan naar behoren te kunnen monitoren, onder meer met het oog op het opsporen en aanpakken van onregelmatigheden, storingen en onverwachte prestaties;

verdict.shared_subject: Verplichtingen inzake informatie-uitwisseling en meldingen
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Beide bepalingen gebruiken een verplichtende formulering en kunnen in ruime zin betrekking hebben op informatie over incidenten of telecommunicatiepartijen. Toch legt A een taak op aan het CSIRT-netwerk, terwijl B een voorafgaande melding over een voorgenomen verkrijging van zeggenschap regelt; de vereiste handelingen, actoren en triggers vallen niet samen.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: A verplicht het CSIRT-netwerk tot het uitwisselen van relevante informatie over incidenten, bijna-incidenten, cyberdreigingen, risico’s en kwetsbaarheden. B verplicht degene met een voornemen om overwegende zeggenschap in een telecommunicatiepartij te verkrijgen tot een melding uiterlijk acht weken vooraf, zodat beide verplichtingen naast elkaar kunnen worden nageleefd zonder tegenstrijdige inhoud, termijn of verbod.
verdict.evidence_span_a: het uitwisselen van relevante informatie over incidenten, bijna-incidenten, cyberdreigingen, risico’s en kwetsbaarheden
verdict.evidence_span_b: De melding in het eerste lid wordt gedaan uiterlijk acht weken voor de beoogde datum van uitvoering van dit voornemen.

verdict.shared_subject: CSIRT-taken concerning cyber-threats, vulnerabilities and incidents
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions impose CSIRT duties, and their wording differs slightly: Provision B expressly adds dissemination to the Minister of Economic Affairs, while Provision A refers more generally to competent authorities and relevant stakeholders. One might therefore ask whether the national implementation changes the recipients or scope of the warning-and-information duty.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The specifically selected norm in Provision A is the duty to provide early warnings, notifications and announcements, whereas the specifically selected norm in Provision B is the duty to monitor and analyse cyber-threats, vulnerabilities and incidents. These are complementary CSIRT functions, and nothing in either provision requires the CSIRT to choose between monitoring and issuing warnings or makes one duty incompatible with the other.
verdict.evidence_span_a: b) het verstrekken van vroegtijdige waarschuwingen, meldingen en aankondigingen en het verspreiden van informatie onder betrokken essentiële en belangrijke entiteiten en aan de bevoegde autoriteiten en andere relevante belanghebbenden over cyberdreigingen, kwetsbaarheden en incidenten, in bijna-realtime indien mogelijk;
verdict.evidence_span_b: a. het monitoren en analyseren van cyberdreigingen, kwetsbaarheden en incidenten op nationaal niveau, en het op verzoek verlenen van bijstand aan de betrokken essentiële entiteit of belangrijke entiteit met betrekking tot het realtime of bijna-realtime monitoren van haar netwerk- en informatiesysteem;

verdict.shared_subject: The CSIRT obligation to provide assistance, on request, concerning real-time or near-real-time monitoring of an essential or important entity’s network and information system.
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: The provisions use slightly different formulations: Provision A refers to assistance to “betrokken essentiële en belangrijke entiteiten” and their “netwerk en informatiesystemen,” while Provision B refers to “de betrokken essentiële entiteit of belangrijke entiteit” and “haar netwerk- en informatiesysteem.” One might argue that the singular possessive wording in B could narrow the scope or create uncertainty about whether assistance may cover multiple systems or entities.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Both provisions impose materially the same obligation on the CSIRT: upon request, it must assist an essential or important entity with real-time or near-real-time monitoring of that entity’s network and information system(s). The grammatical differences do not establish incompatible duties, different benchmarks, different recipients, or different conditions; the obligations can plainly be performed together.
verdict.evidence_span_a: op verzoek, het verlenen van bijstand aan betrokken essentiële en belangrijke entiteiten met betrekking tot het realtime of bijna-realtime monitoren van hun netwerk en informatiesystemen
verdict.evidence_span_b: op verzoek verlenen van bijstand aan de betrokken essentiële entiteit of belangrijke entiteit met betrekking tot het realtime of bijna-realtime monitoren van haar netwerk- en informatiesysteem

verdict.shared_subject: Regulatory obligations concerning regulated entities and competent authorities
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions involve supplying information or documentation to authorities, so one might initially see overlapping administrative burdens. However, they concern different actors, different materials, and different regulatory regimes, with no incompatible instruction.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision A requires central securities depositories to provide competent authorities with copies of ICT business-continuity test results or similar exercises. Provision B requires an authorised representative of a provider of a general-purpose AI model to provide a copy of its mandate to the AI Office on request; these duties can plainly be performed cumulatively and do not regulate the same act or document.
verdict.evidence_span_a: Centrale effectenbewaarinstellingen verstrekken de bevoegde autoriteiten kopieën van de resultaten van de ICT-bedrijfscontinuïteitstests of van soortgelijke oefeningen.
verdict.evidence_span_b: Hij legt op verzoek een kopie van het mandaat over aan het AI-bureau, in een van de officiële talen van de instellingen van de Unie.

verdict.shared_subject: Incident reporting by entities providing electronic communications or other essential/important services
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: A requires the provider to notify the Dutch data-protection authority, while B requires an essential or important entity to notify its service recipients. If the same security incident satisfies both triggers, the actor must make two notifications to different recipients, each without delay; notifying one recipient does not notify the other.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can both be complied with because they address different notification recipients and potentially different incident categories. B applies only to significant incidents adversely affecting service provision, whereas A concerns a security breach with adverse consequences for personal-data protection, so an incident may trigger only one duty.
verdict.concrete_scenario: An entity that is both a provider of a public electronic communications service and an essential or important entity suffers one significant security breach that both adversely affects the provision of its services and has adverse consequences for the protection of personal data processed in connection with those services. It must notify the Autoriteit persoonsgegevens without delay under A and separately notify its service recipients without delay under B; either notification alone does not discharge the other duty.
verdict.evidence_span_a: De aanbieder van een openbare elektronische communicatiedienst stelt de Autoriteit persoonsgegevens onverwijld in kennis van een inbreuk op de beveiliging, bedoeld in artikel 11.3, die nadelige gevolgen heeft voor de bescherming van persoonsgegevens die zijn verwerkt in verband met de levering van een openbare elektronische communicatiedienst in de Europese Unie.
verdict.evidence_span_b: De essentiële entiteit of belangrijke entiteit stelt in voorkomend geval onverwijld de ontvangers van haar diensten in kennis van significante incidenten die een nadelige invloed kunnen hebben op de verlening van die diensten.

verdict.shared_subject: Het verstrekken van informatie en meldingen over cyberdreigingen, kwetsbaarheden en incidenten door het CSIRT.
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Artikel 11, onderdeel b, verplicht het CSIRT tot het verspreiden van vroegtijdige waarschuwingen, meldingen en aankondigingen aan onder meer bevoegde autoriteiten, terwijl artikel 40 een specifieke informatieverstrekking aan de bevoegde autoriteit uit de Wet weerbaarheid kritieke entiteiten voorschrijft. Men zou kunnen aanvoeren dat voor dezelfde melding onduidelijk is of de algemene verspreidingsplicht en de specifieke doorgifteplicht verschillende inhoud, ontvangers of procedures vereisen.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: De bepalingen zijn cumulatief verenigbaar: artikel 11 legt een algemene taak op om informatie onder bevoegde autoriteiten te verspreiden, en artikel 40 concretiseert voor een specifieke categorie essentiële entiteiten dat het CSIRT informatie aan een bepaalde bevoegde autoriteit verstrekt. Niets in de teksten verbiedt die specifieke doorgifte of bepaalt dat naleving van de ene plicht de andere uitsluit.
verdict.evidence_span_a: het verstrekken van vroegtijdige waarschuwingen, meldingen en aankondigingen en het verspreiden van informatie onder betrokken essentiële en belangrijke entiteiten en aan de bevoegde autoriteiten en andere relevante belanghebbenden over cyberdreigingen, kwetsbaarheden en incidenten, in bijna-realtime indien mogelijk
verdict.evidence_span_b: Het CSIRT verstrekt de bevoegde autoriteit, bedoeld in artikel 8 van de Wet weerbaarheid kritieke entiteiten, informatie over een incident, bijna-incident of cyberdreiging dat overeenkomstig artikel 33, eerste lid, onderdeel a, is gemeld door een essentiële entiteit die tevens een kritieke entiteit is als bedoeld in de Wet weerbaarheid kritieke entiteiten.

verdict.shared_subject: Cybersecurity incident preparedness and communication
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A obliges CSIRTs to provide early warnings, notifications and announcements about cyber threats, vulnerabilities and incidents. Provision B assigns the Minister competence to establish a national plan for large-scale cybersecurity incidents and crisis response; one might argue that the plan could prescribe a different institutional approach to such communications.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions regulate different functions and actors: A imposes an operational warning and notification task on CSIRTs, while B empowers the Minister to establish a national crisis-response plan. Nothing in B forbids, replaces, or sets incompatible conditions for the CSIRTs’ warning duty, so both can operate cumulatively.
verdict.evidence_span_a: het verstrekken van vroegtijdige waarschuwingen, meldingen en aankondigingen
verdict.evidence_span_b: Onze Minister stelt een nationaal plan voor grootschalige cyberbeveiligingsincidenten en crisisrespons als bedoeld in artikel 9, vierde lid, van de NIS2-richtlijn vast.

verdict.shared_subject: Submission of regulatory drafts to EU-level and national authorities
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions impose submission duties, so one might initially see overlapping obligations concerning regulatory or decision drafts. However, they concern different actors, different documents, and different regulatory procedures, with no incompatible requirement or deadline.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision A requires the ESAs to submit common draft technical regulatory and implementing standards to the Commission. Provision B requires the ACM to submit a draft decision to the Commission and national regulatory authorities; these duties can both be performed independently and cumulatively.
verdict.evidence_span_a: De ETA’s leggen de gemeenschappelijke ontwerpen van technische reguleringsnormen bedoeld in de eerste alinea, punt a), en de gemeenschappelijke ontwerpen van technische uitvoeringsnormen bedoeld in de eerste alinea, punt b), uiterlijk op 17 juli 2024 voor aan de Commissie.
verdict.evidence_span_b: De Autoriteit Consument en Markt legt een ontwerp van een besluit als bedoeld in het eerste lid voor aan de Europese Commissie en de nationale regelgevende instanties van andere lidstaten.

verdict.shared_subject: Human oversight of high-risk AI processing personal data and an individual's right to object
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Article 21 requires the controller to stop processing when the data subject objects, unless overriding legitimate grounds or legal-claim grounds exist. Article 14(d) requires the high-risk AI system to enable human overseers, where appropriate and proportionate, to intervene in its operation or replace or reverse its output; one might argue that stopping or reversing an AI-supported process after an objection could conflict with continued system operation or reliance on its output.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose cumulative duties rather than incompatible commands: an objection under Article 21 can be handled by stopping the relevant processing, while Article 14(d) requires that human overseers have the capability to intervene or disregard output where appropriate and proportionate. Article 14 does not require continued processing or prohibit stopping the system, and Article 21 itself contains grounds allowing processing to continue.
verdict.evidence_span_a: De verwerkingsverantwoordelijke staakt de verwerking van de persoonsgegevens tenzij hij dwingende gerechtvaardigde gronden voor de verwerking aanvoert die zwaarder wegen dan de belangen, rechten en vrijheden van de betrokkene of die verband houden met de instelling, uitoefening of onderbouwing van een rechtsvordering.

verdict.shared_subject: Incident- or threat-related reporting by regulated entities
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A concerns a voluntary onward transmission by a relevant national competent authority to the ECB, while Provision B requires the entity itself to submit a final report to both its CSIRT and competent authority. If the same underlying event triggers both regimes, the ECB transmission does not appear to discharge the entity’s separate filing duties to the CSIRT and competent authority.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can be complied with cumulatively: the entity may voluntarily report a significant cyber threat, while separately submitting the required final incident report within one month. Provision A’s onward transmission is not framed as replacing or satisfying Provision B’s report, and the provisions concern potentially different triggers and actors.
verdict.evidence_span_a: De relevante bevoegde autoriteit kan dergelijke informatie aan de in lid 6 genoemde andere relevante autoriteiten verstrekken.
verdict.evidence_span_b: De essentiële entiteit of belangrijke entiteit dient uiterlijk één maand na de melding, bedoeld in artikel 27, eerste lid, een eindverslag in bij haar CSIRT en haar bevoegde autoriteit

verdict.shared_subject: Reporting ICT/security incidents by entities potentially covered by both regimes
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: A requires financial entities to report ICT-related incidents as part of their incident-management process, while B separately requires providers of public electronic communications services to notify the Dutch data-protection authority immediately of certain security breaches. If one actor falls within both categories and one incident satisfies both triggers, the provisions could impose two reporting duties, with A giving no recipient or deadline and B specifying the data-protection authority and immediate notification.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can be satisfied cumulatively: the actor can report the incident under A and also notify the data-protection authority under B. A does not identify a different recipient, deadline, or exclusive reporting channel, so nothing in the shown text makes B's notification substitute for A's incident reporting or makes the duties impossible to perform together.
verdict.evidence_span_a: Financiële entiteiten omschrijven een beheerproces voor ICT-gerelateerde incidenten, stellen dit vast en leggen dit ten uitvoer, om ICT-gerelateerde incidenten te detecteren, te beheren en te melden.
verdict.evidence_span_b: De aanbieder van een openbare elektronische communicatiedienst stelt de Autoriteit persoonsgegevens onverwijld in kennis van een inbreuk op de beveiliging, bedoeld in artikel 11.3, die nadelige gevolgen heeft voor de bescherming van persoonsgegevens die zijn verwerkt in verband met de levering van een openbare elektronische communicatiedienst in de Europese Unie.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions impose obligations on public authorities in EU digital-law contexts, so they are topically related. One might loosely argue that an authority’s case-specific enforcement assessment could compete for attention with its notification-administration duties, but neither text makes the duties incompatible.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision A requires an authority, when taking specified enforcement measures, to consider relevant prior infringements by the entity. Provision B requires a notifying authority to inform the Commission and other Member States of relevant changes in a notified body’s notification; the duties concern different actions, triggers, and subject matter and can readily be performed cumulatively.
verdict.evidence_span_a: elke relevante eerdere inbreuken door de betrokken entiteit
verdict.evidence_span_b: De aanmeldende autoriteit stelt de Commissie en de andere lidstaten via het in artikel 30, lid 2, bedoelde elektronische aanmeldingssysteem in kennis van alle relevante wijzigingen in de aanmelding van een aangemelde instantie.

verdict.shared_subject: Cybersecurity governance and oversight
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern institutional responses to cybersecurity risks, so one might initially suspect overlap between the competent authorities’ follow-up measures under DORA and the Minister’s national crisis-response planning duty. However, neither provision assigns the same decision or operational task to the same actor, and the texts do not make the national plan displace or constrain the authorities’ assessment.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision A requires competent authorities, when taking a decision concerning a critical ICT third-party provider, to consider the unremedied risks and seriousness of non-compliance, and to give a financial entity time to adapt contracts. Provision B assigns the Minister the separate competence to establish a national plan for large-scale cybersecurity incidents and crisis response; both duties can operate independently.
verdict.evidence_span_a: De bevoegde autoriteiten nemen na het ontvangen van de in artikel 35, lid 1, punt c), bedoelde meldingen bij het nemen van het in lid 6 van dit artikel bedoelde besluit het soort en de omvang van het risico dat of de risico’s die de kritieke derde aanbieder van ICT-diensten niet heeft verholpen, in aanmerking, alsook de ernst van de niet-naleving, en wel op basis van de volgende criteria:
verdict.evidence_span_b: Onze Minister stelt een nationaal plan voor grootschalige cyberbeveiligingsincidenten en crisisrespons als bedoeld in artikel 9, vierde lid, van de NIS2-richtlijn vast.

verdict.shared_subject: Incident notifications and their processing by public authorities
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern incident notifications, but they impose duties on different authorities and concern different notification channels. Provision A requires the market-surveillance authority to take measures within seven days after receiving a serious-incident notification, while provision B requires the CSIRT to process voluntary notifications under its own procedure and permits prioritisation of mandatory notifications; nothing shown makes the CSIRT's processing duty displace or delay the market-surveillance authority's duty.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The duties are cumulative and directed to different authorities: the market-surveillance authority acts within seven days after receiving the notification, whereas the CSIRT processes voluntary notifications under Article 36. Each authority can perform its own duty, and the texts show no incompatible deadline, recipient, or prohibition.
verdict.evidence_span_a: De markttoezichtautoriteit neemt passende maatregelen, zoals bedoeld in artikel 19 van Verordening (EU) 2019/1020, binnen zeven dagen na de datum waarop zij de in lid 1 van dit artikel bedoelde kennisgeving heeft ontvangen, en volgt de kennisgevingsprocedures waarin die verordening voorziet.
verdict.evidence_span_b: Het CSIRT verwerkt de vrijwillige meldingen, bedoeld in het eerste lid, overeenkomstig de in artikel 36 omschreven procedure. Het CSIRT kan daarbij voorrang geven aan de verwerking van verplichte meldingen als bedoeld in artikel 25 boven vrijwillige meldingen als bedoeld in het eerste lid.

verdict.shared_subject: Reporting incidents involving personal data and serious ICT-related incidents
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: A personal-data breach and a serious ICT-related incident can arise from the same event, requiring the financial entity to notify the GDPR supervisory authority and separately submit DORA reports to the relevant competent authority. The recipients and deadlines are framed separately, so one filing does not clearly discharge the other.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can both be satisfied cumulatively: the entity can make the GDPR notification within 72 hours and submit DORA's initial, interim, and final reports within the Article 20 deadlines. The texts do not require contradictory content or prohibit making both reports.
verdict.concrete_scenario: A financial entity suffers a ransomware attack that both constitutes a personal-data breach likely to risk individuals' rights and freedoms and qualifies as a serious ICT-related incident. It must notify the Article 55 supervisory authority under Article 33 within 72 hours of becoming aware, while separately submitting DORA's initial notification and subsequent reports to the relevant competent authority within the Article 20 deadlines; filing with one authority does not itself make the separate filing to the other authority.
verdict.decisive_exception: The provisions shown do not establish that the GDPR supervisory authority and DORA's relevant competent authority are the same authority, nor that one report satisfies the other. Article 33 also contains an exception where the breach is not likely to pose a risk, but the scenario assumes that exception does not apply.

verdict.evidence_span_b: bei de relevante bevoegde autorität

verdict.shared_subject: Information and human oversight concerning high-risk AI and automated decision-making
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires the controller to inform the data subject about automated decision-making and its underlying logic, significance, and expected consequences. Provision B requires the high-risk AI system to be supplied so that human overseers can understand its capabilities and limitations and, where appropriate and proportionate, decide to replace its output with another decision; these duties could create practical uncertainty about how much explanation and human intervention are required in the same automated-decision context.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different, cumulative duties on different aspects of AI governance: A is a transparency obligation owed by the controller to the data subject, while B is a system-design and human-oversight obligation concerning the user and responsible human overseers. The texts do not say that satisfying one duty substitutes for, overrides, or prevents compliance with the other; both can be fulfilled.

verdict.shared_subject: Incident reporting by entities involved in personal-data and significant cybersecurity incidents
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires a processor to inform the controller, while provision B requires the relevant entity to submit an incident report to the CSIRT or competent authority within 72 hours. For an incident covered by both, these are different communications to different recipients, so the B filing would not itself satisfy A.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can both be complied with: the processor can promptly inform the controller and the relevant entity can separately submit the required report to the CSIRT or competent authority. They concern different recipients and therefore do not impose incompatible content or deadlines.
verdict.concrete_scenario: A processor becomes aware of a significant incident involving a personal-data breach. It must inform the controller 'zonder onredelijke vertraging' under provision A and, as the relevant entity, submit an incident report to the CSIRT or competent authority within 72 hours under provision B. Filing with the CSIRT or competent authority does not inform the controller, so both communications are required.

verdict.evidence_span_b: binnen 72 uur nadat zij kennis hebben gekregen van het significante incident, een incidentmelding indienen

verdict.shared_subject: High-risk AI systems and their processing/conformity-assessment context
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions can apply around a high-risk AI system, but they impose different obligations on different actors: Article 36 requires a controller to consult the supervisory authority before processing where a DPIA identifies an unmitigated high risk, while Article 31 requires notified bodies to remain independent. One might argue that a notified body’s use of a high-risk system for its conformity-assessment activities could involve processing that triggers prior consultation, potentially complicating its independent assessment role.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions regulate distinct duties and actors. Article 36 concerns a controller’s prior consultation with a data-protection supervisory authority when processing presents an insufficiently mitigated high risk; Article 31 concerns the organisational independence of notified bodies and expressly permits their use of assessed high-risk AI systems for activities necessary to conformity assessment or for personal purposes. Nothing in Article 31 exempts a controller from Article 36 or makes consultation incompatible with independence.
verdict.evidence_span_a: raadpleegt de verwerkingsverantwoordelijke voorafgaand aan de verwerking de toezichthoudende autoriteit
verdict.evidence_span_b: Dit belet echter niet dat beoordeelde AI-systemen met een hoog risico die nodig zijn voor activiteiten van de conformiteitsbeoordelingsinstantie worden gebruikt

verdict.shared_subject: Supervisory and enforcement powers concerning ICT and cybersecurity compliance
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern authorities addressing shortcomings by ICT-related entities. One could argue that A requires an essential entity to remedy identified deficiencies or infringements, while B permits the lead overseer to request reports about corrective measures concerning recommendations, potentially creating overlapping supervisory demands for a provider operating across both regimes.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions confer different powers on different authorities and apply to different categories of entities: A concerns competent authorities enforcing NIS2 against essential entities, while B concerns the lead overseer overseeing critical third-party ICT service providers under DORA. A remedial order and a request for a report about corrective measures can both be complied with independently; neither provision forbids compliance with the other or states that one measure substitutes for the other.

verdict.shared_subject: Reporting consequences of a serious ICT-related incident involving personal data and clients’ financial interests
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: The same incident can trigger both duties: Provision A requires the controller to notify the competent supervisory authority within 72 hours, while Provision B requires a financial entity to notify affected clients without delay. These are different recipients and different communications, so notifying one does not discharge the other.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can be complied with cumulatively: the entity can notify the competent supervisory authority under Article 33 and separately inform its clients under Article 19. Nothing in either text prohibits the other notification or makes the duties mutually exclusive.
verdict.concrete_scenario: A financial entity, acting as controller, suffers a serious ICT-related personal-data breach that affects clients’ financial interests and is likely to risk individuals’ rights and freedoms. verdict.shared_subject: Use of personal data in decisions involving a high-risk AI system
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Article 21 gives the data subject a right to object to processing based on Article 6(1)(e) or (f), requiring the controller to stop unless overriding legitimate grounds or legal-claim grounds exist. Article 14(e), as the specified norm, requires the operator to be able, where appropriate and proportionate, to decide to use the high-risk AI system; if exercising that capability entails continuing the objected-to processing, the provisions could appear to pull in opposite directions.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Article 14(e) requires only a capability to decide whether to use or stop the AI system, not actual continued use in every case. Article 21 independently governs whether the underlying personal-data processing must cease, subject to its own overriding-grounds exception; the operator can comply with both by not using the system when the objection requires cessation, or by documenting overriding grounds where applicable.
verdict.decisive_exception: Article 21 itself supplies the decisive qualification: processing may continue if the controller demonstrates compelling legitimate grounds overriding the data subject’s interests, rights and freedoms, or grounds connected with legal claims. Article 14(e) does not require actual use and therefore does not override that right.

verdict.shared_subject: Electronic services involving accessibility and accepted authentication or electronic statements
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A prohibits providing electronic communications services that fail to meet specified accessibility requirements. Provision B obliges certain organisations and courts to accept specified electronic statements when substantial or high authentication is required. If accepting such a statement necessarily entails providing an electronic service that cannot meet the accessibility requirements, the duties might appear difficult to reconcile, but neither text says that acceptance must occur through an inaccessible service or that accessibility may be disregarded.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions can apply to a high-risk AI system whose processing presents an unmitigated high risk. Article 36 GDPR then requires prior consultation, while Article 26 AI Act requires the deployer to use Article 13 information in carrying out the DPIA; the texts do not specify whether using that information changes, replaces, or delays the separate consultation duty.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose sequential and cumulative duties rather than incompatible ones: the deployer can use Article 13 information in its DPIA and, if that DPIA shows an unmitigated high risk, consult the supervisory authority before processing. Nothing in Article 26 exempts the deployer from Article 36 or makes the duties mutually exclusive.

Zelfs bij een entiteit die onder beide categorieën zou vallen, zijn de bevoegdheden cumulatief en inhoudelijk verenigbaar; geen bepaling verplicht of verbiedt iets dat de andere uitsluit.

verdict.shared_subject: Administrative fines for entities participating in an AI regulatory sandbox, where the conditions in Provision B are met and the Member State lacks an administrative-fine system.
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires the Member State to ensure that a fine is imposed by national courts when its legal system does not provide for administrative fines. Provision B says that, where other authorities responsible for other EU or national law actively supervised the AI system and provided compliance guidance, no administrative fines are imposed for that law; this could appear to bar the fine contemplated by A if the same conduct is covered.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision A applies only when the Member State's legal system does not provide for administrative fines and concerns fines under the NIS2 framework, while Provision B concerns fines for violations of the AI Act or other law in the regulatory testing environment. Provision B's no-fine rule is limited to the relevant law and does not expressly prohibit a judicially imposed fine under Provision A, so the provisions can operate cumulatively within their distinct legal bases.
verdict.concrete_scenario: An essential or important entity participating in an AI regulatory sandbox complies with the specific participation plan and guidance, while another authority responsible for other EU or national law has actively supervised the AI system and issued compliance guidance. The same conduct is treated as a violation covered by Provision A in a Member State whose legal system lacks administrative fines: Provision A requires the fine to be imposed by national courts, while Provision B states that no administrative fines are imposed for the relevant law. Whether Provision B's immunity extends to the judicially imposed fine required under Provision A is unresolved by the texts shown.
verdict.decisive_exception: The decisive unresolved issue is whether Provision B's prohibition on imposing administrative fines for the relevant law applies to, or overrides, the judicially imposed fine required under Provision A when the Member State lacks an administrative-fine system, and whether the two provisions concern the same underlying violation.

verdict.shared_subject: Reporting significant or serious incidents involving a high-risk AI system
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires the user of a high-risk AI system to notify the provider first and then the importer or distributor and the relevant market-surveillance authorities of a serious incident. Provision B separately requires an essential or important entity to report every significant incident under Articles 26–29, but it does not identify the recipient, deadline, or whether that report is the same filing required by A; if the same incident qualifies under both regimes, the duties may therefore require cumulative reporting.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can be satisfied cumulatively: the actor can make the notifications required by A and also make the report required by B. Provision B does not state that its report replaces, prohibits, or conflicts with A’s notifications, and its recipient and timing are not shown, so the text does not establish two incompatible or definitively separate filings.

verdict.shared_subject: Incident reporting by an entity that is both a NIS2 ‘betrokken entiteit’ and a DORA financial entity
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions require an interim report after an incident-related initial report, but they belong to different reporting regimes and identify different reporting channels: A requires an incident report to the CSIRT or, where applicable, the competent authority, while B requires a financial entity to report to the relevant competent authority. If the same incident qualifies under both regimes, the entity may have to make separate filings under each regime, on potentially different Article 20 and NIS2 timelines.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can be complied with cumulatively: the entity can submit the NIS2 incident report and the DORA interim report, and nothing in either quoted norm prohibits dual reporting or states that one filing substitutes for the other. Moreover, the excerpts do not establish that the same entity, incident, or reporting event necessarily falls within both regimes, nor do they provide the DORA deadlines needed to prove an actual incompatible timing burden.
verdict.concrete_scenario: A financial entity is also a NIS2 ‘betrokken entiteit’ and suffers one significant ICT incident that is also a serious ICT-related incident. After making the respective initial notifications, it must submit the NIS2 incidentmelding ‘bij het CSIRT of, indien van toepassing, de bevoegde autoriteit’ within 72 hours and also submit the DORA interim report ‘bij de relevante bevoegde autoriteit’ after the first notification when the incident status or handling materially changes. These are potentially separate filings under different regimes and recipients, so filing the DORA report alone would not discharge the NIS2 duty, and filing the NIS2 report alone would not discharge the DORA duty.
verdict.missing_reference: The exact DORA deadlines in Article 20, first paragraph, point a)(ii), and the applicable NIS2 transposition/designation rules are needed to determine whether the clocks or recipients create an additional concrete incompatibility. They are not needed to establish the cumulative dual-reporting burden on the stated overlapping fact pattern.
verdict.decisive_exception: If the applicable national implementation or competent-authority arrangements provide that one filing is legally accepted as satisfying both regimes, the apparent dual-reporting burden would disappear; that substitution rule is not shown here.

verdict.shared_subject: Incident-related documentation and reporting by entities subject to both provisions

verdict.shared_subject: ICT/security incident management by regulated entities
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern serious or security-related ICT incidents, but they impose different duties: Provision A requires financial entities to maintain communication plans enabling responsible disclosure, while Provision B allows the Minister to impose measures concerning the resolution of a security incident. One might argue that incident-resolution measures could constrain or delay disclosure, creating an operational tension.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The duties address different aspects of incident management and can be performed cumulatively: a financial entity can resolve an incident while also using a communication plan to disclose it responsibly. Provision B does not prohibit communication, and Provision A does not prevent compliance with ministerial measures; moreover, Provision B applies only if the Minister imposes such a duty on a covered communications provider, whereas Provision A concerns financial entities.

verdict.shared_subject: Reporting incidents involving personal data and high-risk AI systems
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: A requires the controller to report a qualifying personal-data breach to the competent data-protection supervisory authority within 72 hours where possible. Neither provision forbids the other notification, and B's 'serious incident' trigger is not identical to A's personal-data-breach trigger.

It must report the breach, where possible, within 72 hours to the competent data-protection supervisory authority under A, while separately notifying the provider first and then the importer or distributor and the relevant market-surveillance authorities under B; notifying one set of recipients does not discharge the other duty, and B provides no common deadline that resolves the coordination issue.

verdict.shared_subject: Reporting of serious/significant ICT incidents by an entity subject to both regimes
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions require incident reporting, but A directs the financial entity to report an interim report to the relevant competent authority, while B requires a significant-incident notification to both the CSIRT and the competent authority within 24 hours. If the same incident triggers both regimes, the duties may involve different filings, recipients, content and timing; reporting to the competent authority under B would not itself satisfy A's separate interim-report duty, and reporting under A would not satisfy the CSIRT notification.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can be complied with cumulatively: the entity can submit B's notification within 24 hours and separately submit A's interim report within the applicable Article 20 deadline. The texts do not expressly state that the filings must be separate documents, but they do identify different reporting stages and, for B, an additional CSIRT recipient.
verdict.concrete_scenario: A financial entity that is also an essential or important entity offering a trust service experiences one incident that is both a serious ICT-related incident under A and a significant incident affecting its trust service under B. verdict.shared_subject: High-risk classification and safeguards for regulated processing or AI systems
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions can concern an activity involving a system that is treated differently under the two regimes: Article 36 requires prior consultation where a DPIA identifies high risk, while Article 6 addresses an Annex III AI system that the provider considers not high risk. One might argue that the provider's negative classification could sit uneasily with the GDPR's separate high-risk assessment, especially if the same system's processing presents high risk.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different, cumulative duties triggered by different actors and criteria. Article 36 concerns a data controller's processing and requires consultation when the GDPR DPIA shows high risk absent mitigation; Article 6 requires an AI provider who considers an Annex III system not high-risk to document that assessment. Documenting an AI Act classification does not determine the GDPR DPIA result or discharge the separate consultation duty, so both can be complied with.

verdict.shared_subject: Compliance obligations for high-risk AI systems involving personal-data processing
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions can apply to the same high-risk AI system: Article 35 requires the controller to conduct a prior data-protection impact assessment where processing is likely to create a high risk, while Article 16(c) requires the provider to have a quality-management system. One might argue that the quality-management system could be treated as addressing the relevant risks and therefore make a separate assessment duplicative, but neither text says that it substitutes for the DPIA.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The duties concern different compliance measures and can be performed cumulatively: a controller can conduct the required DPIA before processing, while the provider maintains the required quality-management system. The provisions do not impose incompatible acts, deadlines, or benchmarks, and Article 35 does not state that a quality-management system discharges the DPIA duty.
