verdict.evidence_span_b: blijft zijn dienst onder dezelfde voorwaarden leveren tot de ontvangende aanbieder de levering activeert

verdict.shared_subject: High-risk AI systems involving personal-data processing and their operators
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions impose obligations before or during the operation of a high-risk AI-related activity: Article 36 requires prior consultation where a DPIA identifies an unmitigated high risk, while Article 10 requires data-governance practices for high-risk AI training, validation and test datasets. One might argue that the operator must coordinate a data-governance regime with a separate supervisory-authority consultation, creating additional compliance work.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different, independently satisfiable duties with different triggers and objects. Article 36 concerns a controller’s prior consultation with a supervisory authority when a DPIA shows a high risk absent mitigation; Article 10 concerns subjecting datasets to purpose-aligned data-governance practices. Complying with Article 10 does not eliminate the Article 36 trigger, and consulting under Article 36 does not replace the dataset requirements, but there is no incompatibility or unresolved benchmark conflict.
verdict.evidence_span_a: Wanneer uit een gegevensbeschermingseffectbeoordeling krachtens artikel 35 blijkt dat de verwerking een hoog risico zou opleveren indien de verwerkingsverantwoordelijke geen maatregelen neemt om het risico te beperken, raadpleegt de verwerkingsverantwoordelijke voorafgaand aan de verwerking de toezichthoudende autoriteit.
verdict.evidence_span_b: Datasets voor training, validatie en tests worden onderworpen aan praktijken op het gebied van databeheer die stroken met het beoogde doel van het AI-systeem met een hoog risico.

verdict.shared_subject: ICT-incidenten affecting regulated entities, particularly financial entities
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires an essential or important entity to report each significant incident immediately to its CSIRT or competent authority. Provision B concerns the financial entity’s responsibility for ICT-related incidents reported under Article 19(1), but it does not itself impose a second reporting duty or identify a separate recipient or deadline; at most, it preserves responsibility despite supervisory feedback.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different duties: A is an immediate incident-reporting obligation, while B is a continuing responsibility rule for financial entities after reporting under another provision. A diligent entity can report the significant incident immediately and remain fully responsible for its handling and consequences; neither provision forbids compliance with the other.
verdict.missing_reference: The content of Regulation 2022/2554 Article 19(1) would be needed to assess whether that separate provision creates an additional reporting obligation, recipient, or deadline. The text shown for Article 22 itself does not establish such a second filing.
verdict.evidence_span_a: Elke lidstaat zorgt ervoor dat essentiële en belangrijke entiteiten elk incident dat aanzienlijke gevolgen heeft voor de verlening van hun diensten als bedoeld in lid 3 (significant incident) onverwijld meldt bij zijn CSIRT of, indien van toepassing, zijn bevoegde autoriteit overeenkomstig lid 4.
verdict.evidence_span_b: Onverminderd de ontvangen feedback van toezichthouders blijven financiële entiteiten volledig verantwoordelijk voor de behandeling en de gevolgen van de ICT-gerelateerde incidenten die op grond van artikel 19, lid 1, zijn gerapporteerd.

verdict.shared_subject: Incident-related notifications and measures involving ICT or personal-data breaches
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions may be engaged by the same underlying incident, but they impose different kinds of obligations on different actors: provision A requires competent authorities, where appropriate, to take necessary measures to protect immediate financial-system stability, while provision B empowers the Dutch data-protection authority to require a communications provider to notify the affected person. The strongest possible tension case is that a stability-protective measure could affect or delay individual notification, but neither text expressly requires, forbids, or conditions such a delay.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions are readily cumulative: the competent authorities can take necessary financial-stability measures while the data-protection authority can require the provider to notify the affected person. Provision A does not prohibit notification, and provision B does not prevent stability measures; moreover, they address different actors and functions.
verdict.evidence_span_a: Op basis van die kennisgeving nemen de bevoegde autoriteiten, in voorkomend geval, alle nodige maatregelen om de onmiddellijke stabiliteit van het financiële systeem te beschermen.
verdict.evidence_span_b: kan de Autoriteit persoonsgegevens, indien het van oordeel is dat de inbreuk in verband met persoonsgegevens waarschijnlijk ongunstige gevolgen zal hebben voor de persoonlijke levenssfeer van de persoon wiens persoonsgegevens het betreft, van de aanbieder verlangen dat hij die persoon alsnog in kennis stelt van de inbreuk.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions impose obligations connected with regulated entities and security, so an essential or important entity that is also an electronic-communications provider might be subject to both governance duties and a subscriber-notification duty. However, neither provision requires conduct that the other forbids or sets incompatible timing, content, or recipient requirements.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision A requires Member States to ensure that governing bodies approve and oversee cybersecurity-risk-management measures and may be held liable for breaches of Article 21. Provision B separately requires a provider to notify the affected subscriber before taking a specified measure, or as soon as possible where urgency prevents prior notice; the duties can be performed cumulatively without either discharging or obstructing the other.
verdict.evidence_span_a: de bestuursorganen van essentiële en belangrijke entiteiten de door deze entiteiten genomen maatregelen voor het beheer van cyberbeveiligingsrisico’s goedkeuren om te voldoen aan artikel 21, toezien op de uitvoering ervan en aansprakelijk kunnen worden gesteld voor inbreukendoor de entiteiten op dat artikel
verdict.evidence_span_b: Voorafgaand aan het nemen van een maatregel, bedoeld in het eerste lid, onderdeel g, doet de aanbieder melding aan de betrokken abonnee, en geeft de abonnee daarbij de gelegenheid de in dit onderdeel bedoelde bedreiging van de integriteit en veiligheid van netwerk, dienst of randapparaat weg te nemen.

verdict.shared_subject: Essential entities that are also critical entities and their handling of cybersecurity incidents
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires enforcement authorities to take account of the offender’s intent or negligence when imposing enforcement measures. Provision B requires the CSIRT to provide incident, near-incident, or cyber-threat information to the competent authority, but does not address intent or negligence; one might therefore suspect that information sharing could expose an entity to enforcement without the contextual assessment required by A.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose duties on different actors and operate at different stages: A governs how competent authorities assess enforcement measures, while B governs CSIRT information-sharing about reported events. Nothing in B prohibits or replaces the authority’s obligation under A to consider intent or negligence, so both duties can be fully performed cumulatively.

verdict.shared_subject: Incident or security measure involving a provider and, potentially, a financial-sector entity
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: If the same real-world security event triggers both provisions, the actor could have to make two separate notifications: A to the affected subscriber and B to the designated financial-sector CSIRT. The recipients differ, and neither text says that notifying one recipient discharges the other.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions regulate different notifications serving different purposes: A concerns advance or prompt notice to the affected subscriber before a protective service measure, while B concerns incident reporting by specified financial-sector entities to a CSIRT. They can therefore be performed cumulatively without either duty making the other impossible.

verdict.shared_subject: High-risk AI systems involving personal-data processing and their compliance assessment
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions can apply to the same high-risk AI system, but they impose different obligations on different actors: the GDPR requires the controller to conduct a data-protection impact assessment before processing where the processing is likely to create a high risk, while the AI Act provision requires the provider to use a specified conformity-assessment route and, in certain public-sector-use cases, requires the market-surveillance authority to act as the notified body. The strongest tension case is therefore that one system may require parallel assessments and involve different responsible actors, creating coordination and compliance burdens, but neither text makes the obligations mutually exclusive or substitutes one for the other.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The obligations address different matters and can be performed cumulatively: the GDPR DPIA concerns the impact of intended personal-data processing on individuals’ data-protection rights, whereas Article 43 concerns demonstrating conformity with the AI Act’s requirements through specified procedures. A provider, controller, and—where applicable—market-surveillance authority can each perform their respective duties without violating the other provision.

verdict.shared_subject: Procedural reporting/decision duties, but concerning different actors and triggers
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires a financial entity to submit updated notifications after an initial notification, while provision B requires that a decision be taken immediately after receipt of a notification. If B applied to the same recipient and decision process, the recipient might need to decide immediately even though A contemplates later updated information.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose duties on different actors and address different events: A concerns a financial entity’s reporting of serious ICT incidents to a competent authority, whereas B concerns the timing of a decision after receipt of a notification. Nothing in the shown texts makes the financial entity’s reporting duty incompatible with the recipient’s duty to decide without delay.

verdict.shared_subject: Testing and investigation of ICT/AI systems after or before deployment
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires vulnerability assessments before ICT applications, infrastructure components, or supporting ICT services are deployed or redeployed. Provision B prohibits an investigation that modifies an AI system in a way that could affect later evaluation of an incident’s causes, unless the competent authorities are notified in advance. An investigation under B might involve testing or assessment activity covered by A, creating a possible procedural constraint if that activity modifies the system.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions regulate different triggers and activities: A concerns vulnerability assessments before deployment or redeployment by central securities depositories and central counterparties, while B concerns a provider’s post-serious-incident investigation of an AI system. B does not prohibit vulnerability assessments; it only requires prior notification for investigations involving potentially causally significant modifications, so both duties can be satisfied cumulatively.

verdict.shared_subject: Processing of personal data in high-risk AI systems and the associated information and human-oversight duties
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions can apply to a high-risk AI operator processing personal data: Article 13 requires information to the data subject, including about automated decision-making and related rights, while Article 14 requires human-oversight measures for the AI system. One might argue that system-level oversight measures could be treated as addressing the individual-facing safeguards described in Article 13, creating uncertainty about whether separate transparency and rights information is still required.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different, cumulative duties on different aspects of operation: Article 13 concerns information supplied to the data subject at collection, whereas Article 14 concerns technical or operational human oversight of a high-risk AI system. Nothing in Article 14 states that its oversight measures replace, satisfy, or override the GDPR information duties, so an operator can comply with both.

verdict.shared_subject: Reporting significant or serious ICT incidents
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires a financial entity to inform its clients without delay when a serious ICT-related incident affects clients’ financial interests. Provision B separately requires an essential or important entity to report every significant incident under Articles 26–29; if the same entity and incident fall under both regimes, the duties may involve different reporting channels and procedures, so notifying clients would not necessarily constitute the report required by B.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can both be obeyed cumulatively: the entity can notify affected clients under A and make the report required by B under Articles 26–29. The texts shown do not establish that the same incident necessarily triggers both duties, nor do they identify B’s recipient or deadline, so they do not establish a concrete dual-reporting conflict.
verdict.missing_reference: BWBR0052872 Articles 26–29, especially the provisions specifying the recipient, content and timing of the report required by Article 25; those provisions are needed to determine whether B requires a separate filing from A’s client notification.

verdict.shared_subject: ICT-related/significant incidents involving a financial entity that is also an essential or important entity offering a trust service
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires financial entities to establish processes ensuring that underlying causes of ICT-related incidents are detected, documented, and removed, while provision B requires a qualifying trust-service entity to report a significant incident within 24 hours to its CSIRT and competent authority. A qualifying incident therefore creates both an internal root-cause-remediation duty and an external reporting duty, potentially requiring simultaneous attention and raising timing or sequencing questions.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different, cumulatively satisfiable duties: A concerns internal incident management and root-cause remediation, whereas B concerns notification of a significant incident to specified recipients within a deadline. Nothing in A forbids or substitutes for the report required by B, and B does not prevent the entity from investigating, documenting, and removing underlying causes.

verdict.shared_subject: Incident management and ICT-security governance
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires a financial entity to evaluate the effectiveness of its internal incident escalation after a serious ICT incident. Provision B requires an entity to calibrate the proportionality of its security measures to risks, incident likelihood and severity, which could theoretically lead to different judgments about how much escalation capability is necessary.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose cumulative and compatible duties at different stages: A requires a post-incident evaluation of escalation effectiveness, while B requires risk-proportionate security measures. Performing the evaluation can inform compliance with B, and nothing in either text requires an entity to omit, weaken, or disregard the other duty.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Beide bepalingen kunnen raken aan een hoog-risico-AI-systeem dat persoonsgegevens gebruikt voor geautomatiseerde besluitvorming. Men zou kunnen aanvoeren dat de AVG-informatieplicht over de onderliggende logica en gevolgen een transparantieplicht oplegt, terwijl artikel 14 AI Act vooral vereist dat menselijke toezichthouders het systeem kunnen begrijpen, monitoren en overrulen; die verplichtingen leggen echter geen tegenstrijdige gedragingen op.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: De bepalingen richten zich op verschillende, cumulatief verenigbare verplichtingen: artikel 14 AVG verplicht de verwerkingsverantwoordelijke de betrokkene bepaalde informatie te verstrekken, terwijl artikel 14 AI Act vereist dat het hoog-risico-AI-systeem aan de gebruiksverantwoordelijke wordt verstrekt met mogelijkheden voor menselijk toezicht. Naleving van de ene bepaling verhindert naleving van de andere niet, en geen van beide bepaalt dat de andere verplichting vervalt of door haar wordt vervangen.

verdict.shared_subject: Melding van significante/ernstige ICT-incidenten door entiteiten die onder beide regimes vallen
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Bij een incident dat zowel aanzienlijke gevolgen heeft voor de dienstverlening als een ernstig ICT-gerelateerd incident is, verplicht A de entiteit onverwijld haar dienstontvangers te informeren, terwijl B een eerste kennisgeving aan de relevante bevoegde autoriteit verlangt binnen de op grond van artikel 20 vast te stellen termijnen. Dit zijn verschillende meldingen aan verschillende ontvangers; de ene melding kan de andere niet vervangen.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: De verplichtingen kunnen zonder inhoudelijke tegenstrijdigheid cumulatief worden nageleefd: de entiteit kan haar dienstontvangers onverwijld informeren en daarnaast de eerste kennisgeving aan de bevoegde autoriteit indienen volgens de toepasselijke termijnen. Geen van beide bepalingen verbiedt of vervangt de andere melding.
verdict.concrete_scenario: Een financiële entiteit die tevens een essentiële of belangrijke entiteit is, ondervindt een ernstig ICT-incident dat de verlening van haar diensten aanzienlijk beïnvloedt. Zij moet dan onverwijld haar dienstontvangers informeren op grond van A én een afzonderlijke eerste kennisgeving indienen bij de relevante bevoegde autoriteit op grond van B; de twee meldingen hebben verschillende ontvangers en verschillende tijdstippen, zodat één melding niet aan beide verplichtingen voldoet.
verdict.evidence_span_a: In voorkomend geval stellen de betrokken entiteiten de ontvangers van hun diensten onverwijld in kennis van significante incidenten die een nadelige invloed kunnen hebben op de verlening van die diensten.
verdict.evidence_span_b: Financiële entiteiten dienen, binnen de overeenkomstig artikel 20, eerste alinea, punt a), ii), vast te stellen termijnen, bij de relevante bevoegde autoriteit het volgende in: a) een eerste kennisgeving;

verdict.shared_subject: Incident or threat affecting the integrity or security of a network, service, or device, where the provider is also an essential or important entity offering a trust service
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions can apply to the same provider and event, but they impose different notification requirements. Provision A requires notice to the affected subscriber, while provision B requires a report to the CSIRT and competent authority within 24 hours; the stricter timing in B does not discharge A because the recipients and apparent purposes differ.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The duties are cumulatively satisfiable: the provider can notify the subscriber under A and separately report the significant incident to the CSIRT and competent authority under B. Provision A does not prohibit or replace the authority report, and provision B does not state that its report substitutes for subscriber notification.
verdict.concrete_scenario: A trust-service provider that is an essential or important entity takes an urgent measure to remove a threat to the integrity or security of its network or service, and the event is also a significant incident affecting provision of the trust service. The provider must notify the affected subscriber as soon as possible under A and, within 24 hours of learning of the significant incident, report it to both its CSIRT and competent authority under B; filing with those authorities does not notify the subscriber, and notifying the subscriber does not make the required authority filings.
verdict.evidence_span_a: Voorafgaand aan het nemen van een maatregel, bedoeld in het eerste lid, onderdeel g, doet de aanbieder melding aan de betrokken abonnee, en geeft de abonnee daarbij de gelegenheid de in dit onderdeel bedoelde bedreiging van de integriteit en veiligheid van netwerk, dienst of randapparaat weg te nemen. Wanneer dit wegens de vereiste spoed niet voorafgaand aan het nemen van de maatregel mogelijk is, doet de aanbieder zo snel mogelijk melding van de maatregel.
verdict.evidence_span_b: In afwijking van het eerste lid dient een essentiële entiteit of belangrijke entiteit die een vertrouwensdienst aanbiedt onverwijld of, indien dat niet mogelijk is, binnen 24 uur nadat zij kennis heeft gekregen van het significante incident een melding van het significante incident in bij haar CSIRT en haar bevoegde autoriteit als dat incident gevolgen heeft voor de verlening van haar vertrouwensdienst.

verdict.shared_subject: Reporting of the same ICT incident by certain financial-sector entities
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires a financial entity to submit an initial notification to the relevant competent authority, while Provision B requires specified entities to make the Article 19 notification also to the sectoral CSIRT. Thus, for a covered bank or financial-market infrastructure entity, the same incident appears to require two submissions to different recipients; A's filing does not, on the text shown, discharge B's separate CSIRT filing.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can be complied with cumulatively: the entity submits the initial notification to the relevant competent authority under A and also submits it to the designated sectoral CSIRT under B. Provision B expressly says “tevens” (also), which supports an additional reporting duty rather than an alternative or incompatible procedure.
verdict.concrete_scenario: A bank subject to both provisions suffers a serious ICT-related incident. It must submit the Article 19 initial notification within the applicable Article 20 deadline to “de relevante bevoegde autoriteit” under A, and must also make that notification to the designated CSIRT for the banking and financial-market-infrastructure sectors under B. Filing with the competent authority does not, on the text shown, constitute filing with the CSIRT, and B specifies no deadline, leaving two cumulative filings with different recipients and an unresolved timing relationship.
verdict.evidence_span_a: Financiële entiteiten dienen, binnen de overeenkomstig artikel 20, eerste alinea, punt a), ii), vast te stellen termijnen, bij de relevante bevoegde autoriteit het volgende in: a) een eerste kennisgeving;
verdict.evidence_span_b: Banken, handelsplatformen, centrale effectenbewaarinstellingen en centrale tegenpartijen doen de melding, bedoeld in artikel 19, eerste lid, eerste paragraaf, van de verordening, en de vrijwillige melding, bedoeld in artikel 19, tweede lid, eerste paragraaf, van de verordening, tevens bij het bij of krachtens artikel 16, eerste lid, van de Cyberbeveiligingswet aangewezen CSIRT voor de sectoren bankwezen en infrastructuur voor de financiële markt.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A concerns the enforcement powers of competent authorities toward essential entities, while provision B requires the Minister to establish a national plan. One might argue that both concern national cyber-incident governance, but neither text creates an incompatible duty, deadline, or allocation of authority.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different competences on different institutional actors: A requires Member States to ensure that competent authorities may issue warnings for infringements by essential entities, whereas B requires the Minister to establish a national plan. The Minister can establish the plan while competent authorities retain the stated enforcement power; both can be fully satisfied without one limiting or displacing the other.

verdict.shared_subject: The deadline for issuing a decision on the relevant application/request
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions impose a time limit on issuing a decision, but they prescribe different maximum periods: three months under provision A and two months under provision B. If the same decision and triggering submission fall within both provisions, the actor would face apparently inconsistent deadlines unless the two provisions apply to different procedures or the two-month rule is intended to operate cumulatively as the stricter deadline.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The texts do not establish that they govern the same application, request, decision-maker, or procedure. Provision A concerns an application deemed to arise from a trust-service provider's notification and refers to the eIDAS Regulation, while provision B expressly assigns the duty to the ACM and refers to a request. They may therefore be separate procedures; alternatively, issuing the decision within two months would also satisfy the three-month limit.
verdict.missing_reference: The provisions governing the scope and relationship of the application under article 2.5b, the request under article 5.3, and the identity of the competent decision-maker are needed to determine whether the same decision is subject to both deadlines. In particular, the referenced article 21(2) of the eIDAS Regulation and the relevant provisions defining the ACM's requests/procedure are not shown.
verdict.decisive_exception: If both deadlines apply to the same decision and the same triggering submission, the two-month deadline is the stricter one and can satisfy the three-month deadline; the unresolved issue is whether the procedures overlap at all.
verdict.evidence_span_a: Een beschikking op een aanvraag als bedoeld in het eerste lid, wordt gegeven binnen de termijn van drie maanden, bedoeld in artikel 21, tweede lid, van de eidas-verordening.
verdict.evidence_span_b: De Autoriteit Consument en Markt geeft de beschikking zo spoedig mogelijk, doch uiterlijk binnen 2 maanden na ontvangst van het verzoek.

verdict.shared_subject: Reporting a personal-data breach
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: The same breach can trigger both duties: provision A requires notification to the competent supervisory authority within 72 hours where the breach is likely to risk individuals' rights and freedoms, while provision B requires immediate notification to the affected person where the breach is likely to have adverse consequences for that person's privacy. These are separate notifications to different recipients, on different clocks, so notifying one recipient cannot discharge the other duty.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The duties can be performed cumulatively without contradiction: the controller or provider can notify the affected person immediately and notify the supervisory authority within 72 hours. The different thresholds and exceptions may mean that both duties do not arise in every breach, but where both do arise they remain independently satisfiable.
verdict.concrete_scenario: A telecommunications provider discovers a personal-data breach that is likely both to risk affected individuals' rights and freedoms and to have adverse consequences for their privacy. It must notify the affected person 'onverwijld' under B and separately notify the competent supervisory authority, if possible no later than 72 hours after becoming aware, under A; either notification alone does not satisfy the other recipient's duty.
verdict.evidence_span_a: Indien een inbreuk in verband met persoonsgegevens heeft plaatsgevonden, meldt de verwerkingsverantwoordelijke deze zonder onredelijke vertraging en, indien mogelijk, uiterlijk 72 uur nadat hij er kennis van heeft genomen, aan de overeenkomstig artikel 55 bevoegde toezichthoudende autoriteit, tenzij het niet waarschijnlijk is dat de inbreuk in verband met persoonsgegevens een risico inhoudt voor de rechten en vrijheden van natuurlijke personen.
verdict.evidence_span_b: De aanbieder, bedoeld in het eerste lid, stelt degene wiens persoonsgegevens het betreft onverwijld in kennis van een inbreuk in verband met persoonsgegevens indien de inbreuk waarschijnlijk ongunstige gevolgen zal hebben voor diens persoonlijke levenssfeer.

verdict.shared_subject: Reporting ICT incidents by entities in the banking and financial-market-infrastructure sectors
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: A significant incident may require reporting to the CSIRT or competent authority under Article 23, while provision B requires the Article 19 report to be made additionally to the sectoral CSIRT. If these are separate statutory reporting channels, the same incident could require two filings to different recipients, with Article 23 requiring immediate reporting and B specifying no deadline.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision B may merely designate the same sectoral CSIRT as an additional recipient for the Article 19 report, rather than creating a second report for the same Article 23 significant incident. Moreover, B applies only to the entities and incidents covered by Article 19, and the shown text does not establish that Article 19's report and Article 23's report are triggered by the same event or that both filings are independently required.
verdict.missing_reference: The provisions of the referenced regulation's Article 19, especially Article 19(1)(1) and Article 19(2)(1), and any rule establishing whether an Article 19 report is the same report as, or separate from, the Article 23 significant-incident report. The text is also needed to identify Article 19's recipients, triggers and deadlines.

verdict.shared_subject: Institutional powers and incident-report forwarding under EU digital law

verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose no incompatible commands on the same actor or concerning the same act. A concerns a supervisory authority’s competence to notify judicial authorities and litigate GDPR infringements; B concerns a central contact point’s forwarding of NIS2 incident reports to other Member States’ central contact points when requested. verdict.shared_subject: Reporting ICT/significant incidents by financial-sector entities

Provision B requires an essential or important entity to report a significant incident to its CSIRT and competent authority within 72 hours; if the same entity and incident fall under both provisions, A may require an additional sector-CSIRT filing, while B requires a filing to both its CSIRT and authority.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can be satisfied cumulatively: the entity can make the report required by B to its CSIRT and competent authority and also make the report required by A to the designated financial-sector CSIRT. The texts do not establish that the CSIRT named in A differs from B's CSIRT, nor that A imposes a separate deadline or filing where the recipients overlap.

verdict.shared_subject: Incident- or security-related notifications by network/internet service providers
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: A significant incident must be reported without delay to the CSIRT or competent authority, while B requires the provider to notify the affected subscriber before taking a security measure, or as soon as possible afterward. A single security event could therefore trigger two notifications to different recipients, with neither text stating that one notification substitutes for the other.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose distinct, cumulatively satisfiable duties triggered by different circumstances: A concerns significant incidents affecting service provision, whereas B concerns a contemplated measure to protect network, service, or device integrity and security. A provider can report the incident to the CSIRT or authority and separately notify the subscriber, so there is no incompatibility.
verdict.concrete_scenario: An internet-access provider experiences a significant security incident that materially disrupts service and responds by suspending a subscriber’s access under article 7.6a(1)(g). verdict.shared_subject: Reporting certain security or ICT incidents to designated authorities
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires a public electronic communications service provider to notify the Dutch data-protection authority immediately when a qualifying security breach adversely affects personal-data protection. verdict.shared_subject: Use of a high-risk AI system involving personal-data processing under GDPR Article 21
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Article 21 gives the data subject a right to object and requires the controller to stop processing unless overriding legitimate grounds or legal-claim grounds are established. Article 14 requires the high-risk AI system to be supplied with human-supervision capabilities, including the ability to ignore, replace, reverse, or stop the system's output or operation; those capabilities could support responding to an objection, but Article 14 does not itself determine whether processing must cease or whether Article 21's exception is satisfied.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose cumulative and compatible duties: the controller must comply with the individual objection right under Article 21 while the AI system must be designed or supplied to enable appropriate and proportionate human oversight under Article 14. Article 14 does not deem human-supervision capability to satisfy Article 21, nor does Article 21 prohibit the oversight capabilities required by Article 14.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: A processor must promptly inform the controller of a personal-data breach, while B requires an essential or important entity to report a significant incident to both its CSIRT and competent authority. A single event could satisfy both definitions, creating cumulative duties to notify different recipients on different procedural terms.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can both be obeyed: the processor informs the controller without unreasonable delay and the relevant entity separately reports the significant incident to its CSIRT and competent authority within the applicable period. The texts do not make either notification a substitute for the other, so there is no impossibility of simultaneous compliance.
verdict.concrete_scenario: A company is both a GDPR processor and an essential or important entity. A cyberattack causes unauthorised access to personal data and endangers the confidentiality of data or services, so it is both a personal-data breach and a significant incident. The company must inform the controller without unreasonable delay and also submit the incident report to its CSIRT and competent authority, potentially within 72 hours; notifying the controller does not discharge the two statutory reports to the other recipients.
verdict.evidence_span_a: De verwerker informeert de verwerkingsverantwoordelijke zonder onredelijke vertraging zodra hij kennis heeft genomen van een inbreuk in verband met persoonsgegevens.
verdict.evidence_span_b: De essentiële entiteit of belangrijke entiteit dient onverwijld of, indien dat niet mogelijk is, binnen 72 uur nadat zij kennis heeft gekregen van het significante incident een melding in bij haar CSIRT en haar bevoegde autoriteit

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions use the language of a mandatory notification, and each could involve an operator or provider. However, they concern different triggering events and different regulatory subjects: serious incidents involving high-risk AI systems versus cable-maintenance work on public land. The texts do not establish one event that triggers both duties for the same actor.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The duties are readily cumulative where their separate triggers happen to apply: an AI provider could make the serious-incident notification under Article 73 and separately ensure that any cable-maintenance work on public land is reported in advance under Article 5.6. There is no incompatible deadline, prohibition, recipient conflict, or indication that one notification substitutes for the other.
verdict.evidence_span_a: De in lid 1 bedoelde melding wordt gedaan onmiddellijk nadat de aanbieder een oorzakelijk verband tussen het AI-systeem en het ernstige incident of de redelijke waarschijnlijkheid van een dergelijk verband heeft vastgesteld en in ieder geval uiterlijk 15 dagen nadat de aanbieder of, in voorkomend geval, de gebruiksverantwoordelijke zich bewust wordt van het ernstige incident.
verdict.evidence_span_b: Ingeval de werkzaamheden in verband met de instandhouding van kabels worden verricht in of op openbare gronden, wordt hiervan door de aanbieder tevens voorafgaand aan de uit te voeren werkzaamheden melding gedaan bij de burgemeester van de gemeente binnen wiens grondgebied de werkzaamheden zullen plaatsvinden, of bij een daartoe door hem gemachtigd ambtenaar.

verdict.shared_subject: Reporting significant incidents by essential or important entities
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires a progress report when the incident is still ongoing at the time the final report is due, while provision B separately requires the entity to report every significant incident under articles 26–29. If those are distinct reporting duties under the same incident, the entity might need both an A progress report and a B report, potentially under different procedures or recipients.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision B states only a general obligation to report and does not, in the text shown, prescribe a separate filing, recipient, deadline, or content that would be distinct from the reporting sequence in provision A. Provision A's progress-report duty is a specific stage of the incident-reporting process, and nothing shown establishes that provision B requires an additional filing rather than compliance through the applicable articles 26–29 procedure.
verdict.missing_reference: BWBR0052872 articles 26–29, especially their recipient, deadline, content, and whether the report required by article 25 is separate from or satisfied by the progress report under 32022L2555 article 23(4)(e).
verdict.evidence_span_a: indien het incident nog aan de gang is op het moment dat het in punt d) bedoelde eindverslag wordt ingediend, zorgen de lidstaten ervoor dat de betrokken entiteiten op dat moment een voortgangsverslag indienen
verdict.evidence_span_b: De essentiële entiteit of belangrijke entiteit meldt overeenkomstig de artikelen 26 tot en met 29 ieder significant incident.

verdict.shared_subject: High-risk AI systems that process personal data obtained from sources other than the data subject
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires the controller to inform the data subject about automated decision-making, relevant logic, and expected consequences, while Provision B requires high-risk AI systems to be designed for effective human oversight. One might argue that a system could satisfy the design-level oversight requirement without ensuring that each affected person receives the individual information required by A. However, the provisions impose different, cumulative duties rather than incompatible ones.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can plainly be satisfied together: the controller can provide all Article 14 information, including the automated-decision information in point g, and design the high-risk AI system with effective human oversight. Article 14 is an individual transparency duty triggered by obtaining personal data indirectly; Article 14 of the AI Act is a system-design duty triggered by high-risk classification, and neither text says that compliance with one substitutes for or overrides the other.
verdict.evidence_span_a: g) het bestaan van geautomatiseerde besluitvorming, met inbegrip van de in artikel 22, leden 1 en 4, bedoelde profilering, en, ten minste in die gevallen, nuttige informatie over de onderliggende logica, alsmede het belang en de verwachte gevolgen van die verwerking voor de betrokkene.
verdict.evidence_span_b: AI-systemen met een hoog risico worden zodanig ontworpen en ontwikkeld, met inbegrip van passende mens-machine-interface-instrumenten, dat hierop tijdens de periode dat zij worden gebruikt, op doeltreffende wijze toezicht kan worden uitgeoefend door natuurlijke personen.

verdict.shared_subject: Use of a high-risk AI system in processing personal data where the data subject objects under GDPR Article 21
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Article 21 gives the data subject a right to object to processing based on Article 6(1)(e) or (f), requiring the controller to stop unless overriding legitimate grounds or legal-claim grounds are established. Article 14(4)(d) requires the high-risk AI system to enable a human to replace or override its output, so exercising that capability could result in a different decision while the underlying personal-data processing continues, potentially undermining the objector’s requested cessation.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different, cumulatively satisfiable duties: Article 21 governs whether the controller may continue a particular processing operation after an objection, while Article 14(4)(d) concerns the human overseer’s ability to disregard or replace an AI output. A controller can both stop processing when Article 21 requires it and ensure that, where the system is used, a human can replace or override its output; neither text says that human intervention substitutes for the objection right.
verdict.evidence_span_a: De verwerkingsverantwoordelijke staakt de verwerking van de persoonsgegevens tenzij hij dwingende gerechtvaardigde gronden voor de verwerking aanvoert die zwaarder wegen dan de belangen, rechten en vrijheden van de betrokkene of die verband houden met de instelling, uitoefening of onderbouwing van een rechtsvordering.
verdict.evidence_span_b: in alle specifieke situaties te kunnen besluiten om het AI-systeem met een hoog risico niet te gebruiken of de output van het AI-systeem met een hoog risico op andere wijze te negeren, door een andere beslissing te vervangen of terug te draaien

verdict.shared_subject: Transparantie over geautomatiseerde besluitvorming en menselijk toezicht bij hoog-risico-AI
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Artikel 13 verplicht de verwerkingsverantwoordelijke informatie te verstrekken over geautomatiseerde besluitvorming en de onderliggende logica, terwijl artikel 14 de aanbieder verplicht menselijke toezichthouders in staat te stellen het systeem te begrijpen, te monitoren en zo nodig in te grijpen. Men zou kunnen stellen dat openbaarmaking van logica en operationele toezichtsinformatie spanning kan opleveren met vertrouwelijkheid of beperkte uitlegbaarheid, maar geen van beide aangehaalde bepalingen verbiedt naleving van de andere.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: De bepalingen leggen cumulatieve, goed verenigbare verplichtingen op: artikel 13 ziet op informatieverstrekking aan de betrokkene door de verwerkingsverantwoordelijke, terwijl artikel 14 ziet op het zodanig verstrekken van een hoog-risico-AI-systeem dat verantwoordelijke natuurlijke personen toezicht kunnen houden. Een organisatie kan beide doen door de betrokkene de vereiste informatie te geven en toezichthouders afzonderlijk de nodige operationele mogelijkheden te bieden.
verdict.evidence_span_a: f) het bestaan van geautomatiseerde besluitvorming, met inbegrip van artikel 22, leden 1 en 4, bedoelde profilering, en, ten minste in die gevallen, nuttige informatie over de onderliggende logica, alsmede het belang en de verwachte gevolgen van die verwerking voor de betrokkene.
verdict.evidence_span_b: e) in te grijpen in de werking van het AI-systeem met een hoog risico of het systeem te onderbreken door middel van een stopknop of een vergelijkbare procedure waarmee het systeem op veilige wijze kan worden stopgezet.

No actor is required by one provision to do something incompatible with the other.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: A controller could comply with the prior-consultation duty, and a notified body could separately perform the required full assessment; the provisions have different addressees, triggers, authorities, and subject matter. verdict.shared_subject: Rapportage van significante/ernstige ICT-incidenten door entiteiten die onder beide regimes vallen
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Een financiële entiteit die ook een essentiële of belangrijke entiteit is, kan voor hetzelfde incident onder beide bepalingen vallen. Artikel 23 verlangt onverwijlde melding bij het CSIRT of, indien van toepassing, de bevoegde autoriteit, terwijl artikel 19 melding en daaropvolgende verslagen bij de relevante bevoegde autoriteit verlangt volgens afzonderlijke termijnen en procedures; de teksten bepalen niet dat één melding de andere vervangt.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: De bepalingen kunnen naast elkaar worden nageleefd: de entiteit kan onverwijld melden op grond van artikel 23 en daarnaast de eerste kennisgeving, tussentijdse verslagen en het eindverslag op grond van artikel 19 indienen. Bovendien kan de bevoegde autoriteit een melding onder artikel 23 doorsturen naar het CSIRT, zodat de regimes institutioneel op elkaar kunnen aansluiten, ook al blijkt daaruit niet dat de financiële-entiteit haar afzonderlijke artikel 19-verplichtingen niet meer hoeft na te komen.
verdict.concrete_scenario: Een financiële entiteit die tevens een essentiële of belangrijke entiteit is, ondervindt een ernstig ICT-incident dat ook aanzienlijke gevolgen heeft voor haar diensten. Zij moet hetzelfde incident onverwijld melden bij haar CSIRT of bevoegde autoriteit op grond van artikel 23 én bij de relevante bevoegde autoriteit een eerste kennisgeving en vervolgens de vereiste tussentijdse en eindverslagen indienen binnen de op grond van artikel 20 vast te stellen termijnen op grond van artikel 19. De ontvangers en rapportageprocedures zijn niet volledig identiek; een melding aan het CSIRT onder artikel 23 vervangt niet tekstueel de melding aan de relevante bevoegde autoriteit onder artikel 19.
verdict.decisive_exception: Geen tekstuele regel in de getoonde bepalingen bepaalt dat de artikel 23-melding geldt als de eerste kennisgeving of verslagen van artikel 19, of omgekeerd. De mogelijkheid dat lidstaten bepaalde artikel 19-meldingen ook aan CSIRT’s laten verstrekken, maakt de twee verplichtingen niet automatisch één enkele melding.

verdict.shared_subject: Essential and important entities facing a significant cyber threat or significant incident
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires the entity to inform potentially affected service recipients about the significant cyber threat itself, while Provision B requires a report to the entity’s CSIRT and competent authority about a significant incident. For an event that is both a significant cyber threat and a significant incident, the entity must make communications to different recipients under two distinct duties, with no indication that the authority report substitutes for notifying service recipients.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can readily be complied with cumulatively: the entity can notify affected service recipients under A and separately report the incident to its CSIRT and competent authority under B. They concern different recipients and different information functions, so neither duty prevents performance of the other.

verdict.shared_subject: Incident-related duties concerning an entity or provider and an AI system
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions may apply after a serious or significant incident, but they regulate different conduct: Provision A restricts a particular investigation unless authorities are notified in advance, while Provision B requires supplying the responsible reporting officer’s contact details. The same entity could therefore need to conduct the restricted investigation and provide the contact details, but nothing in either text makes those duties incompatible.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The duties are independently satisfiable and concern different actions and conditions. A provider can refrain from modifying the AI system in the specified way unless it first notifies the competent authorities, while also providing the responsible officer’s contact details in the early warning.

verdict.shared_subject: Significante incidenten of cyberdreigingen affecting an essential or important entity and its service recipients
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires the entity to submit a final incident report to the CSIRT or competent authority within one month after handling the incident. Provision B separately requires the entity, where necessary, to inform potentially affected service recipients about the significant cyberthreat. Thus, one event may generate both an authority filing and recipient communication, with different recipients and no rule that one discharges the other.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different, cumulatively satisfiable communications: A concerns a detailed post-incident report to a CSIRT or competent authority, while B concerns protective information for potentially affected service recipients. Nothing in either text forbids the other communication or makes their deadlines incompatible.
verdict.concrete_scenario: An essential entity suffers a significant cyber incident that is still ongoing and is then handled. The entity must submit the final report to the CSIRT or competent authority within one month after handling the incident under A, while also informing service recipients who may be affected by the related significant cyberthreat, where necessary, under B. These are separate communications to different recipients, and submitting the authority report does not inform the service recipients.

verdict.shared_subject: Toezichthoudende/bevoegde autoriteiten en hun beoordeling van entiteiten of inbreuken
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: A geeft een toezichthoudende autoriteit de bevoegdheid om een verwerkingsverantwoordelijke of verwerker in kennis te stellen van een beweerde inbreuk op de AVG. B verplicht bevoegde autoriteiten bij handhaving tegen essentiële entiteiten rekening te houden met relevante eerdere inbreuken; men zou kunnen vrezen dat een kennisgeving onder A als een eerdere inbreuk moet worden behandeld, terwijl B geen nadere kwalificatieregel geeft.

Niets in B verbiedt de kennisgeving uit A of bepaalt dat die kennisgeving als een eerdere inbreuk moet worden aangemerkt; beide kunnen dus volledig worden nageleefd.

verdict.shared_subject: Incidenten die zowel een significant incident onder Richtlijn (EU) 2022/2555 als een persoonsgegevensinbreuk met waarschijnlijk ongunstige gevolgen voor de persoonlijke levenssfeer vormen.
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Eenzelfde gebeurtenis kan beide meldplichten activeren: de entiteit moet het incident onverwijld melden aan haar CSIRT of bevoegde autoriteit, terwijl zij de betrokken persoon onverwijld moet informeren. Dit zijn afzonderlijke mededelingen aan verschillende ontvangers; de melding aan de autoriteit informeert de betrokkene niet, en de individuele kennisgeving vervangt de melding aan het CSIRT of de bevoegde autoriteit niet.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Beide verplichtingen kunnen zonder inhoudelijke tegenstrijdigheid naast elkaar worden nageleefd en hebben dezelfde termijn, namelijk onverwijld. De teksten verbieden elkaar niet en leggen geen incompatibele inhoud of deadlines op; zij vereisen slechts cumulatieve meldingen wanneer beide triggers zijn vervuld.
verdict.concrete_scenario: Een cloudcomputingaanbieder die een essentiële of belangrijke entiteit is, ondervindt één cyberincident waardoor zijn diensten ernstig worden verstoord en waarbij opgeslagen persoonsgegevens van klanten waarschijnlijk ongunstige gevolgen voor hun persoonlijke levenssfeer ondervinden. De aanbieder moet ditzelfde incident onverwijld melden bij zijn CSIRT of bevoegde autoriteit én iedere betrokken persoon onverwijld informeren; één van die twee mededelingen voldoet niet aan de andere plicht.

verdict.evidence_span_b: De aanbieder, bedoeld in het eerste lid, stelt degene wiens persoonsgegevens het betreft onverwijld in kennis van een inbreuk in verband met persoonsgegevens indien de inbreuk waarschijnlijk ongunstige gevolgen zal hebben voor diens persoonlijke levenssfeer.

verdict.shared_subject: Cybersecurity incident enforcement and CSIRT feedback
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern conduct following a significant incident: the competent authority must consider the offender’s intent or negligence when taking enforcement measures, while the CSIRT must promptly provide feedback after an early warning. One might argue that prompt CSIRT feedback could affect how the entity’s conduct is assessed, creating an interaction between operational response and enforcement.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose duties on different actors and regulate different actions. Article 32 requires competent authorities to take the offender’s intent or negligence into account when imposing enforcement measures; Article 36 requires the CSIRT to respond to the reporting entity within 24 hours. The CSIRT’s response does not prevent the authority from considering intent or negligence, and the enforcement assessment does not prevent the CSIRT from responding.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions impose obligations, but they govern different actors, subject matters, and triggers. Provision A concerns essential or important entities communicating significant cyberthreats to service recipients, whereas provision B concerns municipal executive authorities adopting an approval decision after a telecommunications works notification.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The obligations can readily coexist: an entity could notify its service recipients of a significant cyberthreat while the municipal authority separately adopts an approval decision within the statutory period. Neither provision requires conduct that prevents compliance with the other.

verdict.shared_subject: Governance and assessment of high-risk processing or AI systems
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions impose ex ante organisational controls on activities that may overlap: a GDPR data-protection impact assessment must address risks to natural persons, while the AI Act quality-management system must document design, data, risk-management, monitoring and compliance procedures. An operator might therefore face uncertainty about whether one integrated assessment or system is sufficient, particularly because the provisions use different structures and scopes.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose cumulative, independently satisfiable duties rather than incompatible commands. Article 35 requires a DPIA where the processing is likely to create a high risk to individuals' rights and freedoms; Article 17 requires high-risk AI providers to maintain a documented quality-management system covering specified AI-governance aspects. Nothing in either text says that compliance with one substitutes for or overrides the other; the duties can be integrated while still satisfying each requirement.
verdict.evidence_span_a: Wanneer een soort verwerking, in het bijzonder een verwerking waarbij nieuwe technologieën worden gebruikt, gelet op de aard, de omvang, de context en de doeleinden daarvan waarschijnlijk een hoog risico inhoudt voor de rechten en vrijheden van natuurlijke personen voert de verwerkingsverantwoordelijke vóór de verwerking een beoordeling uit
verdict.evidence_span_b: Aanbieders van AI-systemen met een hoog risico voorzien in een systeem voor kwaliteitsbeheer dat de naleving van deze verordening waarborgt.

verdict.shared_subject: Supervisory authorities’ handling of infringements involving cybersecurity and personal data
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern authorities dealing with infringements, but provision A governs how an authority weighs the offender’s intent or negligence when taking enforcement measures, while provision B requires notification to the Dutch data-protection authority in a specified cross-border GDPR situation. No duty, prohibition, deadline, or decision criterion in B prevents the authority from considering intent or negligence under A.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different, cumulative duties on authorities: A requires consideration of “opzet of nalatigheid” when enforcement measures are taken, whereas B requires notification of the Dutch data-protection authority when the competent GDPR authority is located in another Member State. An authority can make the notification and independently assess intent or negligence, so both duties can be satisfied.

verdict.shared_subject: The obligation of essential and important entities to report significant incidents
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions impose reporting obligations for a significant incident, but Provision A expressly identifies the CSIRT or, where applicable, the competent authority as recipient and requires immediate reporting. Provision B requires reporting in accordance with Articles 26–29, which could theoretically establish a distinct procedure or recipient, so the texts might create cumulative reporting duties if those provisions require a separate filing.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision B appears to restate the same obligation for the same entities and the same category of significant incident, while expressly referring to Articles 26–29 for the applicable reporting procedure. Nothing in the text shown requires a second filing to a different recipient or establishes a different deadline; Provision A also provides that a report made to the competent authority is forwarded to the CSIRT, indicating one coordinated reporting channel rather than two independent filings.
verdict.missing_reference: BWBR0052872 Articles 26–29, especially their specified recipient(s), deadlines, and whether reporting under Article 25 is a separate filing from the Article 23 report.
verdict.decisive_exception: Whether Articles 26–29 establish a distinct recipient or reporting clock, or instead implement the same report to the CSIRT/competent authority, is not shown.
verdict.evidence_span_a: Elke lidstaat zorgt ervoor dat essentiële en belangrijke entiteiten elk incident dat aanzienlijke gevolgen heeft voor de verlening van hun diensten als bedoeld in lid 3 (significant incident) onverwijld meldt bij zijn CSIRT of, indien van toepassing, zijn bevoegde autoriteit overeenkomstig lid 4.
verdict.evidence_span_b: De essentiële entiteit of belangrijke entiteit meldt overeenkomstig de artikelen 26 tot en met 29 ieder significant incident.

verdict.shared_subject: Informing clients/service recipients about ICT incidents or cyberthreats and protective measures
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions can apply to the same financial or essential/important entity and require prompt communication to affected users. However, A concerns a serious ICT-related incident affecting clients’ financial interests and requires informing clients of the incident and mitigation measures, while B concerns a significant cyberthreat and requires informing service recipients of measures and, if necessary, the threat itself; the texts do not establish that the same recipients, trigger, or communication discharges both duties.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose distinct, cumulatively satisfiable information duties rather than incompatible commands. A requires notice to clients about a qualifying serious incident and measures taken, whereas B requires notice to potentially affected service recipients about measures they can take in response to a significant cyberthreat and, if necessary, the threat; an entity can send both communications, and neither provision forbids the other.

verdict.shared_subject: AI-system processing personal data and the resulting compliance obligations
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions may apply to the same high-risk AI system, but they impose different obligations: GDPR Article 35 requires a data-protection impact assessment before processing where processing is likely to create a high risk, while Article 16(i) requires the provider to affix a CE marking. One might argue that the provider faces parallel, potentially burdensome regulatory steps before deployment.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The obligations concern different compliance objects and can readily be performed cumulatively: the controller conducts the required impact assessment, while the provider affixes the CE marking after satisfying the AI Act requirements. Neither provision forbids or substitutes for the other, and the texts do not establish that one assessment or marking discharges the other.

verdict.shared_subject: Cybersecurity and ICT-risk governance by regulated entities
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern governance and monitoring of cyber/ICT risks, so an entity’s governing body and the financial entity may need to coordinate approval, oversight, implementation, and incident-pattern analysis. However, the provisions impose complementary duties rather than incompatible commands: neither requires conduct that the other prohibits, and they do not establish competing benchmarks for the same duty.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision A requires governing bodies of essential and important entities to approve cybersecurity-risk-management measures, oversee their implementation, and face accountability for breaches of Article 21. Provision B requires financial entities to analyse the frequency, types, scale, evolution, and patterns of ICT-related incidents to improve resilience; that analysis can support the governance and oversight required by A, while remaining a separate operational-resilience duty.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires the entity to submit an incident notification within 72 hours for a significant incident. Provision B states that, notwithstanding supervisory feedback, a financial entity remains fully responsible for handling and the consequences of ICT-related incidents reported under Article 19(1); this could be read as imposing an additional responsibility alongside the reporting duty.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Provision B does not require a second filing, a different recipient, or a different deadline. It expressly concerns the entity's continuing responsibility after incidents have been reported, while Provision A concerns submission of an incident notification to the CSIRT or competent authority. The duties therefore operate cumulatively without contradiction: the entity can make the required notification and remain responsible for the incident's handling and consequences.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions require an authority to consider whether non-compliance was intentional or negligent, so the same conduct could be assessed under two overlapping regimes. One might argue that the regimes provide different enforcement frameworks and could lead to inconsistent weighting of that factor, particularly where an entity is both an essential entity and a critical ICT third-party provider.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions apply to different enforcement decisions and different regulated subjects: Article 32 concerns enforcement against essential entities under NIS2, while Article 42 concerns follow-up measures concerning a critical ICT third-party provider under DORA. Even where the same factual conduct is relevant, each authority can independently consider intent or negligence alongside its own distinct criteria; neither provision requires or forbids a result required by the other.

One might argue that regulatory information supplied under B could relate to conduct relevant to A, creating overlapping supervisory involvement, but the texts do not make the duties incompatible.

Each can be fully complied with independently, and neither provision forbids or displaces the other's action.

verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires a final report after a significant incident, while provision B requires notice to the affected subscriber before, or as soon as possible after, a measure. If the same incident leads to such a measure, the provider may face two communications with different recipients, content and timing.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions concern different triggering events and different communications: A concerns a significant incident and a final report to the CSIRT or competent authority, whereas B concerns a provider's measure affecting a subscriber and notice to that subscriber. They can therefore be performed cumulatively without either duty preventing compliance with the other.

verdict.shared_subject: Classification and assessment of potentially high-risk AI or data-processing activities
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions address whether an activity or system presents a high risk, but they impose different obligations based on different triggers. Article 35 GDPR requires the controller to conduct a DPIA before processing where the processing is likely to create a high risk to natural persons’ rights and freedoms, whereas Article 80 AI Act concerns a market-surveillance authority’s review of a provider’s classification under Article 6(3), so the same AI system could fall within one regime’s high-risk assessment while not triggering the other’s procedure.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions can readily operate cumulatively: a controller can perform a DPIA before processing, while a market-surveillance authority can separately review a provider’s low-risk classification. Article 80 does not exempt the provider or controller from GDPR duties, and Article 35 does not prevent the authority from conducting its own AI Act classification review.
verdict.concrete_scenario: A provider classifies an AI system as not high-risk under Article 6(3), so a market-surveillance authority may review that classification under Article 80, while the system’s intended processing of personal data is nevertheless likely to create a high risk to individuals’ rights and freedoms, requiring the controller to complete a GDPR DPIA before processing under Article 35. Conversely, an AI system may be subject to Article 80 review because of the provider’s Article 6(3) classification even though the particular personal-data processing does not independently meet Article 35’s likely-high-risk trigger.

Als A daadwerkelijk een afzonderlijk voortgangsverslag verlangt, zou dat naast het eindverslag van B moeten worden ingediend.

De bepalingen kunnen dus cumulatief worden nageleefd, maar de tekst toont niet dat hetzelfde incident onder beide normen noodzakelijk dezelfde trigger heeft of dat twee afzonderlijke filings bij verschillende ontvangers vereist zijn.

verdict.shared_subject: Incident involving personal data affecting an essential or important entity
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: A requires immediate notification to the affected individual when a personal-data breach is likely to adversely affect that person's privacy. B separately requires the entity to notify both its CSIRT and competent authority of a significant incident, so one incident may require communications to the individual and to two authorities on different bases and potentially different timing/content.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The duties are addressed to different recipients and serve different purposes, so they can be performed cumulatively without either making the other impossible. B's 72-hour outer limit does not excuse A's immediate individual notification, but that is a need to make both notifications, not an incompatibility between them.
verdict.concrete_scenario: An essential entity suffers a cyberattack that compromises customers' personal data and is likely to adversely affect an identified customer's privacy, while also qualifying as a significant incident. The entity must notify that customer immediately under A and, separately, submit the incident notification to its CSIRT and competent authority immediately or within 72 hours under B; notifying the customer does not discharge the two authority/CSIRT filings, and filing with those recipients does not discharge the individual notification.

The separate recipients are decisive; any exceptions to A, such as the encryption exception in the contextual paragraph, could remove A in a particular case but do not make the duties generally compatible.

Provision A requires advance notice of public-ground cable-maintenance works to the municipal mayor or authorised official, while provision B requires an essential or important entity to inform service recipients about measures and, if necessary, the relevant significant cyberthreat; neither duty discharges or obstructs the other. The mere fact that both involve informing someone does not create a conflict.

verdict.shared_subject: Incident reporting by a financial entity that is also a relevant entity under Directive (EU) 2022/2555
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: The provisions may require overlapping reports for the same serious/significant ICT incident: A requires an incident report within 72 hours to the CSIRT or, where applicable, the competent authority, while B requires a first notification and subsequent reports to the relevant competent authority under separately determined deadlines. If the regimes designate different competent authorities or require distinct forms and reporting sequences, one filing would not necessarily discharge the other.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The texts do not establish that the same incident necessarily falls within both regimes, nor that the recipients or reporting forms are different in the concrete case. B's context also expressly permits Member States to require financial entities to provide the DORA reports to authorities or CSIRTs designated under Directive 2022/2555, which could allow coordinated or shared reporting; the provisions can therefore be complied with cumulatively without contradiction.
verdict.missing_reference: The decisive missing material is the applicable Article 20(1)(a)(ii) deadlines and reporting templates/procedures under Regulation (EU) 2022/2554, together with the national designation of the relevant competent authority and any implementation of Article 19(1)'s option to require DORA reports also to NIS2 CSIRTs or authorities. Those provisions are needed to establish whether the two duties require separate filings to different recipients and on different clocks, or whether one filing can satisfy both.

verdict.shared_subject: Reporting/documenting incidents involving an entity that may also operate a high-risk AI system
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Provision A requires the affected entity to submit a final report no later than one month after filing the incident notification, or, for an ongoing incident, a further final report within one month after resolution. Provision B separately requires a user of a high-risk AI system that detects a serious incident to notify the provider first and then the importer or distributor and the relevant market-surveillance authorities immediately; thus, if the same event is both a significant incident under A and a serious AI incident under B, the duties could involve different filings, recipients and timing.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions do not necessarily regulate the same incident: A concerns a 'significant incident' under the NIS2 framework, while B concerns a 'serious incident' involving a high-risk AI system. Even when both apply, the texts do not expressly make the reports mutually exclusive or impossible to perform cumulatively; the operator can submit A's final report and make B's notifications. The extracted A recipient is none, and A's final-report duty is not clearly a filing to a different recipient from B's notifications on the facts shown.
verdict.concrete_scenario: A company operates a high-risk AI system used in network and information systems. A cyber incident compromises the integrity of data processed by those systems and is therefore a significant incident under Provision A, while the same incident also causes a serious, irreversible disruption of critical infrastructure and is therefore a serious incident under Provision B. The company must submit A's final incident report within one month after the incident notification (or, if still ongoing, within one month after handling it), while under B it must immediately notify first the AI provider and then the importer or distributor and the relevant market-surveillance authorities. These are separate reporting duties to the extent B expressly identifies those recipients and A requires a separate final report; making the B notifications does not itself submit A's final report.
verdict.decisive_exception: The decisive uncertainty is whether another provision or competent-authority rule identifies the recipient and procedure for A's final report and provides that a B notification can substitute for, or discharge, A's report. No such substitution rule is shown. If A's final report and B's notifications are in fact directed to the same recipient and the B notification satisfies A's content and deadline, the relationship would instead be compatible.

verdict.shared_subject: Reporting a significant/serious ICT incident by an entity subject to both regimes
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: The same incident could qualify both as a serious ICT-related incident under Provision A and as a significant incident affecting the provision of a trust service under Provision B. A then requires reporting to the relevant competent authority on the Article 20 timetable, while B requires a report to both the entity’s CSIRT and competent authority within 24 hours; the texts do not say that the B filing to the competent authority, or its 24-hour deadline, replaces A’s separate report.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: Both provisions can be obeyed cumulatively: the entity can submit the required A report to the relevant competent authority and separately submit B’s report to its CSIRT and competent authority within 24 hours. The overlap in competent-authority reporting does not itself create a conflict, because neither provision forbids the additional filing and the duties can be performed together.
verdict.concrete_scenario: A financial entity that offers a trust service suffers one incident that is both a serious ICT-related incident and a significant incident affecting that trust service. It must submit Provision A’s initial notification to “de relevante bevoegde autoriteit” within the Article 20 timetable, and also submit Provision B’s notification “bij haar CSIRT en haar bevoegde autoriteit” within 24 hours. The CSIRT filing is an additional filing, and the texts do not establish that one submission discharges the other or resolve which authority’s timetable governs the overlapping competent-authority report.
verdict.decisive_exception: No exception or substitution rule is shown stating that the Provision B notification to the CSIRT and competent authority replaces Provision A’s initial notification, or that one recipient may receive the filing on behalf of the other.

verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions impose different duties on different actors and are triggered by different legal tests. Article 36 GDPR concerns a controller's prior consultation where a data-protection impact assessment shows high residual risk absent mitigation; Article 34 AI Act concerns notified bodies' conformity checks under Article 43. Each duty can be performed independently, and neither text says that one consultation or assessment substitutes for the other.

verdict.shared_subject: Incident or threat-related reporting by an entity subject to both provisions
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions impose reporting duties that could arise around the same security incident or threat, but they require filings to different recipients and on different terms. A provider may therefore have to notify the affected subscriber before or promptly after taking a protective measure and separately submit a detailed final incident report to its CSIRT and competent authority within one month.
verdict.strongest_case_for_compatibility: The provisions concern different reporting events and purposes: A concerns notifying the affected subscriber before or promptly after a measure to remove a threat, while B concerns an entity's final report after an Article 27 incident notification. Each duty can be performed independently, and neither text says that one report substitutes for the other.
verdict.concrete_scenario: An entity subject to both regimes detects a security threat attributable to a subscriber and immediately suspends the subscriber's internet service under the referenced security ground. It must notify the subscriber as soon as possible because prior notice was impracticable, and, if the event is also an Article 27 incident, it must separately file a final report within one month with both its CSIRT and competent authority; notifying the subscriber does not discharge either institutional filing.

verdict.shared_subject: Cybersecurity enforcement and incident-report forwarding
verdict.strongest_case_for_tension: Both provisions concern cybersecurity compliance involving entities and competent authorities. One might argue that an enforcement warning under Provision A and a forwarding duty under Provision B could overlap when the underlying conduct involves a reportable incident.

Provision B imposes a separate duty on the central contact point, triggered by a request from the CSIRT or competent authority, to forward received reports to other Member States’ central contact points.
